# Overview
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started

Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) is a declarative, component-based framework for
building Windows desktop apps in C#. You write components. Each component has a
`Render()` method that returns a description of the UI for the current state.
When the state changes, Reactor updates the real WinUI controls on screen.
There is no XAML, no data binding and no view model to write.

## At a glance [#at-a-glance]

| Topic | What to know |
|---|---|
| **Language** | C# only. Layout, styling, state and logic all live in `.cs` files. |
| **UI model** | Declarative. `Render()` returns a tree of immutable element records, and Reactor keeps the screen in sync with it. |
| **State** | [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) such as `UseState`, `UseReducer` and `UseEffect`, called inside `Render()`. |
| **Output** | Real WinUI controls such as `Button`, `TextBox` and `NavigationView`. No web view and no custom renderer. |
| **Interop** | Host Reactor content in a XAML app, or XAML controls in a Reactor app. They share one visual tree. |
| **Runs on** | Windows 10 version 1809 or later, and Windows 11, with .NET 10. |
| **Status** | Public preview. The `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` package is on NuGet.org. |

## A first look [#a-first-look]

This is a complete component. It shows two lines of text:

```csharp
class HelloWorld : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        return VStack(12,
            TextBlock("Hello from Reactor!").FontSize(24).Bold(),
            TextBlock("No XAML. No data binding. Just C#.")
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

![A window with the bold heading "Hello from Reactor!" above the line "No XAML. No data binding. Just C#."](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/readme/hello-world.png)

Add state with one hook call. `UseState(0)` returns the current value and a
setter. Each click calls the setter, and Reactor renders the component again
with the new value:

```csharp
class QuickCounter : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (count, setCount) = UseState(0);

        return HStack(8,
            Button("- 1", () => setCount(count - 1)),
            TextBlock($"{count}").FontSize(20).SemiBold().Width(40)
                .HAlign(HorizontalAlignment.Center),
            Button("+ 1", () => setCount(count + 1))
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

![A counter: a "- 1" button, the number 0, and a "+ 1" button in one row](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/readme/counter.png)

Text styles and theme colors are built in:

```csharp
class StyledText : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        return VStack(8,
            Heading("Heading element"),
            SubHeading("SubHeading element"),
            TextBlock("Regular text with modifiers")
                .FontSize(14).Foreground(Theme.Accent),
            Caption("Caption for fine print")
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

![Four lines of text in different styles: a heading, a subheading, accent-colored body text and a caption](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/readme/styled-text.png)

## How it works [#how-it-works]

![The Reactor render loop. Your component's Render method returns an element tree of immutable C# records. The reconciler compares it with the previous tree and mounts or updates real WinUI controls, patching only what changed. A user event calls a state setter, and Render runs again.](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/index/render-loop.svg)

1. You write [components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components). A component's `Render()` returns an
   element tree, built from factory methods such as `VStack`, `TextBlock` and
   `Button`.
2. The reconciler compares the new tree with the previous one. It creates the
   WinUI controls on the first render, and after that it changes only the
   properties and children that differ.
3. A user event, such as a click, calls a state setter from a
   [hook](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks). Reactor calls `Render()` again, and the loop repeats.

You do not subscribe to property-changed events or update controls by hand.
[Architecture overview](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/architecture-overview) explains each part of the
runtime in detail.

## Who Reactor is for [#who-reactor-is-for]

- **C# developers who want a Windows desktop UI without XAML.** You stay in
  one language, with full IntelliSense, refactoring and compile-time checks.
- **Developers who know React, SwiftUI or Jetpack Compose.** Components, hooks
  and state that lives next to the render code work the way you expect.
- **XAML, WinUI and WPF developers who want less boilerplate.** You keep the
  same controls and runtime. See [Coming from XAML](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/xaml-developers).

Reactor does not replace XAML and MVVM. If those work well for your app, keep
using them. Reactor is another way to describe the same WinUI content.

## Why pick Reactor [#why-pick-reactor]

- **One language.** There is no markup file and no code-behind split. A
  component is a plain C# class that you can test, refactor and search like
  any other code.
- **The UI follows the state.** You describe what the screen should show. You
  do not write code that changes the screen step by step.
- **Native controls.** Your app uses real WinUI controls, with Fluent
  design, keyboard support and accessibility built in.
- **A fast inner loop.** `dotnet watch` applies code changes to the running
  app and keeps component state. Roslyn analyzers catch common mistakes as
  you type. See [Dev tooling](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools).

## Prefer Rust? [#prefer-rust]

The same idea is also being explored in Rust.
[windows-reactor](https://github.com/microsoft/windows-rs/blob/HEAD/docs/crates/windows-reactor.md)
is a declarative WinUI library in [windows-rs](https://github.com/microsoft/windows-rs),
the Rust for Windows project. Components own their state, controls send typed
messages back, and only the WinUI controls that changed are updated. It is a
separate library with its own model, available on
[crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/windows-reactor). These docs cover
Microsoft.UI.Reactor, the C# library.

## Tips [#tips]

**Try it in one file first.** A single `.cs` file with a few `#:` lines at the
top is a complete Reactor app. See
[One file, no project](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/install#one-file-no-project).

**Learn `UseState` first.** Most components need only `UseState` and plain
C#. Read [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) when you need effects, reducers or memoization.

**Keep components small.** Move each part of the UI into its own component
early. Small components are easier to read, test and reuse.

## Next Steps [#next-steps]

- **[Installation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/install)**: set up your machine, create a project and
  run it.
- **[Your first app](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/first-app)**: build a counter, a list and a todo
  app, one step at a time.
- **[Thinking in Reactor](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/thinking-in-reactor)**: the mental model behind
  components, state and rendering.
- **[Coming from XAML](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/xaml-developers)**: map XAML, bindings and MVVM to
  Reactor.
- **[Guides](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components)**: components, hooks, layout, styling, navigation
  and more, starting with Components.
- **[Controls catalog](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls)**: every built-in control, with examples.
- **[Tools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools)**: the `mur` CLI, hot reload, devtools and
  analyzers.
- **[API reference](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference)**: every hook, component, factory and
  modifier, generated from the source.

# Cheat Sheet
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/cheat-sheet

## Minimum viable app [#minimum-viable-app]

```csharp
class HelloVignette : Component
{
    public override Element Render() =>
        VStack(8,
            Heading("Hello"),
            Button("Click", () => { })
        ).Padding(20);
}
```

![Cheat-sheet vignettes — Hello, State, Effect](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/cheat-sheet/vignettes.png)

Three pieces: a `using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories` import,
a `Component` subclass, and a `ReactorApp.Run<App>(title, ...)` call.
Doc apps inherit `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport=true` from `docs/_pipeline/apps/Directory.Build.props` so `mur` can capture screenshots.

## Hooks [#hooks]

| Hook | Returns | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `UseState<T>(initial)` | `(T, Action<T>)` | Local state that drives re-render. |
| `UseReducer<T>(initial)` | `(T, Action<Func<T,T>>)` | Functional updates from prev. |
| `UseReducer<S,A>(reducer, initial)` | `(S, Action<A>)` | Redux-style state. |
| `UseEffect(setup, deps?)` | void | Side effects after render; cleanup on re-run. |
| `UseMemo<T>(factory, deps)` | `T` | Cache expensive computation across renders. |
| `UseCallback(fn, deps)` | stable delegate | Memoize a callback identity. |
| `UseRef<T>(initial)` | `Ref<T>` | Mutable value that does *not* trigger re-render. |
| `UseContext<T>(ctx)` | `T` | Read a [context](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/context) value. |
| `UsePersisted<T>(key, initial, scope)` | `(T, Action<T>)` | Survive re-mount via [LRU cache](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/persistence). |
| `UseColorScheme()` | `ColorScheme` | Reactive app-global light/dark. Forced colors: `UseHighContrast()`. |
| `UseResource(fetcher, cache, deps, opts?)` | `AsyncValue<T>` | [`async-resources`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/async-resources). |
| `UseFocusTrap(isActive)` | `FocusTrapHandle` | Trap Tab inside a sub-tree. |
| `UseAnnounce()` | `AnnounceHandle` | Push a screen-reader announcement (via `.Announce(string)` method). |
| `UseElementRef<T>()` | `ElementRef<T>` | Reference a realized element for focus, `TeachingTip.Target`, UIA relationships, or XYFocus. |
| `UseDevtools()` | `bool` | [Dev-tooling](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools) gate — true when devtools are enabled. |

```csharp
class StateVignette : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (count, setCount) = UseState(0);
        return Button($"clicked {count}×", () => setCount(count + 1))
            .AutomationName($"Increment counter; clicked {count} times");
    }
}
```

```csharp
class EffectVignette : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (tick, incrementTick) = UseReducer(0, threadSafe: true);
        UseEffect(() =>
        {
            var timer = new System.Timers.Timer(1000);
            timer.Elapsed += (_, _) => incrementTick(t => t + 1);
            timer.Start();
            return () => timer.Dispose();
        }, []);
        return TextBlock($"Tick: {tick}");
    }
}
```

Full coverage on [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks).

| `Slider(value, min, max, set)` | Numeric range. |

| `VStack(spacing, ...children)` / `HStack(spacing, ...children)` | Linear stacks. |

| `Empty()` / `Group(...children)` / `ForEach(items, render)` | Tree helpers. |
| `Memo(ctx => ...)` / `RenderEachTime(ctx => ...)` | Function components. |
| `Component<TComp>()` | Mount a class-based [Component](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components). |

| API | Purpose |

| Token | What it is |

## Patterns at a glance [#patterns-at-a-glance]

**Controlled input.** `var (v, set) = UseState("")` →
`TextBox(v, set)`.

**Effect with cleanup.** Return a cleanup lambda from the effect lambda;
Reactor calls it before the next run (when deps change) and on unmount.

**Conditional render.** `cond ? Element1 : Empty()` keeps the element
out of the tree when `cond` is false; in a container with no keyed
children it still holds its slot, so the siblings after it keep their
state — see the
[modal-dialog recipe](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/modal-dialog).

**List with stable keys.** `ForEach(items, x => Card(x).WithKey(x.Id))`
so the reconciler can move rows rather than rebuild them.

**Reference prop.** `var target = this.UseElementRef<FrameworkElement>()` →
`Button("Open", show).Ref(target)` →
`TeachingTip("Tip", target: target)`. Use reference props, not
`target.Current`, for relationships that must survive late mount or
unmount.

**Memoized subtree.** Wrap the expensive child in `Memo(ctx => …)`;
the function-component cache holds it across parent re-renders.

**Disable submit during async work.** A single `submitting` bool
covers both the button's `.IsEnabled(...)` and the spinner label.

## Rules [#rules]

Five rules cover most analyzer findings (full list on
[Rules of Reactor](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/rules-of-reactor)):

1. Hooks at the top of `Render`, never in a loop or conditional.
2. Setters returned by hooks are stable; you can capture them in
   closures safely.
3. Render functions are pure — side effects go in `UseEffect`.
4. Lists need stable `.WithKey()` for any element that can reorder.
5. Theme-aware modifiers (`.Background`, `.Foreground`, `.WithBorder`)
   want a `Theme.*` token, not a hex literal.

## Tips [#tips]

**Skim the cheat sheet, then jump.** Each row is a one-liner; the
deep-dive page is one click away. Don't try to learn Reactor from
this page — learn it from [getting-started](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/first-app) and
[components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components), and use this card as the recall surface.

**Bookmark the modifier table.** Modifier chains are the easiest thing
to forget mid-keystroke; the modifier table is the highest-traffic
section of this page.

**Copy from the recipes for shape, not from the cheat sheet.** The
recipes are the working compositions; the cheat sheet is the catalog.

# Your first app
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/first-app

In this tutorial you write five small Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) apps.
Each step adds one idea. You start with a [component](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components) that
shows text. Then you add state with the `UseState` [hook](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks), arrange
controls with [layout](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/layout) containers, and show a list where each row
has a key. In the last step you put it all together in a todo app. After each
step you run the app and see the result. You need about 30 minutes, and you
do not need to know XAML or React.

Before you start, follow [Installation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/install) to create a project and
check that `dotnet run` opens a window.

| Step | You learn | You see |
|---|---|---|
| [1. Your first component](#step-1-your-first-component) | `ReactorApp.Run`, `Render()`, elements and modifiers | A greeting that follows what you type |
| [2. Add state](#step-2-add-state) | `UseState`, event handlers, values computed from state | A counter with three buttons |
| [3. Layout basics](#step-3-layout-basics) | `VStack`, `HStack`, spacing and nesting | Rows and columns of controls |
| [4. Lists with keys](#step-4-lists-with-keys) | `ForEach`, `WithKey`, replacing a list in state | A list you can add to and remove from |
| [5. Finish the todo app](#step-5-finish-the-todo-app) | `UseReducer`, `When`, records for data | A complete todo list |

## How to run each step [#how-to-run-each-step]

Step 1 and Step 5 show a complete `App.cs` file. Steps 2 to 4 show one
component class. To run a class, replace the old class in `App.cs` with it.
Then change the `ReactorApp.Run<T>()` line at the top to the class name. The
first comment in each snippet shows the line to use, for example
`ReactorApp.Run<CounterExample>("Counter");`. Keep the `using` lines at the
top of the file. Then run:

```powershell
dotnet run
```

Close the window before you run the next step. To see changes without closing
the window, use `dotnet watch` instead (see
[Hot reload with `dotnet watch`](#hot-reload-with-dotnet-watch)).

## Step 1: Your first component [#step-1-your-first-component]

Replace the contents of `App.cs` with this code:

```csharp
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor;
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core;
using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml;

ReactorApp.Run<GettingStartedApp>("Getting Started");

class GettingStartedApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (name, setName) = UseState("World");

        return VStack(16,
            TextBlock($"Hello, {name}!").FontSize(24).Bold(),
            TextBox(name, setName, placeholderText: "Enter your name")
                .AutomationName("Name")
                .Width(250)
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

Run `dotnet run`. You see a greeting and a text box. Type a name, and the
greeting changes as you type:

![The hello world app: a "Hello, World!" heading above a text box that holds the name](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/getting-started/hello-world.png)

Here is what each part does:

- **`ReactorApp.Run<T>`** opens a window and mounts your root component in it.
- **`class GettingStartedApp : Component`** is a component. Its `Render()`
  method returns the UI as a tree of elements.
- **[`UseState`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hooks/UseState)** returns the current value and
  a setter. When you call the setter, Reactor runs `Render()` again with the
  new value.
- **[`VStack`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/layout)** stacks its children from top to bottom. The `16`
  is the space between them, in pixels.
- **`TextBlock(...).FontSize(24).Bold()`** shows the modifier pattern. Every
  element has chainable modifiers for style and layout.

There is no event wiring and no property-changed notification. The text box
calls `setName`, and the greeting reads `name`. State goes in, and UI comes
out.

## Step 2: Add state [#step-2-add-state]

Every interactive UI needs state. Replace the `GettingStartedApp` class with
this counter, and change the `Run` line to
`ReactorApp.Run<CounterExample>("Counter");`:

```csharp
// Launch with:
//   ReactorApp.Run<CounterExample>("Counter");

class CounterExample : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (count, setCount) = UseState(0);

        return VStack(12,
            TextBlock($"Count: {count}").FontSize(20).SemiBold(),
            HStack(8,
                Button("- 1", () => setCount(count - 1)),
                Button("Reset", () => setCount(0)),
                Button("+ 1", () => setCount(count + 1))
            )
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

Run the app. You see "Count: 0" above three buttons. Click **+ 1** and the
number goes up. Click **Reset** and it goes back to 0:

![The counter app: "Count: 0" above the buttons "- 1", "Reset" and "+ 1"](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/getting-started/counter.png)

Each call to `setCount` makes Reactor render the component again. Reactor
compares the new element tree with the old one and updates only the WinUI
controls that changed. Here, that is the text of one `TextBlock`.

### Several pieces of state [#several-pieces-of-state]

A component can call `UseState` more than once. Each call holds its own value.
Try this example:

```csharp
// Launch with:
//   ReactorApp.Run<MultipleStateExample>("Multiple State");

class MultipleStateExample : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (firstName, setFirstName) = UseState("");
        var (lastName, setLastName) = UseState("");
        var (fontSize, setFontSize) = UseState(16.0);

        var fullName = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(firstName) && string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(lastName)
            ? "Anonymous"
            : $"{firstName} {lastName}".Trim();

        return VStack(12,
            TextBlock($"Hello, {fullName}!").FontSize(fontSize).Bold(),
            TextBox(firstName, setFirstName, placeholderText: "First name")
                .AutomationName("First name")
                .Width(200),
            TextBox(lastName, setLastName, placeholderText: "Last name")
                .AutomationName("Last name")
                .Width(200),
            HStack(8,
                TextBlock("Font size:"),
                Slider(fontSize, 10, 40, setFontSize).Width(200),
                TextBlock($"{fontSize:F0}px")
            )
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

You see two text boxes and a slider. Type a first and last name, and the
greeting shows the full name. Move the slider, and the greeting gets bigger or
smaller.

`fullName` is computed from `firstName` and `lastName` on every render. You do
not need computed properties or bindings. A plain C# expression works,
because `Render()` runs again every time the state changes.

## Step 3: Layout basics [#step-3-layout-basics]

Reactor has a small set of layout containers that you nest inside each other.
Try this example:

```csharp
// Launch with:
//   ReactorApp.Run<LayoutBasicsExample>("Layout");

class LayoutBasicsExample : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        return VStack(16,
            Heading("Layout Demo"),

            SubHeading("Horizontal Stack"),
            HStack(8,
                Button("One"),
                Button("Two"),
                Button("Three")
            ),

            SubHeading("Nested Layout"),
            HStack(16,
                VStack(4,
                    TextBlock("Left Column").Bold(),
                    TextBlock("Item A"),
                    TextBlock("Item B")
                ),
                VStack(4,
                    TextBlock("Right Column").Bold(),
                    TextBlock("Item X"),
                    TextBlock("Item Y")
                )
            )
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

You see a heading, a row of three buttons, and two columns of text side by
side:

![The layout demo: a heading, a row of buttons named One, Two and Three, and two columns of items](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/getting-started/layout-basics.png)

These containers cover most layouts:

| Element | What it does |
|---|---|
| `VStack` | Stacks children from top to bottom. |
| `HStack` | Places children from left to right. |
| `Grid` | Places children in rows and columns, with fixed or proportional sizes. |
| `ScrollView` | Scrolls content that does not fit. |
| `Border` | Draws a background, a corner radius or an outline around one child. |

`VStack` and `HStack` take the spacing as an optional first argument:
`VStack(12, child1, child2)` puts 12 pixels between the children. The
[Layout](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/layout) guide covers `Grid` and the other containers.

## Step 4: Lists with keys [#step-4-lists-with-keys]

Most apps show a list that changes. This example keeps a list of fruit in
state. You can add a fruit or remove one:

```csharp
// Launch with:
//   ReactorApp.Run<KeyedListExample>("Keyed List");

record Fruit(string Id, string Name);

class KeyedListExample : Component
{
    static readonly string[] Names = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry", "Mango", "Pear"];

    static readonly IReadOnlyList<Fruit> StartFruits =
        [new("fruit-1", "Apple"), new("fruit-2", "Banana")];

    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (fruits, setFruits) = UseState(StartFruits);
        var (nextId, setNextId) = UseState(3);

        void AddFruit()
        {
            var name = Names[(nextId - 1) % Names.Length];
            setFruits([.. fruits, new Fruit($"fruit-{nextId}", name)]);
            setNextId(nextId + 1);
        }

        void RemoveFruit(string id) =>
            setFruits([.. fruits.Where(f => f.Id != id)]);

        return VStack(12,
            Button("Add fruit", AddFruit),
            VStack(4,
                ForEach(fruits, fruit =>
                    HStack(8,
                        TextBlock(fruit.Name).Width(120),
                        Button("Remove", () => RemoveFruit(fruit.Id))
                            .AutomationName($"Remove {fruit.Name}")
                    ).WithKey(fruit.Id)
                )
            )
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

You see an **Add fruit** button and two rows, Apple and Banana, each with a
**Remove** button. Click **Add fruit** and a new row appears at the end. Click
**Remove** on a row and only that row goes away.

Three things make this work:

- **`ForEach(fruits, fruit => ...)`** turns each item into an element.
- **`.WithKey(fruit.Id)`** gives each row a stable identity. When you remove
  Apple, Reactor knows which row went away and keeps the other rows as they
  are. Use an ID from your data, not the position in the list. The
  [Rules of Reactor](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/rules-of-reactor#3-lists-need-stable-keys) explain
  why.
- **`setFruits([.. fruits, new Fruit(...)])`** creates a **new** list.
  Reactor renders again only when the setter gets a value that is different
  from the old one. If you change the old list in place and pass it back,
  Reactor sees the same object and does nothing.

The start list is a `static readonly` field. `UseState` uses its argument only
on the first render, so there is no need to build a new list on every render.

## Step 5: Finish the todo app [#step-5-finish-the-todo-app]

Now put the pieces together. A todo app needs a list of items, a way to add
items, and check boxes to mark them done.

Replace the contents of `App.cs` with this code:

```csharp
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor;
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core;
using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml;

ReactorApp.Run<TodoApp>("Todo App");

class TodoApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var initialItems = UseMemo(() => new List<TodoItem>
        {
            new("todo-1", "Learn Reactor basics", true),
            new("todo-2", "Build a todo app", false),
            new("todo-3", "Explore hooks", false),
        });
        var (items, updateItems) = UseReducer(initialItems);
        var (newText, setNewText) = UseState("");
        var (nextId, setNextId) = UseState(4);

        var doneCount = items.Count(i => i.Done);

        return VStack(16,
            Heading("Todo List"),
            TextBlock($"{doneCount}/{items.Count} completed").Opacity(0.6),

            // Input row
            HStack(8,
                TextBox(newText, setNewText, placeholderText: "What needs to be done?")
                    .AutomationName("New todo")
                    .Width(300),
                Button("Add", () =>
                {
                    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(newText))
                    {
                        var text = newText.Trim();
                        updateItems(list => [.. list, new TodoItem($"todo-{nextId}", text, false)]);
                        setNextId(nextId + 1);
                        setNewText("");
                    }
                }).IsEnabled(!(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(newText)))
            ),

            // Item list
            VStack(4,
                items.Select((item, _) =>
                    HStack(8,
                        CheckBox(item.Done, done =>
                            updateItems(list =>
                            {
                                var copy = new List<TodoItem>(list);
                                var itemIndex = copy.FindIndex(i => i.Id == item.Id);
                                if (itemIndex >= 0)
                                    copy[itemIndex] = item with { Done = done };
                                return copy;
                            }),
                            label: item.Text
                        ),
                        Button("Remove", () =>
                            updateItems(list =>
                            {
                                var copy = new List<TodoItem>(list);
                                copy.RemoveAll(i => i.Id == item.Id);
                                return copy;
                            })
                        ).AutomationName($"Remove {item.Text}")
                    ).WithKey(item.Id)
                ).ToArray()
            ),

            // Clear completed button
            When(doneCount > 0, () =>
                Button($"Clear completed ({doneCount})", () =>
                    updateItems(list => list.Where(i => !i.Done).ToList())
                ).AutomationName("Clear completed todos")
            )
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

Then add a record for one todo item at the end of the file:

```csharp
record TodoItem(string Id, string Text, bool Done);
```

Run the app. You see three todo items, and the first one is already checked.
Below the list is a **Clear completed (1)** button. Type a new item and click
**Add**: the item appears at the end of the list. Check an item, and the
"completed" count goes up. The **Add** button is turned off while the text box
is empty:

![The todo app: a "Todo List" heading, a count of completed items, a text box with an Add button, and three items with check boxes and Remove buttons](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/todo-app/todo-app.png)

New ideas in this step:

- **[`UseReducer`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hooks/UseReducer)** is like `UseState`, but
  its setter takes a function of type `Func<T, T>`. The function gets the
  current list and returns the next one. Use it when the new state depends on
  the old state, as when you add an item to a list.
- **[`UseMemo`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hooks/UseMemo)** builds the start list once, on
  the first render, instead of on every render.
- **`items.Select(...).ToArray()`** maps data to elements, like `ForEach` in
  Step 4. Each row still gets a key with `WithKey(item.Id)`.
- **`When(condition, () => element)`** shows an element only when the
  condition is true, without an `if`/`else` in the middle of the tree.
- **`item with { Done = done }`** creates a changed copy of a record. The old
  item stays as it was.

You now have a complete Reactor app.

## Next challenge: a calculator [#next-challenge-a-calculator]

The calculator keeps four pieces of related state and changes them from plain
C# methods. Replace the contents of `App.cs` with this code and run it:

```csharp
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor;
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core;
using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml;

ReactorApp.Run<CalculatorApp>("Calculator");

class CalculatorApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (display, setDisplay) = UseState("0");
        var (operand, setOperand) = UseState<double?>(null);
        var (op, setOp) = UseState<string?>(null);
        var (resetNext, setResetNext) = UseState(false);

        void PressDigit(string digit)
        {
            if (resetNext || display == "0")
            {
                setDisplay(digit);
                setResetNext(false);
            }
            else
            {
                setDisplay(display + digit);
            }
        }

        void PressOp(string nextOp)
        {
            var current = double.Parse(display);
            if (operand.HasValue && op != null)
            {
                var result = Calculate(operand.Value, current, op);
                setDisplay(FormatResult(result));
                setOperand(result);
            }
            else
            {
                setOperand(current);
            }
            setOp(nextOp);
            setResetNext(true);
        }

        void PressEquals()
        {
            if (operand.HasValue && op != null)
            {
                var current = double.Parse(display);
                var result = Calculate(operand.Value, current, op);
                setDisplay(FormatResult(result));
                setOperand(null);
                setOp(null);
                setResetNext(true);
            }
        }

        void PressClear()
        {
            setDisplay("0");
            setOperand(null);
            setOp(null);
            setResetNext(false);
        }

        Element NumButton(string digit) =>
            Button(digit, () => PressDigit(digit))
                .AutomationName($"Digit {digit}")
                .Width(60).Height(48);

        Element OpButton(string label, string opCode) =>
            Button(label, () => PressOp(opCode))
                .AutomationName(opCode switch
                {
                    "+" => "Add",
                    "-" => "Subtract",
                    "*" => "Multiply",
                    "/" => "Divide",
                    _ => $"Operator {label}"
                })
                .Width(60).Height(48);

        return VStack(4,
            // Display
            TextBlock(display)
                .FontSize(32).Bold()
                .HAlign(HorizontalAlignment.Right)
                .Padding(horizontal: 12, vertical: 8),

            // Button grid
            HStack(4, Button("C", PressClear).Width(60).Height(48),
                       NumButton("7"), NumButton("8"), NumButton("9")),
            HStack(4, OpButton("/", "/"),
                       NumButton("4"), NumButton("5"), NumButton("6")),
            HStack(4, OpButton("*", "*"),
                       NumButton("1"), NumButton("2"), NumButton("3")),
            HStack(4, OpButton("-", "-"),
                       NumButton("0"), OpButton("+", "+"),
                       Button("=", PressEquals)
                          .AutomationName("Equals")
                          .Width(60).Height(48))
        ).Padding(16);
    }

    static double Calculate(double a, double b, string op) => op switch
    {
        "+" => a + b,
        "-" => a - b,
        "*" => a * b,
        "/" => b != 0 ? a / b : 0,
        _ => b,
    };

    static string FormatResult(double value) =>
        value == Math.Floor(value) ? $"{value:F0}" : $"{value:G10}";
}
```

![The calculator app: a display above a grid of digit and operator buttons](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/calculator/calculator.png)

Methods, `switch` expressions and local functions all work inside a component.
You do not need a command pattern. A button calls a method, the method calls
`setDisplay(...)`, and the UI updates. Try to add a percent key or a
backspace key.

> **Caveat:** The argument you pass to `UseState` or `UseReducer` is the **initial** value.
> Reactor reads it only on the first render. If you pass a different value
> later, the state does not change. Call the setter instead. Hooks are also
> matched by the order you call them, so call them at the top of `Render()`,
> never inside an `if` or a loop.

## Patterns [#patterns]

### Hot reload with `dotnet watch` [#hot-reload-with-dotnet-watch]

The fastest way to work is to run `dotnet watch` from the project folder.
When you save `App.cs`, Reactor runs `Render()` again without restarting the
window. State in `UseState` is kept, so a counter at 42 stays at 42 after you
change the layout. Static fields keep their values too, because the process
keeps running. See [Hot reload](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/hot-reload) for what resets state.

### First event, first state [#first-event-first-state]

Every interactive app has the same two parts: an event handler that calls a
setter, and a value that `Render()` reads from state. In Step 1, the text box
calls `setName`, and the `TextBlock` reads `name`. That round trip is the
whole model. The other [hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) build on it: `UseReducer` for updates
that depend on the old value, `UseEffect` for side effects, and `UseRef` for
values that do not cause a render.

### Running with devtools [#running-with-devtools]

The dev menu needs **two** separate signals. Neither one is `#if DEBUG`.

1. **Build-time capability.** The `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport` feature switch.
   `dotnet new reactor` sets it in Debug builds, together with the
   `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools` package.
2. **Session opt-in.** A command-line argument:

   ```powershell
   dotnet run -- --devtools app
   ```

`dotnet run` passes everything after `--` to the app, and a packaged app still
gets it. The default profile in the template's
`Properties/launchSettings.json` passes no arguments, so a plain
`dotnet run -c Debug` starts the app **without** the dev menu. Keep the word
`app`: a bare `--devtools` means `--devtools run`, the heavier session behind
[`mur devtools`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools#mcp-server) that also starts an MCP endpoint.

`UseDevtools()` returns `true` only when both signals are present. The
signals do not draw anything by themselves. The menu is the `DevtoolsMenu(...)`
element, so it appears only if your tree renders one. To add it to the title
bar, see [In-app dev menu](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools#in-app-dev-menu). Release builds
leave out the package and the switch, so the devtools code is trimmed away.

## Common Mistakes [#common-mistakes]

### Changing a list in place [#changing-a-list-in-place]

```csharp
// Don't: this changes the old list and passes the same object back
names.Add("Ada");
setNames(names);
```

The setter compares the new value with the old one. The same list object
counts as "no change", so the screen does not update. Build a new list
instead, as in Step 4: `setNames([.. names, "Ada"])`.

### Calling a setter twice and expecting two updates [#calling-a-setter-twice-and-expecting-two-updates]

```csharp
// Don't: both calls read the same count, so the result is count + 1
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1);
```

`count` is a normal local variable. It keeps the value from the current
render until `Render()` runs again. To change a value based on its latest
state, use `UseReducer` and pass a function, as the todo app does:
`updateItems(list => [.. list, item])`.

### Using the list position as the key [#using-the-list-position-as-the-key]

```csharp
// Don't: the key moves to another item when a row is removed
items.Select((item, index) => Row(item).WithKey(index.ToString()))
```

When you remove a row, every row after it gets a new index, so Reactor matches
rows to the wrong items. The `REACTOR_DSL_002` analyzer flags index keys, and
`REACTOR_DSL_001` warns when a list item has no key. Use an ID from the data.
See [Collections](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/collections#stable-identity-with-withkey).

### Editing files under `bin/` [#editing-files-under-bin]

Reactor does not read the build output. Edit the source files in your
project, such as `App.cs`, and run `dotnet run` or `dotnet watch` again. The
build replaces the `bin/` folder each time, so changes there are lost.

### Writing Reactor elements in a XAML `Page` [#writing-reactor-elements-in-a-xaml-page]

`ReactorApp.Run<T>` opens a window and owns the whole tree. Reactor elements
are C# records, so there is no XAML loader for them, and you cannot write them
in a `Page` or `UserControl` file. To show a Reactor component inside an
existing WinUI page, add a `ReactorHostControl` to the page and name the
component:

```xml
<reactor:ReactorHostControl ComponentType="local:StatsCard" />
```

Declare the prefix with `xmlns:reactor="using:Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Hosting"`.
See [Coming from XAML](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/xaml-developers). For WinForms, see
[WinForms interop](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/winforms-interop).

### Using `INotifyPropertyChanged` out of habit [#using-inotifypropertychanged-out-of-habit]

If you come from XAML, you may reach for a view model. In Reactor, state is
the binding: `UseState` returns a value and a setter, and the setter causes
the render. You can still connect an existing `INotifyPropertyChanged` source
with `UseObservable` (see [Advanced patterns](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/advanced)), but for new code
hooks are shorter. [Coming from XAML](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/xaml-developers) maps each XAML idea
to Reactor.

## Tips [#tips]

**Think in functions, not objects.** `Render()` turns state into UI. It runs
again from the top every time the state changes. Do not change the UI
directly.

**Keep state as high as it needs to be, but no higher.** If only one
component uses a value, keep it in that component. If two sibling components
need the same value, move it to their parent.

**Use records for data.** C# records are immutable and compare by value. Use
`with` to make a changed copy, as the todo app does.

**Build small components.** Give each component one job, then combine them in
a parent component. See [Components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components).

**Use modifiers for simple styling.** Instead of wrapping an element in a
container, chain modifiers: `TextBlock("hi").Margin(8).Bold()`.

  `Component<TProps>` and typed props.

  [UseReducer](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hooks/UseReducer),
  [UseEffect](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hooks/UseEffect),

# Installation
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/install

This page takes you from a clean Windows machine to a running
Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) app in about five minutes. You need the .NET
SDK and, for packaged apps, Developer Mode. You do not need to clone the
Reactor repository: the package is on NuGet.org, and the project templates
ship in the Windows App SDK template pack.

> **Public preview.** `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` 0.1.0-preview.18 is on
> NuGet.org. The project templates ship in the official Windows App SDK
> `dotnet new` pack (`Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK.WinUI.CSharp.Templates`).
> Broader signed distribution is tracked in
> [spec 022](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/specs/022-packaging-and-distribution.md).

## Requirements [#requirements]

| Requirement | Why you need it | How to check |
|---|---|---|
| Windows 10 version 1809 (build 17763) or later, or Windows 11 | The oldest Windows version Reactor supports. | Run `winver`. |
| .NET 10 SDK or later | Reactor targets `net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0`. Single-file apps (`dotnet run app.cs`) are also a .NET 10 feature. | Run `dotnet --list-sdks` and look for a line that starts with `10.` or higher. |
| Windows App Runtime 2.x | Apps are framework-dependent by default, so they load the runtime that is installed on the machine. | Run `winget list --id Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.2`. |
| Developer Mode | Needed to run **packaged** apps with `dotnet run`. Unpackaged apps do not need it. | Settings → System → For developers. |
| An editor (optional) | The `dotnet` CLI is enough to build and run an app. | See [Choose an editor](#choose-an-editor). |

If the Windows App Runtime is missing, install it with
`winget install Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.2`. This one winget package
covers every 2.x release, so if an older 2.x runtime is installed, update it
with `winget upgrade Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.2`.

You do not need Visual Studio workloads or a separate Windows App SDK
install. NuGet restore brings in the Windows App SDK packages and build tools.

## Create a project [#create-a-project]

Use the `winapp` CLI, plain `dotnet new`, or a coding agent. Each way gives you
the same project.

**winapp**

The fastest way is the WinApp CLI, `winapp`.

1. **Install winapp**

    ```powershell
    winget install Microsoft.WinAppCli
    ```

2. **Create the project**

    ```powershell
    winapp new -t reactor -n MyApp
    ```

    `winapp new` installs the template pack the first time you use it, and
    offers to update a stale one. There is no separate install step and no
    version to pin. `winapp new --list` prints all templates. If you leave out
    `-t`, it asks you to pick one.

3. **Run it**

    ```powershell
    cd MyApp
    dotnet run
    ```

**dotnet new**

If you prefer plain .NET tooling, install the template pack yourself.

1. **Install the template pack**

    ```powershell
    dotnet new install Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK.WinUI.CSharp.Templates::<version>
    ```

    The pack is prerelease-only today. `dotnet new install` picks only stable
    versions unless you pin one, so the `::<version>` part is required. This is
    the step that `winapp new` does for you.

2. **Create the project**

    ```powershell
    dotnet new reactor -n MyApp
    ```

3. **Run it**

    ```powershell
    cd MyApp
    dotnet run
    ```

**With an agent**

Give this prompt to GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, or another coding agent. It
points the agent at these docs first, so it uses the real API. To give the
agent the Reactor skills too, see [Build with AI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/build-with-ai).

**Read https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/latest/llms.txt first. Then create a Reactor app named MyApp: install the winapp CLI with `winget install Microsoft.WinAppCli` if it is missing, run `winapp new -t reactor -n MyApp`, and start the app with `dotnet run` from the MyApp folder. Fix any build errors before you stop.**

> Read https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/latest/llms.txt first.
> Then create a Reactor app named MyApp: install the winapp CLI with
> `winget install Microsoft.WinAppCli` if it is missing, run
> `winapp new -t reactor -n MyApp`, and start the app with `dotnet run` from the
> MyApp folder. Fix any build errors before you stop.

### Templates [#templates]

| Template | What you get |
|---|---|
| `reactor` | A blank app with one component. |
| `reactor-mvu` | A Model-View-Update app built on `UseReducer`. |
| `reactor-navview` | An app shell with a `NavigationView`. |
| `reactor-tabview` | An app shell with a `TabView`. |
| `reactor-singlefile` | One `.cs` file and no project. See [One file, no project](#one-file-no-project). |

The project templates set up the `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` package reference, the
WinUI target framework, MSIX packaging, and an `App.cs` that mounts one
component. There is no `App.xaml` and no `MainWindow.xaml.cs`.

> **Why a custom template?** `dotnet new console` does not produce a WinUI
> app. It builds a console target with no UI thread, no `OutputType=WinExe`,
> no Windows App SDK reference and no `[STAThread]` entry point. The
> `reactor` template sets all of these, plus the Reactor package reference,
> MSIX packaging and a backdrop-aware root component. So the first
> `dotnet run` opens a window, not a console.

### Packaged or unpackaged [#packaged-or-unpackaged]

Apps created from a project template are **packaged** (single-project MSIX) by
default. `dotnet run` registers a loose-layout package and launches the app
with full package identity, the same as F5 in Visual Studio. This needs
**Developer Mode**.

For a plain unpackaged `.exe`, add `--packaging Unpackaged` to any of the four
project templates:

```powershell
dotnet new reactor -n MyApp --packaging Unpackaged
```

`winapp new` has no matching switch, so use `dotnet new` for this. An
unpackaged app has no package identity, so `Package.Current` and `ms-appx:`
URIs are not available. [Packaging](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/packaging) explains how the two shapes
differ and how to publish each one.

## Check that it works [#check-that-it-works]

`dotnet run` builds the app and opens a window with the template's starter
component. To check the whole loop, replace the contents of `App.cs` with this
small app:

```csharp
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor;
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core;
using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml;

ReactorApp.Run<GettingStartedApp>("Getting Started");

class GettingStartedApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (name, setName) = UseState("World");

        return VStack(16,
            TextBlock($"Hello, {name}!").FontSize(24).Bold(),
            TextBox(name, setName, placeholderText: "Enter your name")
                .AutomationName("Name")
                .Width(250)
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

Run `dotnet run` again. You see a greeting and a text box. Type in the box,
and the greeting changes as you type:

![The hello world app: a "Hello, World!" heading above a text box that holds the name](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/getting-started/hello-world.png)

If you see this window, your setup is complete.
[Your first app](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/first-app) explains this code line by line.

## One file, no project [#one-file-no-project]

A Reactor app does not need a `.csproj`. .NET 10 runs a single `.cs` file
directly, and `#:` directives at the top of the file give the settings that a
project file would otherwise hold:

```csharp
#:package Microsoft.UI.Reactor@0.1.0-preview.18
#:package Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp@0.7.0
#:property OutputType=WinExe
#:property TargetFramework=net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0
#:property UseWinUI=true

using Microsoft.UI.Reactor;
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core;
using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories;

ReactorApp.Run<MyApp>("Hello Reactor");

class MyApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (count, setCount) = UseState(0);

        return VStack(
            Heading($"Count: {count}"),
            HStack(8,
                Button("-", () => setCount(count - 1)),
                Button("+", () => setCount(count + 1))
            )
        );
    }
}
```

Save it as `counter.cs` and run it:

```powershell
dotnet run counter.cs
```

That is the whole app: one file, with no scaffolding and no build output to
manage. It is the fastest way to try an idea, reproduce a bug, or paste a
complete example into an issue.

Like an app from a project template, it runs packaged.
`Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp` makes `dotnet run` create an app
manifest from the `#:property` values, register the app, and launch it with
package identity. This needs **Developer Mode**. If you have the
[winapp CLI](https://github.com/microsoft/winappCli) 0.7.0 or later,
`winapp run counter.cs` does the same.

`Microsoft.UI.Reactor` brings in the Windows App SDK, just as in the
[minimal `.csproj`](#minimal-project-setup). The other directives are all
required:

| Directive | Why it is required |
|---|---|
| `Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp` | Lets `dotnet run` package the app. It carries its own copy of the winapp CLI, so you do not need to install that. Without it, `dotnet run` cannot package the app, and the app fails at startup with `COMException … REGDB_E_CLASSNOTREG`. That error does not mention the missing package. To avoid it without this package, run the app unpackaged (see below). |
| `OutputType=WinExe` | Links the app for the Windows GUI subsystem. Without it the build still succeeds, but the `.exe` is a console program, so Windows opens a console window next to your UI for as long as the app runs. |
| `TargetFramework=net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0` | Reactor ships for `net10.0-windows10.0.22621`. A lower Windows version compiles against nothing, and you get `CS0234: the namespace 'Reactor' does not exist`, as if the package were missing. |
| `UseWinUI=true` | Brings in the WinUI build targets. |

You do not have to type the header. `dotnet new reactor-singlefile -n Counter`
creates `Counter/Counter.cs` with the same five directives and a starter
component. Run `dotnet run Counter.cs` from that folder to launch it. The
template's pins differ from the block above: it targets a newer Windows SDK
(`windows10.0.26100.0`) and lets the `Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp`
version float (`@*`). Both headers work.

### Running it unpackaged [#running-it-unpackaged]

`WindowsPackageType` decides whether the app runs packaged. `dotnet run` and
`winapp run` both follow it. To run the app as a plain `.exe`, declare it
unpackaged:

```csharp
#:property WindowsPackageType=None
```

An unpackaged app has no package identity, so `Package.Current` and `ms-appx:`
URIs are not available. It does not need Developer Mode.

Packaged or not, the app is framework-dependent: it uses the Windows App
Runtime that is installed on the machine. To ship the runtime with the app
instead, add `#:property WindowsAppSDKSelfContained=true`. That mode also needs
an architecture, given with `-r win-x64` or `-r win-arm64`, because the runtime
it copies is native code built for each CPU.

## Minimal Project Setup [#minimal-project-setup]

The templates above create all of this for you. To set up a project by hand
instead, create a console project and edit the `.csproj`:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>WinExe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0</TargetFramework>
    <UseWinUI>true</UseWinUI>
    <WindowsPackageType>None</WindowsPackageType>
    <!-- Windows App SDK needs a concrete architecture; without this an
         unqualified `dotnet build` / `dotnet run` fails with
         "WindowsAppSDKSelfContained requires a supported Windows architecture". -->
    <RuntimeIdentifier Condition="'$(RuntimeIdentifier)' == '' And ('$(Platform)' == '' Or '$(Platform)' == 'AnyCPU')">$(NETCoreSdkPortableRuntimeIdentifier)</RuntimeIdentifier>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.UI.Reactor" Version="0.1.0-preview.18" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

One package reference is enough. `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` brings in the Windows
App SDK, so add `Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK` yourself only to pin a specific WinUI
patch or to bundle the runtime with `WindowsAppSDKSelfContained`. Pin WinUI
through that full package. Do not reference `Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK.WinUI` on
its own, because it fails the Windows App SDK's version check.
[Packaging](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/packaging) covers the `<Platforms>`, ARM64 and self-contained
shapes that the project template uses.

Then replace `Program.cs` with an `App.cs` that holds a component and a
`ReactorApp.Run<T>()` call:

```csharp
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor;
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core;
using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories;

ReactorApp.Run<MyApp>("My App");

class MyApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        return VStack(12,
            TextBlock("Hello, Reactor!").FontSize(24).Bold(),
            TextBlock("Your setup works.")
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

Run it with `dotnet run`. A window opens with the two lines of text.

## Choose an editor [#choose-an-editor]

Any editor works, because the `dotnet` CLI builds and runs every Reactor app.
These editors add more:

- **Visual Studio 2026.** Open the project and press F5 to build and debug
  it. The experimental [Visual Studio extension](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/vs-extension) adds an
  embedded live preview of a component.
- **VS Code.** The C# Dev Kit is all you need. The Reactor Preview extension
  adds a live preview panel; see the [VS Code extension](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/vs-extension#vs-code-extension).
- **Any editor and a terminal.** Run `dotnet watch` to apply code changes to
  the running app without a restart. See [Hot reload](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/hot-reload).

## Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting]

### The app fails at startup with `REGDB_E_CLASSNOTREG` [#the-app-fails-at-startup-with-regdb_e_classnotreg]

This happens with a single-file app that has no
`#:package Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp` line. Without that package,
`dotnet run` cannot package the app. Add the package line, or run the app
unpackaged with `#:property WindowsPackageType=None`. See
[One file, no project](#one-file-no-project).

### `dotnet run` cannot register or deploy a packaged app [#dotnet-run-cannot-register-or-deploy-a-packaged-app]

Packaged apps need Developer Mode. Turn it on in Settings → System → For
developers, then run `dotnet run` again. If you cannot turn it on, run the app
unpackaged (see [Packaged or unpackaged](#packaged-or-unpackaged)).

### `CS0234: the namespace 'Reactor' does not exist` [#cs0234-the-namespace-reactor-does-not-exist]

The target framework names a Windows version that is too low. Use
`net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0` or higher. This error looks like a missing
package, but the package is there.

### A console window opens next to the app [#a-console-window-opens-next-to-the-app]

`OutputType` is `Exe`, not `WinExe`. Set `<OutputType>WinExe</OutputType>` in
the `.csproj`, or `#:property OutputType=WinExe` in a single-file app.

### `WindowsAppSDKSelfContained requires a supported Windows architecture` [#windowsappsdkselfcontained-requires-a-supported-windows-architecture]

The build has no concrete architecture. The
[minimal `.csproj`](#minimal-project-setup) sets `RuntimeIdentifier` to fix
this. You can also pass the platform on the command line, for example
`dotnet build -p:Platform=x64` (or `ARM64`).

### `dotnet new` does not know `--packaging` or `reactor-singlefile` [#dotnet-new-does-not-know-packaging-or-reactor-singlefile]

The installed template pack is older than these options. Update it with
`winapp new --list --template-version latest`.

### The app starts and then reports a missing Windows App Runtime [#the-app-starts-and-then-reports-a-missing-windows-app-runtime]

The Windows App Runtime on the machine is missing or too old. Run
`winget install Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.2`, or `winget upgrade` if an
older 2.x runtime is installed. To avoid the machine-wide dependency, publish
the app self-contained; see [Packaging](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/packaging).

### The build fails with `MSB3073` or `PRI210` under a deep folder [#the-build-fails-with-msb3073-or-pri210-under-a-deep-folder]

The Windows App SDK's XAML and resource compilers have no long-path support.
A long project path can push `obj` and `bin` output past the 260-character
`MAX_PATH` limit. Move the project to a short path such as `C:\src\MyApp`, and
avoid OneDrive-synced folders. See
[issue #678](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/issues/678).

> **Caveat:** The template pack is prerelease-only today. `winapp new -t reactor` installs
> the newest pack and creates the project in one step. With plain `dotnet new`,
> run `dotnet new install Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK.WinUI.CSharp.Templates::<version>`
> first: without the explicit version pin, `dotnet new install` does not find the
> pack.

## Tips [#tips]

**Set the first window size.** `ReactorApp.Run<T>` takes an optional width
and height in device-independent pixels. Leave them out to let Windows choose.

```csharp
ReactorApp.Run<MyApp>("My App", width: 800, height: 600);
```

**Try an idea without a class.** For a quick test, pass a render function
instead of a component class. `ctx` gives you the same hooks a component has.

```csharp
ReactorApp.Run("Quick Test", ctx =>
{
    var (count, setCount) = ctx.UseState(0);
    return Button($"Clicked {count} times", () => setCount(count + 1));
});
```

**Keep a single-file app for bug reports.** A complete `.cs` file with the
`#:` header is the easiest repro to share in an issue.

# Rules of Reactor
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/rules-of-reactor

The five core rules:

1. [Hook order is stable across renders.](#1-hook-order-is-stable-across-renders)
2. [Render functions are pure.](#2-render-functions-are-pure)
3. [Lists need stable keys.](#3-lists-need-stable-keys)
4. [Setters returned by hooks are stable; deps must be stable too.](#4-setters-are-stable-and-deps-must-be-stable-too)
5. [Theme-aware modifiers want a token, not a literal.](#5-theme-aware-modifiers-want-a-token-not-a-literal)

```csharp
// REACTOR_HOOKS_001 — hooks must run unconditionally on every render.
// Wrapping a hook in `if` shifts the hook indices when the branch flips,
// and the next render reads slot N expecting `UseEffect` but finds
// `UseState`. The HookOrderException it raises is loud, but the bug
// can ship if the conditional is rarely true.
class HookOrderBad : Component
{
    public bool ShouldCount;

    public override Element Render()
    {
        if (ShouldCount)
        {
            var (count, _) = UseState(0);             // REACTOR_HOOKS_001
            return TextBlock($"Count: {count}");
        }
        return TextBlock("No counter.");
    }
}
```

![Trivial app — rules-of-reactor doc-app shell](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/rules-of-reactor/ok.png)

## Rule index [#rule-index]

| Rule | Analyzer | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Hook order is stable | `REACTOR_HOOKS_001`, `REACTOR_HOOKS_002` | [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) |
| Hooks called from Render only | `REACTOR_HOOKS_005` | [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) |
| Deps are stable | `REACTOR_HOOKS_004` | [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) |
| Debounced commands need UseCommand | `REACTOR_HOOKS_009` | [Commanding](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/commanding) |
| Render is pure | *(convention)* | [Components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components) |
| Lists need stable keys | `REACTOR_DSL_001..004` | [Collections](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/collections) |
| Theme tokens not literals | `REACTOR_THEME_001`, `REACTOR_THEME_004` | [Theming Tokens](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/theming-tokens) |
| Lightweight styling | `REACTOR_THEME_002` | [Styling](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/styling) |
| Accessible names | `REACTOR_A11Y_001..004` | [Accessibility](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/accessibility) |

Each rule below covers one row in the index with the before / after
shape and the analyzer's catch.

## 1. Hook order is stable across renders [#1-hook-order-is-stable-across-renders]

Hooks store their state at a slot index in the component's hook list.
The reconciler walks the list by ordinal on every render — so if
`UseState` was at slot 0 on render 1 and slot 1 on render 2, the
state migrates to the wrong slot and the value silently corrupts.

**The rule:** call every hook unconditionally at the top of `Render()`,
in the same order, every time. No `if`, no `for`, no `try/catch`
around a hook call, no early return.

**Analyzer:** `REACTOR_HOOKS_001` (conditional hook call),
`REACTOR_HOOKS_002` (hook after an early-return guard), and
`REACTOR_HOOKS_005` (hook called outside a `Render()` override or a
`Use*` helper).

Before:

```csharp
// REACTOR_HOOKS_001 — hooks must run unconditionally on every render.
// Wrapping a hook in `if` shifts the hook indices when the branch flips,
// and the next render reads slot N expecting `UseEffect` but finds
// `UseState`. The HookOrderException it raises is loud, but the bug
// can ship if the conditional is rarely true.
class HookOrderBad : Component
{
    public bool ShouldCount;

    public override Element Render()
    {
        if (ShouldCount)
        {
            var (count, _) = UseState(0);             // REACTOR_HOOKS_001
            return TextBlock($"Count: {count}");
        }
        return TextBlock("No counter.");
    }
}
```

After:

```csharp
class HookOrderGood : Component
{
    public bool ShouldCount;

    public override Element Render()
    {
        // Hook always runs; the conditional moves into the render output.
        var (count, _) = UseState(0);
        return ShouldCount
            ? TextBlock($"Count: {count}")
            : TextBlock("No counter.");
    }
}
```

The hook runs unconditionally; the branch moves into the element tree
returned by `Render()`. Same UI, stable hook order.

Full coverage on [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks).

## 2. Render functions are pure [#2-render-functions-are-pure]

`Render()` runs *every* time the component re-renders — which can be
many times per second under animation or input. A side effect inside
`Render()` (writing to a static counter, calling a logger, opening a
file) fires on each render, including dev-mode double-renders that
catch the bug. The right place for a side effect is inside `UseEffect`,
which runs once per render commit after the tree is materialized.

**The rule:** `Render` reads state and returns elements. It does not
mutate, call I/O, or fire telemetry. Side effects go in `UseEffect`.

Before:

```csharp
// Render must be pure. Side effects (file I/O, mutation of static state,
// timers) belong inside UseEffect, which runs after the render commits.
// A logger call inside Render mounts will fire on every re-render,
// including ones triggered by the debugger — and it makes snapshot tests
// flaky because the rendered output now depends on a side effect.
static class TelemetryBad
{
    public static int CardRenders;
}

class CardBad : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        TelemetryBad.CardRenders++;                    // side effect in Render
        return TextBlock("Card");
    }
}
```

After:

```csharp
static class Telemetry
{
    public static int CardRenders;
}

class CardGood : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        UseEffect(() =>
        {
            Telemetry.CardRenders++;
            return () => { };
        });
        return TextBlock("Card");
    }
}
```

The counter still increments on every render, but it does so inside
the effect — which means a snapshot test of `CardGood` doesn't have a
side-effect-on-render bug; the effect fires after the test inspects
the tree. Full coverage on [Effects](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/effects) and
[Components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components).

## 3. Lists need stable keys [#3-lists-need-stable-keys]

When the items in a `ForEach` / `ListView` / `Select(...).ToArray()`
reorder, the reconciler diffs the old tree against the new one.
Without keys, it diffs positionally — and a row that swapped places
gets the previous row's local state (focus, scroll offset, in-flight
edit). With `.WithKey(id)`, the reconciler matches by key and moves
the right state to the right row.

**The rule:** every element produced inside a list-like construct gets
a `.WithKey(stableId)` whose value persists across re-renders. The id
must be the record's primary key, not the array index. If the item
implements `IReactorKeyed`, `ForEach` fills the key for you — write it
only when you mean something other than `item.Key`.

**Analyzer:** `REACTOR_DSL_001` (dynamic list item missing `.WithKey`),
`REACTOR_DSL_002` (non-stable `.WithKey`),
`REACTOR_DSL_003` (typed collection `keySelector` never keys by item), and
`REACTOR_DSL_004` (a `.WithKey` that only restates the key `ForEach`
already supplies for an `IReactorKeyed` item).

Before:

```csharp
// A list reorder without keys forces the reconciler to walk both lists in
// order and reuse slot 0 for whatever new item lands first. Local state
// (focus, scroll position, in-flight edits) gets attached to the wrong
// row. WithKey on each child binds state to identity rather than slot.
class TodoListBad : Component
{
    public TodoItem[] Items = System.Array.Empty<TodoItem>();

    public override Element Render() => VStack(4,
        Items.Select(i =>
            // No .WithKey — reorder is destructive.
            TextBox(i.Title, title => Rename(i, title), header: i.Id.ToString())
        ).ToArray()
    );

    void Rename(TodoItem item, string title)
    {
        var index = System.Array.IndexOf(Items, item);
        if (index >= 0)
            Items[index] = item with { Title = title };
    }
}
public record TodoItem(int Id, string Title);
```

After:

```csharp
class TodoListGood : Component
{
    public TodoItem[] Items = System.Array.Empty<TodoItem>();

    public override Element Render() => VStack(4,
        Items.Select(i =>
            TextBox(i.Title, title => Rename(i, title), header: i.Id.ToString())
                .WithKey(i.Id.ToString())                  // stable identity
        ).ToArray()
    );

    void Rename(TodoItem item, string title)
    {
        var index = System.Array.IndexOf(Items, item);
        if (index >= 0)
            Items[index] = item with { Title = title };
    }
}
```

Full coverage on [Collections](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/collections) and
[Reconciliation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reconciliation).

## 4. Setters are stable, and deps must be stable too [#4-setters-are-stable-and-deps-must-be-stable-too]

The `Action<T>` setter returned by `UseState`, `UseReducer`, and
`UsePersisted` keeps the same delegate identity across renders. You
can safely close over it inside a `UseEffect` cleanup, a captured
event handler, or a `Task` — the captured reference is the live
setter.

The same can't be said of dependency arrays. A freshly-allocated
array or a freshly-allocated record passed as `deps` differs by
reference on every render, so the effect re-fires every time:

```csharp
// Wrong:
UseEffect(Setup, new[] { name, version });    // freshly-allocated array
// REACTOR_HOOKS_004 flags this.
```

```csharp
// Right:
UseEffect(Setup, name, version);              // params overload — items
                                              // compared by value.
```

**The rule:** pass `deps` via the `params` overload of `UseEffect`/
`UseMemo`/`UseCallback`, not as a freshly-allocated array. The
analyzer catches the common shape; for cases the analyzer can't see
(a `Tuple<...>` allocated inline), assign the deps to a local first.

**Analyzer:** `REACTOR_HOOKS_004` (unstable deps),
`REACTOR_HOOKS_007` (`UseMemoCells` builder missing a captured
dependency).

Full coverage on [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks).

## 5. Theme-aware modifiers want a token, not a literal [#5-theme-aware-modifiers-want-a-token-not-a-literal]

`.Background`, `.Foreground`, and `.WithBorder` take a brush. A hex
literal works for the demo but breaks the moment the user flips
themes — the literal is locked to the value you typed, so the
brand-blue button stays blue on a now-dark background and the
contrast collapses.

**The rule:** pass a `Theme.*` token (or `Theme.Ref("CustomKey")` for
a custom XAML resource key) to any theme-aware modifier. Reserve hex
literals for the rare case where the color is *intentionally*
theme-invariant (a brand mark, a print preview) — and leave a comment
saying so.

**Analyzer:** `REACTOR_THEME_001` (hard-coded color string on a
theme-aware modifier) and `REACTOR_THEME_004` (hard-coded
`Brush`/`Color` object bypasses theme tokens).

```csharp
// Don't:
Button("Save", () => { }).Background("#0066CC");   // REACTOR_THEME_001
```

```csharp
// Do:
Button("Save", () => { }).Background(Theme.Accent);
```

Full coverage on [Theming Tokens](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/theming-tokens).

## Reference [#reference]

| Rule | Analyzer | Where the page lives |
|---|---|---|
| Hook order is stable | `REACTOR_HOOKS_001`, `REACTOR_HOOKS_002` | [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) |
| Hooks called from `Render` only | `REACTOR_HOOKS_005` | [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) |
| Deps must be stable | `REACTOR_HOOKS_004` | [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) |
| UseResource fetcher is idempotent | `REACTOR_HOOKS_006` | [Async Resources](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/async-resources) |
| UseMemoCells builder must close over deps | `REACTOR_HOOKS_007` | [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) |
| Debounced commands routed through UseCommand | `REACTOR_HOOKS_009` | [Commanding](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/commanding) |
| Render must be pure | *(convention — no analyzer)* | [Components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components), [Effects](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/effects) |
| Lists need stable keys | `REACTOR_DSL_001..004` | [Collections](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/collections), [Reconciliation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reconciliation) |
| Theme-aware modifiers want a token | `REACTOR_THEME_001`, `REACTOR_THEME_004` | [Theming Tokens](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/theming-tokens) |
| Lightweight styling, not implicit resources | `REACTOR_THEME_002` | [Styling](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/styling) |
| `RequestedTheme` is a render input, not a setter | `REACTOR_THEME_003` | [Styling](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/styling) |
| XML docs on public APIs | `REACTOR_DOC_001` | (framework code) |
| `<see cref="..."/>` resolves | `CS1574` | (framework code) |
| Accessible name on interactive elements | `REACTOR_A11Y_001..004` | [Accessibility](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/accessibility) |

## Tips [#tips]

**Treat analyzer warnings as build errors in CI.** Every rule with an
analyzer has a known false-positive rate near zero; the cost of a
suppression is small, the cost of a regression that the analyzer
would have caught is large.

**The "pure render" rule is conventional, not enforced.** No
analyzer catches it; review and snapshot tests are the safety net.
The [testing](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/testing) page covers the snapshot pattern that makes
purity visible.

**`.WithKey` is cheap; reach for it whenever a list reorders.** Even
when the analyzer doesn't flag the omission, a missing key is one of
the bugs most likely to ship to a customer (it's invisible at small
list sizes and devastating at scale).

  reconciler level.

- **[Accessibility](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/accessibility)** — The A11Y_001..004 rules.

# Samples
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/samples

This page lists the samples in the
[`samples/`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/tree/main/samples)
folder by group, says
what each one shows, and gives the command that runs it.

![The samples in a suggested order: start with ReactorGallery, TodoApp and StylingGallery, then the feature demos, then the full apps. The windowing, interop, charting, animation and performance, and Native AOT samples can be picked by topic](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/samples/sample-map.svg)

## Before you run a sample [#before-you-run-a-sample]

The samples build Reactor from source. They reference `src/Reactor` as a
project, not the NuGet package, so you need a clone of the repository and the
tools that build it.

| You need | Why | How to get it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A clone at a short path, such as `C:\src\microsoft-ui-reactor` | The Windows App SDK build tools have no long-path support. A deep or OneDrive-synced path fails with `MSB3073` or `PRI210`. | `git clone https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor.git` |
| The .NET 11 SDK | `global.json` pins it, and Reactor uses C# 15. | Run `bootstrap.ps1` from the clone. |
| The .NET 10 Desktop runtime | The samples target `net10.0`. | `bootstrap.ps1` installs it with the SDK. |
| The Windows App Runtime 2.x | Most samples are framework-dependent, so they load the runtime that is installed on the PC. | `winget install Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.2` |
| A platform flag | `AnyCPU` is not a supported WinUI app platform. | Pass `-p:Platform=x64`, or `-p:Platform=ARM64` on an Arm PC. |

`bootstrap.ps1` checks for the two .NET pieces and installs them with winget
when they are missing. See
[Setting up a source checkout](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#setting-up-a-source-checkout).
Two samples, `minesweeper` and the internal `Reactor.TestApp`, are
self-contained. They carry the Windows App Runtime with them.

## Run a sample [#run-a-sample]

Run each command from the root of the clone. Pass the sample's folder to
`--project`. When a folder holds more than one project, pass the `.csproj`
file instead.

```powershell
dotnet run --project samples/TodoApp -p:Platform=x64
```

The commands on this page use `x64`. On an Arm PC, use `ARM64`. A few
commands also set `-p:RuntimeIdentifier=win-x64`, as the sample's README does.
Change that value to `win-arm64` when you change the platform.

Debug builds of the samples also reference `Reactor.Devtools`, so you can add
a `--devtools` argument after `--`:

```powershell
dotnet run --project samples/TodoApp -p:Platform=x64 -- --devtools app
```

See [Devtools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools) for the other launch modes.

### Extra setup [#extra-setup]

- **headtrax** reads its data from `service/headtrax.db`. Create that file
  once. The service needs Node.js `^20.19.0`, `^22.13.0` or `^23.5.0`.

  ```powershell
  cd samples/apps/headtrax/service
  npm install
  npm run generate
  ```

  To use the GraphQL source, also run `npm start` in the same folder. The app
  connects to `http://localhost:4000/graphql`.
- **demo-script-tool** and **widget-creator** call GitHub Copilot. Sign in
  first with `gh auth login --web`, using an account that has Copilot.
- **widget-creator** builds the apps it creates against the packages in
  `local-nupkgs/`. Run `mur pack-local` (or `bootstrap.ps1`) first. Its
  [README](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/samples/apps/widget-creator/README.md)
  lists the full setup.
- **regedit** edits the real registry of your PC. Try it on keys you can
  lose, or in a virtual machine.
