### `RequestedTheme` [#requestedtheme]

Sets [`FrameworkElement.RequestedTheme`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.frameworkelement.requestedtheme) on the control, forcing a subtree to render in a specific theme variant (e.g., dark sidebar in a light app). Applied before ThemeRef bindings resolve so that theme resources pick up the correct variant.

### `ToolTipPlacement` [#tooltipplacement]

`ToolTipService.Placement` — which side of the element the tooltip opens on. Applies to both [`ElementModifiers.ToolTip`](#tooltip) and [`ElementModifiers.RichToolTip`](#richtooltip). `PlacementMode` has exactly five members (`Top`, `Bottom`, `Left`, `Right`, `Mouse`); the edge-aligned placements belong to the separate `FlyoutPlacementMode` enum and are not expressible here.

```csharp
public PlacementMode? ToolTipPlacement  // get, init
```

### `ToolTipPlacementTargetRef` [#tooltipplacementtargetref]

`ToolTipService.PlacementTarget` — position the tooltip relative to a different element than the one it is attached to. Resolved through the same deferred reference-edge machinery as the XYFocus refs, so the target does not have to be mounted before this element.

```csharp
public ElementRef? ToolTipPlacementTargetRef  // get, init
```

# Modifiers: Focus and keyboard
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/focus-and-keyboard

Modifiers are extension methods that return a changed copy of the element, so you can chain them.

**Learn more:** [Input and gestures](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/input-and-gestures), [Accessibility](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/accessibility)

## `AccessKey` [#accesskey]

Sets UIElement.AccessKey — the Alt+Key shortcut (underlined hint shown on Alt press). When used on a button bound to a [`Command`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/Command), this per-site access key overrides [`Command.AccessKey`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/Command#accesskey) (per-site override always wins).

```csharp
T AccessKey<T>(this T el, string key) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | `string` |  |

**Example**

```csharp
Button("File", onClick).AccessKey("F")
```


> **Obsolete.** Use OnAccessKeyDisplayRequested. See #260.

| `AccessKeyDisplayRequested<T>(T, Action<UIElement, AccessKeyDisplayRequestedEventArgs>)` | Handler for UIElement.AccessKeyDisplayRequested with full event args. |

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `handler` | `Action` or `Action<UIElement, AccessKeyDisplayRequestedEventArgs>` |  |

## `DraggableWhen` [#draggablewhen]

Gates an attached `.OnDragStart` — when `canDrag` returns false, the drag is cancelled in `DragStarting` before any UI feedback appears. Merge with an existing [`DragSourceConfig`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/drag-and-drop#dragsourceconfig) so previously-set allowed ops / onEnd are preserved.

```csharp

```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `canDrag` | `Func<bool>` |  |

## `IsDragRegion` [#isdragregion]

Marks how this element participates in a window title bar's drag region (`Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Controls.TitleBar.IsDragRegion`, WinApp SDK ≥ 2.1.3): `true` = draggable, `false` = clickable, `null` = defer to the title bar (interactive controls are auto-excluded from the drag region). Only meaningful for an element inside a `TitleBar`'s content; inert elsewhere. The nullable parameter lets callers forward a `bool?` state without branching.

```csharp
T IsDragRegion<T>(this T el, bool? isDragRegion = true) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `isDragRegion` | `bool?` | `true` |  |

**Example**

```csharp
Button(Icon(FontIcon("\uE713", fontSize: 16)), OnSettings)
    .AutomationName("Settings").IsDragRegion(false)
```

## `OnDragStart` [#ondragstart]

```csharp
T OnDragStart<T>(this T el, Func<DragData> getData, DragOperations? allowedOperations = null, Action<DragEndContext>? onEnd = null) where T : Element
T OnDragStart<T, TPayload>(this T el, Func<TPayload> getPayload, DragOperations? allowedOperations = null, Action<DragEndContext>? onEnd = null) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `OnDragStart<T>(T, Func<DragData>, DragOperations?, Action<DragEndContext>?)` | Raw drag source — the caller builds the [`DragData`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/drag-and-drop#dragdata) directly. Useful when advertising multiple formats at once (Phase 6b) or attaching additional metadata. |
| `OnDragStart<T, TPayload>(T, Func<TPayload>, DragOperations?, Action<DragEndContext>?)` | Typed drag source. Auto-sets [`UIElement.CanDrag`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.uielement.candrag) so the element reports as draggable. `getPayload` is called each time a drag starts; the returned value is wrapped in a typed-payload [`DragData`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/drag-and-drop#dragdata) keyed by `TPayload`. Use `allowedOperations` to declare which final operations (Copy/Move/Link) the source will accept. `onEnd` fires after `DropCompleted` with the final negotiated operation (or [`DragOperations.None`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/drag-and-drop#values) on cancel). |

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `getData` | `Func<DragData>` |  |  |
| `allowedOperations` | `DragOperations?` | `null` |  |
| `onEnd` | `Action<DragEndContext>?` | `null` |  |
| `getPayload` | `Func<TPayload>` |  |  |

## `OnDrop` [#ondrop]

```csharp
T OnDrop<T>(this T el, Action<DragTargetArgs> onDrop, DragOperations acceptedOps = DragOperations.All) where T : Element
T OnDrop<T, TPayload>(this T el, Action<TPayload> onDrop, DragOperations acceptedOps = DragOperations.All) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `OnDrop<T>(T, Action<DragTargetArgs>, DragOperations)` | Raw drop handler — receives the full [`DragTargetArgs`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/drag-and-drop#dragtargetargs) so multi-format targets can inspect available formats and accept operation manually. |
| `OnDrop<T, TPayload>(T, Action<TPayload>, DragOperations)` | Typed drop target. Auto-sets [`UIElement.AllowDrop`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.uielement.allowdrop). The handler is invoked when a drag with a matching typed payload is dropped on this element; the accepted operation is set to the intersection of `acceptedOps` and the source's allowed operations (preferring Move \> Copy \> Link). |

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `onDrop` | `Action<DragTargetArgs>` or `Action<TPayload>` |  |  |
| `acceptedOps` | [`DragOperations`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/drag-and-drop#dragoperations) | `DragOperations.All` |  |

## `OnLongPress` [#onlongpress]

```csharp
T OnLongPress<T>(this T el, Action onTriggered, TimeSpan? minimumDuration = null, double cancelDistance = 10, bool enableMouseEmulation = false) where T : Element
T OnLongPress<T>(this T el, Action<LongPressGesture> onTriggered, TimeSpan? minimumDuration = null, double cancelDistance = 10, bool enableMouseEmulation = false) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `OnLongPress<T>(T, Action, TimeSpan?, double, bool)` | Zero-argument convenience overload for long-press. Use when you don't need the gesture snapshot (Position, Duration, Phase). Fires exactly ONCE per recognized long-press, at the moment it triggers ([`GesturePhase.Began`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/gestures#values)) — not again on release ([`GesturePhase.Ended`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/gestures#values)) or cancel. The underlying `OnTriggered` contract fires Began then Ended/Cancelled; a phase-agnostic convenience action must filter to Began or it double-fires. (This was previously masked when a per-render capturing action went stale across a skipped render — both calls became idempotent; the skip-path closure refresh in #721 exposed it, so the filter makes the single-fire contract explicit.) |
| `OnLongPress<T>(T, Action<LongPressGesture>, TimeSpan?, double, bool)` | Attaches a long-press gesture recognizer (spec 027 Tier 3 Part 2). Touch and pen route through [`UIElement.Holding`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.uielement.holding) (`IsHoldingEnabled = true` is auto-set). Mouse input is ignored by default — WinUI's `Holding` event does not raise for mouse pointers. Pass `enableMouseEmulation` `true` to arm a dispatcher timer on [`UIElement.PointerPressed`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.uielement.pointerpressed) that fires after `minimumDuration` and cancels on motion \> `cancelDistance`, pointer release, or capture loss. |

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `onTriggered` | `Action` or `Action<LongPressGesture>` |  |  |
| `minimumDuration` | `TimeSpan?` | `null` |  |
| `cancelDistance` | `double` | `10` |  |
| `enableMouseEmulation` | `bool` | `false` |  |

**Example**

```csharp
card.OnLongPress(g => ShowContextMenu(g.Position))
```

## `OnPan` [#onpan]

Attaches a pan (single-finger translation) gesture recognizer. The reconciler wires [`UIElement.ManipulationDelta`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.uielement.manipulationdelta) and computes [`UIElement.ManipulationMode`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.uielement.manipulationmode) based on the chosen `axis` and `withInertia` flag. `minimumDistance` gates callbacks until the cumulative translation exceeds that distance — on first crossing, `onBegan` fires once with [`GesturePhase.Began`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/gestures#values), then a [`GesturePhase.Changed`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/gestures#values) follows.

```csharp
T OnPan<T>(this T el, Action<PanGesture> onChanged, Action<PanGesture>? onEnded = null, Action<PanGesture>? onBegan = null, Action<PanGesture>? onCancelled = null, double minimumDistance = 0, PanAxis axis = PanAxis.Both, bool withInertia = false) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `onChanged` | `Action<PanGesture>` |  |  |
| `onEnded` | `Action<PanGesture>?` | `null` |  |
| `onBegan` | `Action<PanGesture>?` | `null` |  |
| `onCancelled` | `Action<PanGesture>?` | `null` |  |
| `minimumDistance` | `double` | `0` |  |
| `axis` | [`PanAxis`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/gestures#panaxis) | `PanAxis.Both` |  |
| `withInertia` | `bool` | `false` |  |

# Modifiers: Layout and spacing
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/layout-and-spacing

Modifiers are extension methods that return a changed copy of the element, so you can chain them.

**Learn more:** [Layout](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/layout), [Flex Layout](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/flex-layout)

## `Canvas` [#canvas]

```csharp
T Canvas<T>(this T el, double left = 0, double top = 0) where T : Element
T Canvas<T>(this T el, double left, double top, double anchorX, double anchorY) where T : Element
```

Declared in `CanvasExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Canvas<T>(T, double, double)` | Sets Canvas attached properties (left, top) on this element. Only meaningful when the element is a child of a Canvas. |
| `Canvas<T>(T, double, double, double, double)` | Sets Canvas attached properties with an anchor. `anchorX`/`anchorY` are 0..1 fractions of the element's rendered size; the reconciler subtracts that fraction of the actual width/height from `left`/`top` after layout. 0,0 = top-left (legacy), 0.5,0.5 = centered on (left, top), 1,1 = bottom-right. |

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `left` | `double` | `0` |  |
| `top` | `double` | `0` |  |
| `anchorX` | `double` |  |  |
| `anchorY` | `double` |  |  |

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

## `CenterAt` [#centerat]

Centers this element on (`x`, `y`) within its parent Canvas. Equivalent to `.Canvas(x, y, anchorX: 0.5, anchorY: 0.5)`. Position is recomputed after layout, so the element does not need a known size at construction time.

```csharp
T CenterAt<T>(this T el, double x, double y) where T : Element
```

Declared in `CanvasExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x` | `double` |  |
| `y` | `double` |  |

# LayoutModifiers
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/LayoutModifiers

Layout-related modifiers (sizing, alignment, spacing, visibility, theme, logical-direction insets). Stored as a lazy sub-record on [`ElementModifiers`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/ElementModifiers) so that the common case of a few fields set allocates a small bucket rather than bloating the parent record. Public properties on [`ElementModifiers`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/ElementModifiers) (Padding, Margin, Width, …) read from / write into this sub-record transparently — most callers never see this type.

```csharp
public record LayoutModifiers
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core`.

**Learn more:** [Modifier System](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/modifier-system)

## Remarks [#remarks]

Spec 034 §A. The field set may grow but won't shrink — additions are always backwards-compatible.

# Modifiers: Lifecycle and identity
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/lifecycle

Modifiers are extension methods that return a changed copy of the element, so you can chain them.

**Learn more:** [Components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components), [Context](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/context)

## `OnMount` [#onmount]

Runs an action once when the element is first mounted (not on re-renders). Use this instead of .Set() when attaching event handlers to avoid accumulation. Usage: Button("Go", null).OnMount(fe =\> \{ ((Button)fe).Click += ...; \})

```csharp
T OnMount<T>(this T el, Action<FrameworkElement> action) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `action` | `Action<FrameworkElement>` |  |

## `OnMountAdd` [#onmountadd]

Like [`OnMount`](#onmount), but composes with any mount action already on the element instead of overwriting it. Useful for framework code that wants to apply defensive defaults (e.g. `IsHitTestVisible = false`) to a caller-supplied [`Element`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/Element) without silently dropping the caller's own mount-time wiring. The pre-existing action runs first, then the new one.

```csharp
T OnMountAdd<T>(this T el, Action<FrameworkElement> action) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `action` | `Action<FrameworkElement>` |  |

## `OnSizeChanged` [#onsizechanged]

```csharp
T OnSizeChanged<T>(this T el, Action<object, SizeChangedEventArgs> handler) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `handler` | `Action<object, SizeChangedEventArgs>` |  |

## `OnUnmount` [#onunmount]

Runs an action once when the element is unmounted (removed from the tree), receiving the native control. The teardown half of [`OnMount`](#onmount) — the React `useEffect` cleanup / Compose `DisposableEffect { onDispose }` shape — for controls that need an imperative stop/dispose (e.g. stopping a camera preview, releasing a media session). Runs on genuine unmount, not on re-render/update. Disposing the host drops its tree without unmounting it, so this callback is not guaranteed to run then. Release anything that must not outlive the host from a `UseEffect` cleanup, which disposal does run. Usage: CameraPreview(...).OnMount(fe =\> Start(fe)).OnUnmount(fe =\> Stop(fe))

```csharp
T OnUnmount<T>(this T el, Action<FrameworkElement> action) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `action` | `Action<FrameworkElement>` |  |

## `OnUnmountAdd` [#onunmountadd]

Like [`OnUnmount`](#onunmount), but composes with any unmount action already on the element instead of overwriting it (pre-existing action runs first).

```csharp
T OnUnmountAdd<T>(this T el, Action<FrameworkElement> action) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `action` | `Action<FrameworkElement>` |  |

## `Provide` [#provide]

Provides a context value to this element's subtree. Any descendant can consume it via UseContext(). Multiple .Provide() calls on the same element merge into a single dictionary. Providing the same context twice on the same element is last-write-wins.

```csharp
T Provide<T, TValue>(this T element, Context<TValue> context, TValue value) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ContextExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `context` | [`Context<TValue>`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/components/Context) |  |
| `value` | `TValue` |  |

## `Ref` [#ref]

```csharp
T Ref<T>(this T el, ElementRef target) where T : Element
T Ref<T, TElement>(this T el, ElementRef<TElement> target) where T : Element where TElement : FrameworkElement
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Ref<T>(T, ElementRef)` | Binds this element to an imperative [`ElementRef`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/element-refs#elementref). Obtain the ref from `ctx.UseElementFocus()` (or construct one manually) and use [`FocusManager.Focus`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/FocusManager#focus) to imperatively focus the referenced element after mount. |
| `Ref<T, TElement>(T, ElementRef<TElement>)` | Strongly-typed overload of [`Ref`](#ref). Accepts a typed [`ElementRef<T>`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/element-refs#elementreft) and forwards to the untyped form via the implicit conversion. |

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | [`ElementRef`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/element-refs#elementref) or [`ElementRef<TElement>`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/input/element-refs#elementreft) |  |

**Remarks**

Spec 033 §3. Behaviorally identical to passing the inner untyped ref; the typed overload exists so callers see the typed surface in IntelliSense and so the reconciler's DEBUG mismatch-assert can fire on a wrong-type binding.

**Example**

```csharp
var (inputRef, requestFocus) = ctx.UseElementFocus();
return TextBox(value, setValue).Ref(inputRef);
```

## `WithKey` [#withkey]

```csharp
T WithKey<T>(this T el, string key) where T : Element
T WithKey<T, TKey>(this T el, TKey item) where T : Element where TKey : IReactorKeyed
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `WithKey<T>(T, string)` | Assigns a stable reconciliation key. Reuses the element when it already holds the same string reference; otherwise returns an immutable copy. |
| `WithKey<T, TKey>(T, TKey)` | Assigns the stable identity from an [`IReactorKeyed`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/components/IReactorKeyed) data item directly to a hand-built element — equivalent to `el.WithKey(item.Key)` but lets call sites avoid hoisting the item to read `.Key`. (spec 042 §5) |

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | `string` |  |
| `item` | `TKey` |  |

**Remarks**

Typical use: `FlexColumn(items.Select(item => TextBlock(item.Name).WithKey(item)))`. The `TKey` parameter is independent of the element type so the usual fluent inference (return the element type) is preserved.

## `ProfilePicture` [#profilepicture]

Sets the avatar image from an absolute URI string, such as an `https://` address or an `ms-appx:///` asset path. A `null`, empty, malformed, or relative value shows no picture, so the control falls back to its initials or the generic person glyph; removing the picture on a later render clears the previous image.


# Control modifiers: Navigation
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/navigation

Modifiers are extension methods that return a changed copy of the element, so you can chain them.

**Learn more:** [Navigation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/navigation)

## `AutoRefreshDragRegions` [#autorefreshdragregions]

When `true`, the title bar re-derives its drag regions on every layout pass — the right fit for content that changes across renders. WinApp SDK ≥ 2.1.3. Interactive controls are auto-excluded from the drag region either way; use [`IsDragRegion`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/input-and-events#isdragregion) on a child to override per element.

```csharp
TitleBarElement AutoRefreshDragRegions(this TitleBarElement el, bool value = true)
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** [`TitleBarElement`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#titlebarelement).

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `bool` | `true` |  |

## `FillContentArea` [#fillcontentarea]

Makes the tab content area fill the space the parent gives the TabView, instead of collapsing to the content's own height (issue #914).

```csharp
TabViewElement FillContentArea(this TabViewElement el, bool fill = true)
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** [`TabViewElement`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#tabviewelement).

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fill` | `bool` | `true` |  |

**Remarks**

WinUI's default TabView style sets `VerticalAlignment="Top"` on the control, so by default the tab body is sized to its content and a tab child with its own background paints only a band. An explicit `.VAlign(…)` on the TabView element always wins over this opt-in. See [`TabViewElement.FillContentArea`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#tabviewelement).

## `HeightOption` [#heightoption]

Sets the system caption height for the hosting window. (issue #917)

```csharp
TitleBarElement HeightOption(this TitleBarElement el, WindowTitleBarHeight height)
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** [`TitleBarElement`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#titlebarelement).

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `height` | [`WindowTitleBarHeight`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hosting/window-options#windowtitlebarheight) |  |

**Remarks**

Applies both halves — the native caption (`AppWindow.TitleBar.PreferredHeightOption`) and, for [`WindowTitleBarHeight.Tall`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hosting/window-options#values_12), the control's own 48 DIP height, which the WinUI `TitleBar` control does not derive from the caption. An explicit `.Height(...)` on this element still wins. [`WindowSpec.TitleBarHeight`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hosting/WindowSpec#titlebarheight), when set, wins over this.

## `Icon` [#icon]

```csharp
TitleBarElement Icon(this TitleBarElement el, IconData icon)
TitleBarElement Icon(this TitleBarElement el, string imageUri)
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Icon(TitleBarElement, IconData)` | Sets the icon shown in the leading slot. Pass a [`SymbolIconData`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/controls/icons#symbolicondata), [`FontIconData`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/controls/icons#fonticondata), [`ImageIconData`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/controls/icons#imageicondata), or [`BitmapIconData`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/controls/icons#bitmapicondata). |
| `Icon(TitleBarElement, string)` | Convenience overload — sets the icon to a bundled image / .ico via a Uri string (e.g. `"ms-appx:///Assets/AppIcon.ico"`). |

**Applies to:** [`TitleBarElement`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#titlebarelement).

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `icon` | [`IconData`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/controls/icons#icondata) |  |
| `imageUri` | `string` |  |

**Remarks**

Only needed to show something *other* than the app's own icon — with no explicit icon the title bar inherits the window's (`WindowSpec.Icon`, else `Assets\AppIcon.ico`). Use [`NoIcon`](#noicon) to show none at all.

## `WithNavigation` [#withnavigation]

```csharp
TitleBarElement WithNavigation<TRoute>(this TitleBarElement el, NavigationHandle<TRoute> nav) where TRoute : notnull
NavigationViewElement WithNavigation<TRoute>(this NavigationViewElement el, NavigationHandle<TRoute> nav, Func<TRoute, string?> routeToTag, Func<string, TRoute> tagToRoute, Func<TRoute>? settingsRoute = null) where TRoute : notnull
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `WithNavigation<TRoute>(TitleBarElement, NavigationHandle<TRoute>)` | Auto-syncs this TitleBar's back button with a NavigationHandle: sets `IsBackButtonVisible` and `IsBackButtonEnabled` from `CanGoBack`, and wires `OnBackRequested` to `GoBack`. |
| `WithNavigation<TRoute>(NavigationViewElement, NavigationHandle<TRoute>, Func<TRoute, string?>, Func<string, TRoute>, Func<TRoute>?)` | Auto-syncs this NavigationView with a NavigationHandle: sets `SelectedTag` from the current route, navigates on selection change, wires `OnBackRequested` to `GoBack`, and `IsBackEnabled` to `CanGoBack`. NavigationView's recommended transition is forwarded to the navigation host, so pane navigation uses WinUI's entrance motion and top navigation slides horizontally according to the selected item's position.  Selection is wired through an internal transition-aware callback rather than the public [`NavigationViewElement.OnSelectedTagChanged`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#navigationviewelement), which this deliberately leaves null: setting that property yourself afterwards then takes precedence and suppresses the auto-navigation, so an author can observe selection without this fighting them. The same applies to [`NavigationViewElement.OnSettingsSelected`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#navigationviewelement).  The built-in settings item is opt-in: pass `settingsRoute` to make selecting it navigate. It is a separate parameter rather than a [`NavigationViewElement.SettingsTag`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#navigationviewelement) lookup through `tagToRoute` because that delegate must return a route for every string it is handed — callers typically throw on an unrecognized tag — so there is no way for it to decline. Left null, settings selection does not navigate.  To show the settings item as selected while its route is current, return [`NavigationViewElement.SettingsTag`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#navigationviewelement) from `routeToTag`. |

**Applies to:** [`TitleBarElement`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#titlebarelement), [`NavigationViewElement`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#navigationviewelement).

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nav` | [`NavigationHandle<TRoute>`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/navigation/NavigationHandle) |  | The navigation handle obtained from `UseNavigation`. |
| `routeToTag` | `Func<TRoute, string?>` |  | Maps a route to its NavigationViewItem tag. Return null for routes without a corresponding menu item, or [`NavigationViewElement.SettingsTag`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#navigationviewelement) for the built-in settings item. |
| `tagToRoute` | `Func<string, TRoute>` |  | Maps a NavigationViewItem tag back to a route for `OnSelectedTagChanged`. Never called with [`NavigationViewElement.SettingsTag`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#navigationviewelement) — that value is reserved and routed via `settingsRoute` instead, so an ordinary item must not carry it or it will select without navigating. |
| `settingsRoute` | `Func<TRoute>?` | `null` | Route to navigate to when the built-in settings item is selected. Null (the default) leaves settings selection unrouted. |

## `IsPaneOpen` [#ispaneopen]

```csharp
NavigationViewElement IsPaneOpen(this NavigationViewElement el, bool isPaneOpen, Action<bool> onPaneOpenChanged)
SplitViewElement IsPaneOpen(this SplitViewElement el, bool isPaneOpen, Action<bool> onPaneOpenChanged)
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `IsPaneOpen(NavigationViewElement, bool, Action<bool>)` | Controlled pane state: sets `IsPaneOpen` and wires the matching change handler in one call. The handler is required because the control opens and closes its own pane (light dismiss, adaptive display-mode changes on resize) — driving `IsPaneOpen` from state without feeding those changes back leaves the state stale, so the next toggle writes a value the control already holds and appears to do nothing (issue #916). Use the `IsPaneOpen` initializer directly only for a pane whose state the app never changes. |
| `IsPaneOpen(SplitViewElement, bool, Action<bool>)` | Controlled pane state: sets `IsPaneOpen` and wires the matching change handler in one call. The handler is required because the control closes its own pane (a light dismiss tap in `Overlay`/`CompactOverlay` mode) — driving `IsPaneOpen` from state without feeding those changes back leaves the state stale, so the next toggle writes a value the control already holds and appears to do nothing (issue #916). Use the `IsPaneOpen` initializer directly only for a pane whose state the app never changes. |

**Applies to:** [`NavigationViewElement`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/navigation#navigationviewelement), [`SplitViewElement`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/layout#splitviewelement).

**Parameters**

| --- | --- | --- |
| `isPaneOpen` | `bool` |  |
| `onPaneOpenChanged` | `Action<bool>` |  |

## `TransformOrigin` [#transformorigin]

Sets the pivot for `.Scale()` and `.Rotation()` as a fraction of the element's laid-out size: `(0.5f, 0.5f)` is the centre, `(0, 0)` the leading top corner. The pivot follows resizes and size animations, and `x` is flow-relative, so `0` is the right edge in a right-to-left layout. A `.CenterPoint()` on the same element is added as a pixel offset. Without this modifier the pivot is the `.CenterPoint()` value, or the leading top corner.

**Grow from the centre on hover:** `Border(card).TransformOrigin(0.5f, 0.5f).InteractionStates(s => s.PointerOver(scale: 1.05f))`

```csharp
T TransformOrigin<T>(this T el, float x, float y) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x` | `float` |  |
| `y` | `float` |  |

**Remarks**

Spec 066 §8. The pivot is an expression on the element's composition visual, so the modifier takes the visual (like the other transform modifiers). While `.LayoutAnimation()` animates the size, the pivot follows the animating size, not the final layout size.

## `ToolTipPlacement` [#tooltipplacement]

Sets `ToolTipService.Placement` — which side of the element the tooltip opens on. Pairs with either [`ToolTip`](#tooltip) or [`WithToolTip`](#withtooltip).

`PlacementMode` is the tooltip-specific enum and has exactly five members — `Top`, `Bottom`, `Left`, `Right`, `Mouse`. The edge-aligned placements (`TopEdgeAlignedLeft` and friends) live on the separate `FlyoutPlacementMode` enum and are not expressible for tooltips — use a flyout if you need them.


**Applies to:** any element.

## `FontSize` [#fontsize]

```csharp
RichTextBlockElement FontSize(this RichTextBlockElement el, double size)
RichTextHyperlink FontSize(this RichTextHyperlink link, double size)

RichTextRun FontSize(this RichTextRun run, double size)
TextBlockElement FontSize(this TextBlockElement el, double size)
T FontSize<T>(this T el, double size) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ElementExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `FontSize(RichTextBlockElement, double)` | Sets the root font size on a [`RichTextBlockElement`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/text#richtextblockelement).  This overload is required, not sugar. Without it `.FontSize(n)` on a `RichTextBlockElement` binds the generic `FontSize<T>` modifier, which routes through `ElementModifiers` — and `ApplyModifiers` writes FontSize only to a `Control` or a `TextBlock`. `RichTextBlock` is neither, so the call would compile and silently do nothing. Mirrors the sibling `FontFamily`/`FontWeight`/`FontStyle` overloads, which set the record property and reach the control through the generated descriptor's auto-map. |
| `FontSize(RichTextHyperlink, double)` |  |
| `FontSize(RichTextParagraph, double)` |  |

# Modifiers: Validation
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/validation

Modifiers are extension methods that return a changed copy of the element, so you can chain them.

**Learn more:** [Forms and Input](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/forms)

## `Immediate` [#immediate]

Requests that the control commit its value on every keystroke instead of on blur. Has no effect on controls whose default already fires per-keystroke (TextBox, PasswordBox, AutoSuggestBox, etc.).

```csharp
T Immediate<T>(this T el) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ImmediateExtensions`.

**Applies to:** any element.

Configures custom styling to apply when the field has an error. The configure action receives the element builder and can set any modifier.

## `Validate` [#validate]

```csharp
T Validate<T>(this T el, string fieldName, params IValidator[] validators) where T : Element
T Validate<T>(this T el, string fieldName, object? value, params IValidator[] validators) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ValidateExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Validate<T>(T, string, IValidator[])` | Attaches validators to this element. The element's value will be validated against the provided validators, with results pushed to the nearest ValidationContext. |
| `Validate<T>(T, string, object?, IValidator[])` | Attaches validators to this element along with the current field value, and — when called from inside a component's `Render()` — runs them immediately against the enclosing [`ValidationContext`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext).  Running during render rather than during reconcile is what makes the results readable by the same `Render()` that produced them, so `When(ctx.IsTouched(f) && ctx.HasError(f), …)` placed after this call sees the current verdict instead of the previous pass's.  The validators are still attached, so `FormField` keeps working for elements built outside a render pass. Re-running them is harmless: results are applied with a structural diff. The visualizers only \*display\* what a context already holds — they never run attached validators — so an element that reaches neither a render pass nor a `FormField` contributes no verdict. |

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fieldName` | `string` | Field name for validation messages. |
| `validators` | [`IValidator[]`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/IValidator) | One or more validators to apply. |
| `value` | `object?` |  |

## `ValidateAsync` [#validateasync]

```csharp
T ValidateAsync<T>(this T el, string fieldName, params IAsyncValidator[] asyncValidators) where T : Element
T ValidateAsync<T>(this T el, string fieldName, object? value, params IAsyncValidator[] asyncValidators) where T : Element
```

Declared in `ValidateExtensions`.

| Overload | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `ValidateAsync<T>(T, string, IAsyncValidator[])` | Attaches async validators to this element (in addition to any sync validators). |
| `ValidateAsync<T>(T, string, object?, IAsyncValidator[])` | Attaches async validators to this element along with the current field value, and registers the field so `MarkAllTouched()` covers it.  This overload is **attach-only**: it does not run the validators. Nothing consumes [`ValidationAttached.AsyncValidators`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/attached#asyncvalidators) automatically — not the render scope, which must stay synchronous, and not `FormField`. Run them yourself from an effect via [`ValidationReconciler.ValidateFieldAsync`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationReconciler#validatefieldasync), which carries the generation guard that discards a result superseded by a newer value.  Registration happens here for an element built during a render, and again when `FormField` mounts or updates it, which is the only chance an element assembled outside a render pass gets. |

**Applies to:** any element.

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fieldName` | `string` |  |
| `asyncValidators` | [`IAsyncValidator[]`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/IAsyncValidator) |  |
| `value` | `object?` |  |

## `NavigationDiagnostics` [#navigationdiagnostics]

Diagnostic events for the navigation system. Subscribe to these events to observe navigation operations for debugging and telemetry. All events fire synchronously on the UI thread.

Each event also emits to the `Microsoft-UI-Reactor` ETW provider under the `Keywords.Navigation` keyword (spec 044 §4.2). Use `dotnet-trace`/`PerfView` for capture in Release; the in-process [`ReactorTrace.Subscribe`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/diagnostics/ReactorTrace#subscribe) helper exposes the same stream programmatically.

PII: ETW payloads carry only the destination route's type name (a developer-authored identifier), the navigation mode, and structural values like cache reasons. Concrete route instances, deep-link paths, and any user-controllable strings are intentionally omitted per §6.2.1.

```csharp
public static class NavigationDiagnostics
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Navigation`.

# NavigationHandle<TRoute>
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/navigation/NavigationHandle

```csharp
public sealed class NavigationHandle<TRoute> where TRoute : notnull
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Navigation`.

**Learn more:** [Navigation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/navigation)

## Remarks [#remarks]

**Thread safety (issue #234).** The mutating methods ([`NavigationHandle.Navigate`](#navigate), [`NavigationHandle.GoBack`](#goback), [`NavigationHandle.GoForward`](#goforward), [`NavigationHandle.Replace`](#replace), [`NavigationHandle.Reset`](#reset), [`NavigationHandle.PopTo`](#popto), [`NavigationHandle.SetState`](#setstate)) are thread-safe by default. When called from the UI thread the cost is a single thread-id compare. When called off-thread (e.g. from `Task.Run` or after `await … ConfigureAwait(false)`) the whole mutation — stack edit, [`NavigationHandle.Navigated`](#navigated)/`RouteChanged` events, and the component re-render — is auto-marshaled onto the captured UI dispatcher, mirroring the `UseState`/`UseReducer` contract from issue #212. An off-thread call throws [`InvalidOperationException`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.invalidoperationexception) loudly — rather than corrupting the back/forward stacks — in two cases: when no UI dispatcher is available (unit-test / headless contexts), and when the captured dispatcher refuses the enqueue (its `TryEnqueue` returns `false`, e.g. once it has begun shutting down near window close). The bool-returning mutators return `true` when an off-thread call is accepted and scheduled; the actual guard/empty-stack outcome is then resolved on the UI thread. Off-thread callers must therefore not treat that `true` as confirmation that the navigation actually happened — only that it was scheduled. (On the UI thread the bool keeps its original meaning: whether the navigation succeeded.)

## Methods [#methods]

### `GetState` [#getstate]

Returns a snapshot of the full navigation state — back stack, current route, and forward stack — as a plain POCO. Persist it however you like (JSON, MessagePack, hand-rolled binary): Reactor intentionally does not pick a serialization format for you.

```csharp
public NavigationState<TRoute> GetState()
```

**Remarks**

For JSON persistence, declare a `JsonSerializerContext` covering [`NavigationState<TRoute>`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/navigation/NavigationState) and your route type so the call is AOT-safe. For polymorphic route hierarchies, annotate the base route type with `[JsonPolymorphic]` and `[JsonDerivedType]`.

### `GoBack` [#goback]

Go back to the previous route.

```csharp
public bool GoBack()
```

**Returns:** On the UI thread, `true` if navigation succeeded, or `false` if the back stack is empty or a guard cancelled it. When called off the UI thread, `true` means the call was marshaled and scheduled onto the UI dispatcher — not that it succeeded; the empty-stack/guard outcome is resolved later on the UI thread (see the type-level thread-safety remarks).

### `GoForward` [#goforward]

```csharp
public bool GoForward()
```

**Returns:** On the UI thread, `true` if navigation succeeded, or `false` if the forward stack is empty or a guard cancelled it. When called off the UI thread, `true` means the call was marshaled and scheduled onto the UI dispatcher — not that it succeeded; the empty-stack/guard outcome is resolved later on the UI thread (see the type-level thread-safety remarks).

#### `Slide` [#slide]

Slide transition. With no arguments this is WinUI's slide specification — vertical, 600 ms, exponential easing.

```csharp
public static NavigationTransition Slide(SlideDirection direction = SlideDirection.FromBottom, TimeSpan? duration = null, CompositionEasingFunction? easing = null, float? distance = null)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `direction` | [`SlideDirection`](#slidedirection) | `SlideDirection.FromBottom` |  |
| `duration` | `TimeSpan?` | `null` |  |
| `easing` | `CompositionEasingFunction?` | `null` |  |
| `distance` | `float?` | `null` |  |

**Remarks**

Supplying `duration`, `easing`, or `distance` switches to Reactor's customizable simultaneous slide, which is a structurally different animation — not the WinUI slide with one value changed. [`SlideDirection.FromTop`](#values) is Reactor-only and always takes that path. Note the default direction is [`SlideDirection.FromBottom`](#values); pass [`SlideDirection.FromRight`](#values) explicitly for a horizontal push.

#### `Spring` [#spring]

Spring-physics slide transition. A Reactor extension with no WinUI counterpart, so it keeps a horizontal default rather than following [`NavigationTransition.Slide`](#slide)'s vertical one.

```csharp
public static NavigationTransition Spring(float dampingRatio = 0.6f, float period = 0.08f, SlideDirection direction = SlideDirection.FromRight)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `dampingRatio` | `float` | `0.6f` |  |
| `period` | `float` | `0.08f` |  |
| `direction` | [`SlideDirection`](#slidedirection) | `SlideDirection.FromRight` |  |

### Fields [#fields]

#### `Default` [#default]

The transition a host or navigation gets when it doesn't ask for one. Currently resolves to [`NavigationTransition.Entrance`](#entrance), which is what WinUI's `Frame` plays when `Navigate` is called with no `NavigationTransitionInfo`.

```csharp
public static readonly NavigationTransition Default
```

**Remarks**

This is a policy alias, not a motion — it means "whatever Reactor defaults to". Use [`NavigationTransition.Entrance`](#entrance) when you want the entrance motion specifically and don't want the call site to silently follow a future change of default.

# BackdropChoice
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/theming/BackdropChoice

Tagged value stored in [`ElementModifiers.Backdrop`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/ElementModifiers#backdrop). Holds either a [`BackdropKind`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/theming/enums#backdropkind) selector (the common case, materialized by the host into a built-in WinUI backdrop) or a custom factory delegate (escape hatch for tinted Mica or third-party [`SystemBackdrop`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.media.systembackdrop) subclasses) — never both, never neither. The "exactly one set" invariant is enforced by the private constructor; construct via [`BackdropChoice.Of`](#ofbackdropkind) or [`BackdropChoice.Of`](#offuncsystembackdrop).

```csharp
public sealed record BackdropChoice
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core`.

**Learn more:** [Styling and Theming](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/styling)

## Remarks [#remarks]

Equality is value-based on [`BackdropChoice.Kind`](#kind) and reference-based on [`BackdropChoice.Factory`](#factory) — matching the change-detection in `BackdropApplier`, which uses `ReferenceEquals` on the factory. Two factory choices compare equal only if they hold the same delegate instance; callers who want stable identity across re-renders should hold the factory in a captured local or a hook state cell.

## Properties [#properties]

### `Factory` [#factory]

Custom factory; null when this choice carries a kind selector.

```csharp
public Func<SystemBackdrop?>? Factory  // get
```

### `Kind` [#kind]

The kind selector, or null when this choice carries a factory.

```csharp

```

# BrushHelper
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/theming/BrushHelper

Color and brush parsing utilities. Supports named colors, hex (#RRGGBB, #AARRGGBB), and direct Color values. Parsed colors are cached by string (an immutable value type, safe to share), but a fresh [`SolidColorBrush`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.media.solidcolorbrush) is created per call: a brush is a DependencyObject with thread affinity and mutable Color/Opacity, so a single instance cannot be safely shared across controls.

```csharp
public static class BrushHelper
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor`.

**Learn more:** [Styling and Theming](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/styling)

## Methods [#methods]

### `Parse` [#parse]

Parses a color string into a fresh [`SolidColorBrush`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.media.solidcolorbrush) owned by the caller. Supports named colors (red, green, blue, white, black, gray, lightgray, transparent) and hex codes (#RRGGBB or #AARRGGBB). The parsed color is cached, but a new brush instance is returned on every call, so callers may safely mutate it and a brush is never shared between controls. Any other string silently yields a gray brush; the REACTOR_DYM_006 analyzer flags constant strings that do.

```csharp
public static SolidColorBrush Parse(string color)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `color` | `string` |  |

# Enums
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/theming/enums

**Learn more:** [Styling and Theming](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/styling)

## `BackdropKind` [#backdropkind]

Declarative selector for the WinUI [`SystemBackdrop`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.media.systembackdrop) applied to a Reactor-hosted [`Window`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.window). Set via the [`Backdrop`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/modifiers/appearance#backdrop) modifier on a Reactor root tree.

```csharp
public enum BackdropKind
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core`.

### Remarks [#remarks]

Spec 033 §6. Mica/Acrylic backdrops are a Windows 11 (build 22000+) feature. On Windows 10 the WinUI [`Window.SystemBackdrop`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.window.systembackdrop) setter no-ops; we delegate to that behavior rather than reimplementing the fallback ladder.

### Values [#values]

| Name | Value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `None` | `0` | No backdrop. Clears any previously-set backdrop on the host window. |
| `Mica` | `1` | Mica (window-tint material). Best for primary application surfaces on Win11. |
| `MicaAlt` | `2` | Mica (alt). The same material with a slightly different luminance/tint balance. |
| `DesktopAcrylic` | `3` | Desktop Acrylic (translucent blur). Best for transient surfaces — flyouts, dialogs. |
| `AcrylicThin` | `4` | Acrylic (thin variant). Subtler blur than [`BackdropKind.DesktopAcrylic`](#values). |
| `Transparent` | `5` | Transparent backdrop. Requires Windows App SDK support; unsupported platforms fall back to no backdrop. |

## `ColorScheme` [#colorscheme]

Represents a color scheme variant a component can adapt its rendering to.

Note that [`UseColorScheme`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hooks/UseColorScheme) reports the app-global theme and only ever returns [`ColorScheme.Light`](#values_1) or [`ColorScheme.Dark`](#values_1); [`ColorScheme.HighContrast`](#values_1) is produced solely by the [`ElementTheme.Default`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.elementtheme.default) mapping arm below. Use [`UseHighContrast`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hooks/UseHighContrast) to detect forced-colors mode.

```csharp
public enum ColorScheme
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core`.

### Values [#values_1]

| Name | Value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Light` | `0` | The standard light theme. |
| `Dark` | `1` | The standard dark theme. |
| `HighContrast` | `2` | Windows High Contrast mode is active. |

# ResourceBuilder
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/theming/ResourceBuilder

Fluent builder for per-control resource overrides (WinUI lightweight styling). Each `Set()` call registers a resource key override that will be injected into the control's [`FrameworkElement.Resources`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.frameworkelement.resources) dictionary at mount time.

Lightweight styling lets you override built-in control resources (e.g., `ButtonBackground`, `ButtonBackgroundPointerOver`) without replacing the entire control template. The control's [`VisualStateManager`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.visualstatemanager) continues to function normally, so hover/pressed/disabled states respect the overrides automatically.

**Example — brand-colored button:**

```csharp
Button("Submit").Resources(r => r
    .Set("ButtonBackground", "#0078D4")
    .Set("ButtonBackgroundPointerOver", "#106EBE")
    .Set("ButtonBackgroundPressed", "#005A9E")
    .Set("ButtonForeground", "#FFFFFF"))
```

```csharp
public sealed class ResourceBuilder
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Elements`.

**Learn more:** [Styling and Theming](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/styling)

## Methods [#methods]

### `NotifyResourcesChanged` [#notifyresourceschanged]

Tells Reactor that application resources were edited at runtime, so theme references resolve again and every live host re-renders with the new values.

```csharp
public static void NotifyResourcesChanged()
```

**Remarks**

Call it after changing `Application.Current.Resources` in a way that is *not* a theme change — replacing a brush in a `ThemeDictionaries` entry, merging or removing a brand dictionary, or an inspector's live resource edit. Reactor caches each resolved `(resource key, theme)` brush and only drops that cache when the effective theme or the system palette changes, so without this call such an edit is not seen. Not needed for a Light/Dark/high-contrast switch (`RequestedTheme`) or for mutating an existing brush's `Color`; both are already picked up.

What it does: clears the resolution cache behind [`ThemeRef`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/theming/ThemeRef), then asks every live [`ReactorHost`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hosting/ReactorHost) and [`ReactorHostControl`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/hosting/ReactorHostControl) for a full re-render that bypasses component memoization and the reconciler's skip of unchanged elements, so memoized and reused subtrees are refreshed too. That re-resolves `.Resources(...)` theme overrides, re-applies [`ThemeRef`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/theming/ThemeRef) modifiers such as `.Background(Theme.Accent)`, and re-runs any [`ThemeRef.Resolve`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/theming/ThemeRef#resolve) call in a `Render` method.

Callable from any thread; the re-renders are scheduled on each host's UI thread. Await a host's `WaitForIdleAsync()` to observe the result.

On a host's UI thread, a host that has no content yet re-renders inline, and its render can throw. Every other host is still notified; then the exception is rethrown (an [`AggregateException`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.aggregateexception) when several hosts threw).

## Methods [#methods]

### `Resolve` [#resolve]

Resolves a theme resource using an explicit isDark flag. Useful for resolving during Render() before controls are in the tree.

```csharp
public static Brush? Resolve(string resourceKey, bool isDark)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `resourceKey` | `string` |  |
| `isDark` | `bool` |  |

**Remarks**

The brush is the one a `{ThemeResource}` reference gets on an element in that theme, so either theme can be resolved whatever theme the app uses. WinUI does the lookup, so its rules apply, including the `Default` fallback. For a key WinUI cannot resolve for that theme (one an app dictionary defines only for some themes), Reactor reads the app's Light, Dark and Default theme dictionaries, then does a plain lookup, which uses the app's theme: a key defined only for the app's theme therefore resolves to that brush for the other theme too, and a key defined only for the other theme resolves to null for the app's theme. Returns null when the key is not found or is not a [`Brush`](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/windows-app-sdk/api/winrt/microsoft.ui.xaml.media.brush). Call it on the UI thread.

#### `HasValue` [#hasvalue]

True when a value overload of `.Validate()`/`.ValidateAsync()` supplied [`ValidationAttached.Value`](#value).

`null` is a legitimate value, so the property alone cannot distinguish "the field is empty" from "no value was ever attached". Without that distinction `FormField` validated `null` for the validator-only overload and reported a required-field error for a control that plainly had text in it.

### `MarkAllTouched` [#markalltouched]

Marks all registered fields as touched. Typically called on form submit.

Also records that a submit was attempted, which is what [`ShowWhen.AfterFirstSubmit`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/enums#values_1) waits for. The framework has no other notion of "submit": this is the call the guide tells you to make on a submit attempt, so tying the two together is what makes that policy reachable on a `FormField` at all — before this it could never show an error, behaving identically to [`ShowWhen.Never`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/enums#values_1) (issue #1262).

```csharp
public void MarkAllTouched()
```

### `NotifyValueChanged` [#notifyvaluechanged]

Notifies the context of a field value change. Clears external messages for the field, because a server-side verdict about the old value says nothing about the new one.

The clear is conditional on the value actually having moved. It used to be unconditional, which was survivable only while validation ran rarely: now that validators run on every render, an unconditional clear here would destroy any [`ValidationContext.AddExternal`](#addexternalstring-string-severity) message on the very next repaint, before the user could read it.

An async verdict is retired for the same reason, mirroring [`ValidationContext.ApplyValidation`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext). A field validated only through `.ValidateAsync(...)` never reaches that method, so without this an error computed for a value the user has already replaced would stay on screen, and a pass opened against the old value could still install its result afterwards.

```csharp
public void NotifyValueChanged(string field, object? value)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `field` | `string` |  |
| `value` | `object?` |  |

### `SetInitialValue` [#setinitialvalue]

Stores the initial value for a field. Called at field registration time.

The current value is seeded only the first time the field is seen. Re-seeding it on every call would rewind whatever the user has since typed — harmless while nothing watched the context, but with change notification it becomes a permanent repaint loop for the common `SetInitialValue(...)` + `NotifyValueChanged(...)` pair that components run on each render: the rewind and the re-notify would take turns forever. Use [`ValidationContext.Reset`](#reset) to deliberately return a field to its baseline.

```csharp
public void SetInitialValue(string field, object? value)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `field` | `string` |  |
| `value` | `object?` |  |

## Events [#events]

### `Changed` [#changed]

Raised after any mutation that actually changed observable state — a message appearing or disappearing, a field becoming touched, a reset.

`UseValidationContext()` subscribes to this so that mutating the context from an event handler (the canonical case being [`ValidationContext.MarkAllTouched`](#markalltouched) on a submit attempt) repaints the form. Without it, an invalid submit changes nothing the user can see.

Two rules keep this from driving a render loop. First, re-running the same validators over an unchanged value is silent: results are applied with a structural diff, so an idempotent re-validation raises nothing. Second, mutations made while a render is in flight are not announced *inline* — the rendering component reads the new state later in the same pass, and notifying there would re-enter the reconciler's re-render path from inside `Render()`. They are held and delivered once the pass finishes, so other subscribers — a parent rendering `IsValid()`, say — still hear about them; a pass that ends with the state it started with is dropped rather than delivered, since there is nothing to announce.

```csharp
public event Action? Changed
```

# ValidationReconciler
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationReconciler

```csharp
public static class ValidationReconciler
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Controls.Validation`.

**Learn more:** [Forms and Input](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/forms)

## Methods [#methods]

### `EvaluateRules` [#evaluaterules]

#### `EvaluateRules(ValidationContext, ValidationRuleElement[])` [#evaluaterulesvalidationcontext-validationruleelement]

Evaluates ValidationRuleElements and pushes their results to the context.

Each rule owns its own slot, identified by its field and the call site of its predicate, so re-running the same rules replaces each verdict rather than accumulating. Rules evaluated here are independent of each other and of any other caller using the same context.

Callers are independent of one another as long as their predicates differ, which they do for the ordinary lambda case — each call site compiles to its own method. Two callers that pass the same \*named method\* as the predicate, for the same field and position, share a slot; give those a `setId` instead.

This overload does not withdraw a rule that disappears from the list — nothing re-evaluates a rule that no longer exists. Use the [`ValidationReconciler.EvaluateRules`](#evaluaterulesvalidationcontext-string-validationruleelement) overload when a set shrinks or empties, or mount the rules in the element tree, where unmount retracts them.

```csharp
public static void EvaluateRules(ValidationContext ctx, params ValidationRuleElement[] rules)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ctx` | [`ValidationContext`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext) |  |
| `rules` | [`ValidationRuleElement[]`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/forms#validationruleelement) |  |

#### `EvaluateRules(ValidationContext, string, ValidationRuleElement[])` [#evaluaterulesvalidationcontext-string-validationruleelement]

Evaluates a named rule set: the call owns that set for the context, so a producer from the previous call under the same `setId` that is absent this time has its contribution withdrawn.

The identity is explicit because ownership is destructive. Two unrelated callers sharing one context must not silently retract each other's rules, which is what an implicit per-context set would do.

Each rule is keyed by its position within the set, so two rules stay independent even if they carry the same message, and re-running the set replaces each verdict rather than accumulating.

```csharp
public static void EvaluateRules(ValidationContext ctx, string setId, params ValidationRuleElement[] rules)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ctx` | [`ValidationContext`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext) |  |
| `setId` | `string` |  |
| `rules` | [`ValidationRuleElement[]`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/forms#validationruleelement) |  |

### `EvaluateRulesAsync` [#evaluaterulesasync]

#### `EvaluateRulesAsync(ValidationContext, ValidationRuleElement[])` [#evaluaterulesasyncvalidationcontext-validationruleelement]

The asynchronous counterpart to [`ValidationReconciler.EvaluateRules`](#evaluaterulesvalidationcontext-validationruleelement), for rules built by `ValidationRuleAsync`. Synchronous rules are evaluated normally.

Rules run in order rather than concurrently, so the resulting message order for a field is the order the rules were given in — `GetMessages` exposes that order and callers read the first message.

Each rule is ordered against itself by its own async generation, so two overlapping evaluations of the same rule cannot install out of order. Rules remain independent of each other. No lock is held across a caller's predicate.

```csharp
public static Task EvaluateRulesAsync(ValidationContext ctx, params ValidationRuleElement[] rules)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ctx` | [`ValidationContext`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext) |  |
| `rules` | [`ValidationRuleElement[]`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/forms#validationruleelement) |  |

#### `EvaluateRulesAsync(ValidationContext, string, ValidationRuleElement[])` [#evaluaterulesasyncvalidationcontext-string-validationruleelement]

The asynchronous counterpart to [`ValidationReconciler.EvaluateRules`](#evaluaterulesvalidationcontext-string-validationruleelement).

Every verdict is computed before any is installed, and nothing is installed if the set has been re-evaluated in the meantime, or if a field's value changed while a predicate was running — each rule opens a per-producer async generation before its predicate runs, and those are verified at the moment of application.

```csharp
public static Task EvaluateRulesAsync(ValidationContext ctx, string setId, params ValidationRuleElement[] rules)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ctx` | [`ValidationContext`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext) |  |
| `setId` | `string` |  |
| `rules` | [`ValidationRuleElement[]`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/elements/forms#validationruleelement) |  |

# ValidationRuleDsl
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationRuleDsl

```csharp
public static class ValidationRuleDsl
```

Namespace: `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Controls.Validation`.

**Learn more:** [Forms and Input](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/forms)

## Methods [#methods]

### `Evaluate` [#evaluate]

Evaluates the validation rule against a ValidationContext. Adds or clears messages based on the predicate result.

The result is applied as one diffed replacement rather than clear-then-add. `Mount/UpdateValidationRule` calls this during reconcile — after the component's render scope has closed — so with clear-then-add a failing rule raised [`ValidationContext.Changed`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext#changed) on every pass, each notification drove another render, and the reconciler tripped its re-render re-entrancy limit. Re-evaluating to the same verdict is now silent.

```csharp
public static void Evaluate(this ValidationRuleElement rule, ValidationContext ctx)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ctx` | [`ValidationContext`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext) |  |

### `EvaluateAsync` [#evaluateasync]

Evaluates the async validation rule against a ValidationContext.

The previous verdict is kept while the check is in flight and replaced once, at the end. Clearing first would raise [`ValidationContext.Changed`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext#changed) twice per evaluation for an already-failing rule, and would briefly report the field as valid in between.

Overlapping evaluations are ordered by a generation token taken before the predicate is awaited. Without it, a slow failing check started first could resolve after a fast passing one and reinstate an error the newer run had already cleared.

```csharp
public static Task EvaluateAsync(this ValidationRuleElement rule, ValidationContext ctx, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ctx` | [`ValidationContext`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/validation/ValidationContext) |  |  |
| `cancellationToken` | `CancellationToken` | `default` |  |

## Factories [#factories]

- [`ValidationRule`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/factories/forms#validationrule)
- [`ValidationRuleAsync`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/reference/factories/forms#validationruleasync)

![The Reactor inner dev loop. 1 Create, with project templates and mur --create. 2 Edit live, with dotnet watch, hot reload, and live preview. 3 Inspect, with devtools. 4 Catch mistakes early, with analyzers and mur check. 5 Debug and measure, with diagnostics. An arrow labeled next change goes back to Edit live. In the center, Work with AI agents has dashed arrows to each stage.](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/dev-tooling/inner-loop.svg)

## Create a project [#create-a-project]

Start from a project template. `winapp new -t reactor -n MyApp` creates a
packaged app with the `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` package already referenced.
[Install Reactor](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/install) lists every template and the `dotnet new`
commands.

If you work inside a clone of the Reactor repository, `mur --create MyApp`
writes a minimal project (`Program.cs`, a `.csproj`, a `.sln`, and an app
icon) that references the Reactor source instead of the package. See
[mur CLI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/mur-cli#create-a-project).

To try an idea quickly, you do not need a component class. `ReactorApp.Run`
also takes an inline function component:

```csharp
// Alternative: inline function component, no class needed
// ReactorApp.Run("Quick Test", ctx =>
// {
//     var (n, setN) = ctx.UseState(0);
//     return VStack(12,
//         TextBlock($"Count: {n}").FontSize(20),
//         Button("+1", () => setN(n + 1))
//     ).Padding(24);
// });
```

## Edit live [#edit-live]

Run the app under `dotnet watch`. When you save a file, .NET hot reload
applies the edit to the running process and Reactor re-renders every
component. Hook state stays: a counter keeps its value while you change the
layout around it. If an edit can't be applied in place, `dotnet watch`
restarts the app.

The Visual Studio extension and the VS Code extension run the same loop and
show the live app next to your code.

- [Hot reload and live preview](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/hot-reload): what survives a reload, rude
  edits, and limits.
- [Visual Studio and VS Code extensions](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/vs-extension): install and use the
  live preview.

## Inspect the running app [#inspect-the-running-app]

Devtools let you look inside a running Debug build. Add the
`Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools` package, then launch the app with
`--devtools app` for the in-app dev menu, or `--devtools run` to also start a
local MCP server. With the MCP server running, `mur devtools` can take
screenshots, read the visual tree and hook state, and click or type into the
app from a terminal.

Your own debug-only UI can check the same gate. `UseDevtools()` returns `true`
only when devtools are on for this session:

```csharp
static class DevGate
{
    // UseDevtools() is a RenderContext extension, so it is reached from a
    // function component's ctx (or any helper you hand the ctx to) — there is
    // no Component-level forwarder. It returns true only when BOTH the
    // Reactor.DevtoolsSupport build switch and `--devtools app` (or `run`) are set.
    //
    // UseDevtools() uses no hook slot, but it is still a Use* call:
    // REACTOR_HOOKS_005 only permits Use* calls from Render() or a Use*-named
    // method, so a helper called `Shell` here would warn.
    public static Element UseShell(RenderContext ctx)
    {
        var dev = ctx.UseDevtools();

        return VStack(8,
            MainContent(),
            dev ? DebugOverlay() : Empty()
        );
    }

    private static Element MainContent() => TextBlock("App content");

    // Only *constructed* when dev is true. In retail the ternary costs one
    // bool read plus one branch — no element tree, no children reconciled.
    private static Element DebugOverlay() =>
        TextBlock("debug overlay").Opacity(0.6);
}
```

Read [Devtools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools) for setup, the dev menu, overlays, the MCP
server, and how devtools stay out of Release and AOT builds.

## Catch mistakes early [#catch-mistakes-early]

Reactor's Roslyn analyzers ship inside the `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` package.
They report `REACTOR_*` diagnostics in the editor and in `dotnet build`, and
many come with a code fix. For example, `REACTOR_HOOKS_001` flags a hook
inside an `if`. The fix keeps the hook call unconditional and moves the
condition into the output:

```csharp
class HookOrderGood : Component
{
    public bool ShouldCount;

    public override Element Render()
    {
        // Hook always runs; the conditional moves into the render output.
        var (count, _) = UseState(0);
        return ShouldCount
            ? TextBlock($"Count: {count}")
            : TextBlock("No counter.");
    }
}
```

`mur check` runs the same build and adds a hint under each diagnostic.

- [Analyzers](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/analyzers): every rule ID, its severity, and the code fixes.
- [Rules of Reactor](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/rules-of-reactor): the rules behind the most common
  diagnostics.

## Work with AI agents [#work-with-ai-agents]

AI coding agents can do every stage of this loop. The Reactor agent plugin and
the skill kit teach an agent the DSL, the hooks rules, and the tools on this
page. `mur check` gives the agent build feedback with fix hints, and
`mur devtools` lets it see and drive the running app. The docs site also
publishes `llms.txt` and a Markdown copy of each page.

Read [Build with AI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/build-with-ai) for install steps for each agent.

## Debug and measure [#debug-and-measure]

In Release builds, Reactor reports swallowed exceptions and failed HRESULTs
through the `Microsoft-UI-Reactor` EventSource. Capture them with environment
variables, `dotnet-trace`, the Visual Studio profiler, or in process. During a
devtools session, the `logs` tool returns the same events next to stdout and
debug output.

- [Diagnostics](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/diagnostics): capture and read Reactor's events and traces.
- [Performance](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/performance): find and fix slow renders.
- [Testing](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/testing): unit tests and UI tests for components.

## How it works [#how-it-works]

These pages explain the machinery behind the tools. You do not need them to
use the tools.

- [Devtools internals](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/devtools-internals): the MCP server, tree walker, and
  selectors.
- [Analyzer architecture](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/analyzer-architecture): how the analyzers and
  code fixes are built.
- [Source mapping](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/source-mapping): how a control maps back to the line of
  code that created it.
- [Perf instrumentation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/perf-instrumentation): the EventSource, keywords,
  and counters.

## Tips [#tips]

- Keep `dotnet watch` running in its own terminal. Its output tells you when an
  edit was applied and when the app restarted.
- Build small components. A small `Render()` is quick to re-render and easy to
  inspect.
- Treat analyzer warnings as bugs. Most of them point at a real runtime
  problem, such as lost state or a missed update.
- On an ARM64 machine, pass the runtime explicitly if `dotnet run` picks the
  wrong one: `dotnet run -r win-arm64`.

# Analyzers
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/analyzers

You don't install anything extra. The analyzers are inside the
`Microsoft.UI.Reactor` NuGet package, in its `analyzers/dotnet/cs` folder,
so every project that references the package runs them.

## Where the warnings show up [#where-the-warnings-show-up]

![Your code is checked by the REACTOR analyzers. The results show up in three places: the editor, the dotnet build output, and mur check.](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/analyzers/two-surfaces.svg)

- **In the editor.** Visual Studio and VS Code with the C# extension show
  a squiggle while you type. Press `Ctrl+.` on the squiggle to see the code
  fix, if the rule has one.
- **In the build.** `dotnet build` and CI print the same warnings and
  errors.
- **In `mur check`.** It runs the build and prints each diagnostic on one
  line, with a hint on how to fix it. See [`mur check`](#mur-check).
