## Change the severity [#change-the-severity]

Set the severity of one rule in an `.editorconfig` file at the root of your
project or solution:

```ini
[*.cs]
# Fail the build when a hook is called conditionally.
dotnet_diagnostic.REACTOR_HOOKS_001.severity = error

# Turn off one rule.
dotnet_diagnostic.REACTOR_DSL_004.severity = none

# Raise every rule in one category.
dotnet_analyzer_diagnostic.category-Reactor.Hooks.severity = error
```

The values are `error`, `warning`, `suggestion`, `silent`, and `none`. The
category names are in the [table](#all-rules).

To turn off a rule for one line, wrap the line in
`#pragma warning disable REACTOR_DSL_004` and
`#pragma warning restore REACTOR_DSL_004`. To make every warning fail the
build, set `<TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>` in the
project file.

## Examples [#examples]

Each example shows code that a rule flags, and the code that fixes it.
[Rules of Reactor](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/rules-of-reactor) explains why these rules exist.

**Hooks must run on every render.** This code calls `UseState` only when
`ShouldCount` is true, so `REACTOR_HOOKS_001` fires:

```csharp
// Wrong: REACTOR_HOOKS_001
if (ShouldCount)
{
    var (count, _) = UseState(0);
    return TextBlock($"Count: {count}");
}
return TextBlock("No counter.");
```

Call the hook every time, and move the condition into the output:

```csharp
class HookOrderGood : Component
{
    public bool ShouldCount;

    public override Element Render()
    {
        // Hook always runs; the conditional moves into the render output.
        var (count, _) = UseState(0);
        return ShouldCount
            ? TextBlock($"Count: {count}")
            : TextBlock("No counter.");
    }
}
```

**Items in a dynamic list need a key.** Without `.WithKey`, the reconciler
matches rows by position. `REACTOR_DSL_001` fires:

```csharp
// Wrong: REACTOR_DSL_001
Items.Select(i => TextBox(i.Title, title => Rename(i, title))).ToArray()
```

Key each row by a stable ID. The code fix adds the `.WithKey(...)` call:

```csharp
class TodoListGood : Component
{
    public TodoItem[] Items = System.Array.Empty<TodoItem>();

    public override Element Render() => VStack(4,
        Items.Select(i =>
            TextBox(i.Title, title => Rename(i, title), header: i.Id.ToString())
                .WithKey(i.Id.ToString())                  // stable identity
        ).ToArray()
    );

    void Rename(TodoItem item, string title)
    {
        var index = System.Array.IndexOf(Items, item);
        if (index >= 0)
            Items[index] = item with { Title = title };
    }
}
```

**Use theme tokens, not hard-coded colors.** A hex color does not follow
light, dark, or high-contrast themes. `REACTOR_THEME_001` fires and
suggests a token:

```csharp
// Wrong: REACTOR_THEME_001
Button("Save", () => { }).Background("#0078D4");
```

The code fix replaces the color with the token:

```csharp
// Do:
Button("Save", () => { }).Background(Theme.Accent);
```

## mur check [#mur-check]

[`mur check`](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/mur-cli#check-your-code) runs `dotnet build`, so it sees
every diagnostic the analyzers report. It does not run a second copy of the
rules. It changes how the results are shown:

- In the default mode, it prints errors and `REACTOR_` warnings. It hides
  info-level rules and most other warnings, including `REACTOR0050`, whose ID
  has no underscore. `--final` prints everything. `--strict` ranks every
  warning as an error, so all warnings print.
- For 11 rules it adds a pointer to the skill section that explains the fix:
  `REACTOR_HOOKS_001`, `REACTOR_HOOKS_004`, `REACTOR_HOOKS_005`,
  `REACTOR_HOOKS_006`, `REACTOR_HOOKS_009`, `REACTOR_THEME_001`,
  `REACTOR_THEME_002`, `REACTOR_A11Y_001`, `REACTOR_DSL_001`,
  `REACTOR_DOCK_001`, and `REACTOR_ITEMS_002`.
- For compiler errors such as `CS0103` and `CS1061`, it suggests the Reactor
  name you probably meant (`→ try: ...`). These suggestions cover mistakes
  that the analyzers can't see, because the code does not compile.
- It has seven rules of its own for common mistakes. One of them mirrors
  `REACTOR_DYM_006` and prints the hex value for an unknown color name.

The
[`mur check` design notes](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/reference/mur-check-did-you-mean.md)
describe each tier and rule.

## Rule reference [#rule-reference]

Each entry says what the rule catches and what to do instead. The anchor of
each entry is the rule ID in lower case, for example
`analyzers.md#reactor_hooks_001`.

### Hooks [#hooks]

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_001 [#reactor_hooks_001]

A hook is called inside an `if`, a loop, a `switch`, or a lambda. Reactor
matches hooks by call order, so the order must be the same on every render.
Call the hook every time and branch on its result.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_002 [#reactor_hooks_002]

A hook comes after an early `return`. On renders that return early, the
hooks below it are skipped and the order breaks. Move every hook above the
first `return`.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_003 [#reactor_hooks_003]

The `UseEffect` lambda is `async`, so it compiles as `async void`.
Exceptions escape, the cleanup does not wait for the work, and a setter can
run after the component unmounts. Move the async work into a method and
start it from a normal effect. The code fix does this.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_004 [#reactor_hooks_004]

A hook dependency is a new object, such as an array or a lambda, on every
render. It never equals the previous value, so the hook runs every time.
Wrap it in `UseMemo`, move it to a field, or pass a simple value instead.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_005 [#reactor_hooks_005]

A hook is called outside `Render` or a custom hook. Only call hooks from a
`Render` override or from a method whose name starts with `Use`.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_006 [#reactor_hooks_006]

A resource fetcher calls something that looks like a write. Resources run
again when their dependencies change, on retry, and on focus. Use
`UseMutation` for writes. See [Async resources](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/async-resources).

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_007 [#reactor_hooks_007]

The builder passed to `UseMemoCells`, `UseMemoCellsByKey`, or
`UseMemoCellsByIndex` uses a value that is not in its dependency list. The
cell does not update when that value changes. Add the value to the
dependencies.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_008 [#reactor_hooks_008]

A state variable is read right after its setter in the same handler. The
setter only schedules a new render, so the variable still has the old value.
Use the value you passed to the setter.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_009 [#reactor_hooks_009]

A `Command` sets `DebounceMs`, but it is not created with `UseCommand`. The
debounce state lives in that hook, so the command does not debounce. Create
it with `UseCommand(...)`. See [Commanding](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/commanding).

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_010 [#reactor_hooks_010]

An object or collection is changed in place, and the same instance is
passed back to its setter. The setter sees an equal value and does not
re-render. Pass a new instance, for example with a `with` expression or a
copy of the list.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_011 [#reactor_hooks_011]

An input such as a `TextBox` shows a value from state, but its change
callback is empty or ignores the new value. The user's edits are lost.
Update state in the callback, or make the control read-only.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_012 [#reactor_hooks_012]

A `Memo` dependency is a new object on every render, so the memo never
reuses its result. Make it stable with `UseMemo` or a field, or pass a
simple key.

#### REACTOR_HOOKS_013 [#reactor_hooks_013]

The initial value of `UseState` or `UsePersisted` allocates a new object on
every render, but the hook only reads it once. Wrap it in
`UseMemo(() => ..., [])`.

### State and context [#state-and-context]

#### REACTOR_STATE_001 [#reactor_state_001]

A component implements `INotifyPropertyChanged`. Reactor never listens to
it, so raising `PropertyChanged` does nothing. Keep state in `UseState`, or
use one of the observable bridges in [State management](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/data-system).

#### REACTOR_CTX_001 [#reactor_ctx_001]

A context value is a new object on every render, so every component that
reads the context re-renders. Wrap the value in `UseMemo`. See
[Context](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/context).

#### REACTOR_PERSIST_001 [#reactor_persist_001]

`UsePersisted` is called without a scope, so it uses
`PersistedScope.Application` and is shared by every window. Pass
`PersistedScope.Window` or `PersistedScope.Application` so the scope is
clear. See [Persistence](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/persistence).

### Lists and keys [#lists-and-keys]

#### REACTOR_DSL_001 [#reactor_dsl_001]

An item built in a dynamic list has no `.WithKey(...)`. The reconciler
matches rows by position, so an insert or a reorder re-creates the rows and
loses focus and state. Add a key from the item's ID.

#### REACTOR_DSL_002 [#reactor_dsl_002]

`.WithKey(...)` uses the list index, or a value such as `Guid.NewGuid()`
or `DateTime.Now`. These keys change when the list changes, so the rows are
re-created. Use the item's ID.

#### REACTOR_DSL_003 [#reactor_dsl_003]

A key selector, for example in a typed `ListView<T>`, ignores its item and
returns the same key for every item. Return a unique key for each item,
such as `item.Id`.

#### REACTOR_DSL_004 [#reactor_dsl_004]

The item implements `IReactorKeyed`, so `ForEach` already keys it. The
`.WithKey(...)` call repeats that key and can be removed.

#### REACTOR_ITEMS_001 [#reactor_items_001]

`.Set(...)` assigns `ItemsSource` on a collection element that Reactor
fills itself. This fights the keyed diff. Pass the data through the
element's `items` argument. See [Collections](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/collections).

#### REACTOR_ITEMS_002 [#reactor_items_002]

An `ItemsView` view builder returns something other than an
`ItemContainer`. `ItemsView` needs an `ItemContainer` root. The code fix
wraps the result in `ItemContainer(...)`.

#### REACTOR_MEMO_001 [#reactor_memo_001]

A modifier is applied to a keyed `Memo(key, factory)` wrapper. A wrapper
with modifiers can't use the cache that virtualized lists use when they
recycle rows. Move the modifiers inside the factory.

### Modifiers and .Set [#modifiers-and-set]

#### REACTOR_MOD_001 [#reactor_mod_001]

A placement modifier, such as `.Grid(...)` or `.Canvas(...)`, is applied
more than once in one chain. The last call replaces the earlier ones. Merge
them into one call.

#### REACTOR_MOD_002 [#reactor_mod_002]

`.Set(...)` writes a property that has a Reactor modifier. `.Set` runs on
every render and is never undone. Use the modifier instead.

#### REACTOR_MOD_003 [#reactor_mod_003]

The modifier does nothing on this control type. For example, `.Background`
has no effect on a `Rectangle`, because shapes use `.Fill`. Use the
modifier that the control supports.

#### REACTOR_PERF_001 [#reactor_perf_001]

`.Width(...)` and `.Height(...)` are chained on a built-in element. Each call
copies the element, so one `.Size(width: ..., height: ...)` call saves a copy.
The code fix makes the change and keeps the arguments in their original
order. This is a small allocation saving, not a bug. See
[Analyzer architecture](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/analyzer-architecture#combined-sizing-without-extra-copies).

#### REACTOR_POOL_001 [#reactor_pool_001]

`.Set(...)` writes a property that Reactor resets when it returns the
control to the pool. The value is lost on a later render. Use the matching
modifier. See [Element pooling](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/element-pool).

#### REACTOR_VIS_001 [#reactor_vis_001]

`.Set(c => c.Visibility = ...)` is not tracked, so the value is lost on the
next render or when the control is reused. Use `.IsVisible(bool)`.

#### REACTOR_EVENT_001 [#reactor_event_001]

An event is subscribed inside `.Set(...)`, which runs on every render and
adds a new handler each time. Use the event modifier if there is one.
Otherwise, subscribe in `.OnMountAdd(...)` and unsubscribe in
`.OnUnmountAdd(...)`.

### Controls and selection [#controls-and-selection]

#### REACTOR_CTRL_001 [#reactor_ctrl_001]

The control's selection is controlled by `SelectedIndex`, and
`.Set(x => x.SelectedItem = ...)` sets it a second way. The two fight.
Remove the `.Set(...)` call.

#### REACTOR_OPT_001 [#reactor_opt_001]

A selection property of type `Optional<T>` gets a sentinel value such as
`-1`. That forces the value on every render. Use `Optional<T>.Unset` to let
the control own the selection.

#### REACTOR_CMD_001 [#reactor_cmd_001]

An element sets both `Command` and its own callback, such as `OnClick`.
Reactor runs the callback, so the command never runs. Remove one of them.
See [Commanding](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/commanding).

#### REACTOR_PERF_FUNCREF [#reactor_perf_funcref]

A `new Command { ... }` is created in `Render` on every render. Wrap it in
`UseMemo(() => new Command { ... }, deps)` to keep one instance. The code
fix does this and works out the dependencies.

#### REACTOR_INPUT_001 [#reactor_input_001]

`.OnKeyDown` checks for a Ctrl or Alt shortcut. `.OnKeyDown` only runs while
the element has focus, so the shortcut doesn't work elsewhere. Register a
command with an accelerator instead. See
[Input and gestures](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/input-and-gestures).

#### REACTOR_INPUT_002 [#reactor_input_002]

A drop handler calls `TryGetFiles`, which can return network paths, device
paths, links, and virtual files from the drag source. Use
`TryGetSafeLocalFiles` to keep only safe local files.

### Theming [#theming]

#### REACTOR_THEME_001 [#reactor_theme_001]

A color is hard-coded, for example `"#0078D4"`. It does not change with the
light, dark, or high-contrast theme. Use a `Theme` token, such as
`Theme.Accent`. See [Theming tokens](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/theming-tokens).

#### REACTOR_THEME_002 [#reactor_theme_002]

`.Set(...)` writes a control property that also has a lightweight styling
resource key. The hover and pressed states keep their own colors. Set the
resource with `.Resources(r => r.Set(...))` instead.

#### REACTOR_THEME_003 [#reactor_theme_003]

`RequestedTheme` is set through `.Set(...)`. Use the
`.RequestedTheme(...)` modifier.

#### REACTOR_THEME_004 [#reactor_theme_004]

A brush, such as `new SolidColorBrush(Colors.White)`, is created inline. It
does not follow the theme. Use a `Theme` token.

### Accessibility [#accessibility]

#### REACTOR_A11Y_001 [#reactor_a11y_001]

A button shows only an icon or an element, not text. Screen readers can't
announce it. Add `.AutomationName("...")`. See
[Accessibility](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/accessibility).

#### REACTOR_A11Y_002 [#reactor_a11y_002]

An image has no accessible name. Add `.AutomationName("...")` as alt text,
or `.AccessibilityHidden()` if the image is only decoration.

#### REACTOR_A11Y_003 [#reactor_a11y_003]

A form field has no label. Add a `header:` argument, `.Header(...)`,
`.AutomationName(...)`, or `.LabeledBy(...)`.

#### REACTOR_A11Y_004 [#reactor_a11y_004]

A container has `.OnTapped(...)` but is not a tab stop, so keyboard users
can't reach it. Add `.IsTabStop(true)`, and handle Enter and Space in
`.OnKeyDown(...)`.

### Did you mean [#did-you-mean]

These rules catch names and arguments that are close to a real Reactor
API, usually typed by a person or an AI agent that guessed.

#### REACTOR_DYM_001 [#reactor_dym_001]

A Reactor property is called with parentheses, as if it were a method.
Remove the parentheses.

#### REACTOR_DYM_002 [#reactor_dym_002]

The `Theme` background token does not exist. The message names the token
you probably meant.

#### REACTOR_DYM_003 [#reactor_dym_003]

The name is not defined, but it is close to a Reactor factory name. The
message and the code fix suggest the factory.

#### REACTOR_DYM_004 [#reactor_dym_004]

A factory call is missing a required argument. The message shows the call
with the argument added.

#### REACTOR_DYM_005 [#reactor_dym_005]

A factory expects an element, but you passed a string. Wrap the string in a
text factory such as `TextBlock(...)`.

#### REACTOR_DYM_006 [#reactor_dym_006]

A color string, such as `"orange"`, is not a format Reactor can read, so the
color renders gray. The message suggests a hex value. Better still, use a
`Theme` token.

### Animation [#animation]

#### REACTOR_ANIM_002 [#reactor_anim_002]

The trigger passed to `.Keyframes(...)` changes on every render, so the
animation restarts each time and flickers. Pass a value that changes only
when you want to replay it, such as a counter in state. See
[Animation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/animation).

#### REACTOR_ANIM_003 [#reactor_anim_003]

An `async` lambda is passed to `WithAnimation`. Changes after the first
`await` are not animated. Use one `WithAnimation` call for each step, around
each `await`.

#### REACTOR_ANIM_004 [#reactor_anim_004]

`.Set(...)` or `.OnMount(...)` writes `Rotation`, `Scale`, `CenterPoint`,
`RotationAxis`, `TransformMatrix` or a `*Transition` property, or calls
`StartAnimation`, on an element whose modifiers already own its composition
visual, such as `.Scale(...)`, `.Rotation(...)` or `.Keyframes(...)`. WinUI
rejects the write. Use the matching modifier, such as `.Rotation(...)` or
`.OpacityTransition()`; the code fix rewrites the simple cases. The rule also
flags a `.Set` that writes `Translation` on an element that uses
`.Translation(...)`. See [Animation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/animation).

### Layout and media [#layout-and-media]

#### REACTOR_GRID_001 [#reactor_grid_001]

A `Grid` declares a row or column that no child is placed in. Remove the
track, or place a child in it. See [Layout](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/layout).

#### REACTOR_MEDIA_001 [#reactor_media_001]

A `WebView2` is a direct child of a stack and has no `.Width` and
`.Height`. It sizes itself to the page and keeps changing size. Set
`.Width` and `.Height`, or put it in a fixed-size grid cell.

### Lifecycle and threading [#lifecycle-and-threading]

#### REACTOR_LIFECYCLE_002 [#reactor_lifecycle_002]

A `UseEffect` creates a long-lived object, such as a timer or a
subscription, and returns no cleanup. It keeps running after the component
unmounts. Return a cleanup action that disposes it. See
[Effects](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/effects).

#### REACTOR_DIALOG_001 [#reactor_dialog_001]

`ContentDialog.ShowAsync()` opens a dialog outside the Reactor tree. Use the
`ContentDialog(...)` element with `IsOpen` instead. See
[Dialogs and flyouts](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/dialogs-and-flyouts).

#### REACTOR_NAV_001 [#reactor_nav_001]

A `UseNavigation` handle is stored in a static field or property. It
outlives the page and holds on to its dispatcher. Read it with
`UseNavigation<TRoute>()` where you need it, or pass it through context.

#### REACTOR_THREAD_001 [#reactor_thread_001]

A member that must run on the UI thread is called inside a background task.
Move the call back to the UI thread with
`ReactorApp.UIDispatcher?.TryEnqueue(...)`. See
[Threading and dispatch](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/threading-and-dispatch).

#### REACTOR_THREAD_002 [#reactor_thread_002]

`Render` or an effect blocks on a task, for example with `.Result` or
`.Wait()`. That freezes the UI. Use `UseResource`, or `await` inside an
effect.

### Advanced features [#advanced-features]

#### REACTOR_DOCK_001 [#reactor_dock_001]

`OnLiveLayoutChanged` passes the live dock layout straight into a setter.
The dock host already owns that layout, so writing it back breaks drag,
tab, and splitter behavior. Only read the layout in this callback. See
[Docking](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/docking).

#### REACTOR_ICON_001 [#reactor_icon_001]

A `WindowIcon` is passed to a surface that can't use its kind. For example,
the tray icon can't read a `FromResource` icon. The icon is dropped at run
time. The message names the kind to use instead.

#### REACTOR_WIN2D_001 [#reactor_win2d_001]

A Win2D canvas draws resources from `UseCanvasResources`, which live on the
shared device, but the canvas does not call `.UseSharedDevice()`.
This crashes at run time. Add `.UseSharedDevice()` to the canvas. See
[Win2D canvas](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/win2d-canvas).

### Custom controls [#custom-controls]

These rules apply when you write your own control descriptors or handlers.
See [Extending Reactor controls](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/extending-reactor-controls).

#### REACTOR0050 [#reactor0050]

A OneWay descriptor entry uses `Optional<T>` but has no `dp:` argument.
Without the dependency property, `Unset` skips the write instead of clearing
the value. Add `dp:`. This is the only rule with a help link today. It
points to
[spec 050](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/specs/050-controlled-prop-authority-and-optional-t.md).

#### REACTOR_DESC_001 [#reactor_desc_001]

The handler factory passed to `ControlRegistry.Register` is not a `static`
lambda. Mark it `static`, and move any captured state out, so trimming and
[Native AOT](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/native-aot) stay safe.

#### REACTOR_REF_001 [#reactor_ref_001]

`ElementRef.Current` is read to set a reference property. That value is a
snapshot, so it breaks when the target mounts late or unmounts. Declare the
reference through `descriptor.Reference` or `binding.Reference`.

#### REACTOR_LIFECYCLE_003 [#reactor_lifecycle_003]

A handler calls `Reconciler.UpdateChild`, which does not check that the
child's element type is the same, and does not unmount a control it
replaces. Call `Reconcile` and install its result when it differs from the
current control.

## How it works [#how-it-works]

[Analyzer architecture](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/analyzer-architecture) explains how the
analyzers are built, tested, and packed.

## Tips [#tips]

- Treat analyzer warnings as real bugs. Most of them point at code that
  compiles but behaves wrongly at run time.
- In CI, set `TreatWarningsAsErrors`, or run
  `mur check -- -p:TreatWarningsAsErrors=true`, so new warnings fail the
  build. `mur check --strict` shows every warning but keeps the build's exit
  code.
- Info-level rules don't fail a build. Run `mur check --final` before you
  merge to see them.
- If a rule is wrong for your code, turn it off for that line with
  `#pragma`, not for the whole project.

## Next Steps [#next-steps]

- **[Rules of Reactor](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/rules-of-reactor)**: the rules the analyzers enforce, and why
- **[mur CLI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/mur-cli)**: run `mur check` and its modes
- **[Analyzer architecture](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/analyzer-architecture)**: how the analyzers work inside
- **[Developer tools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools)**: where analyzers fit in the inner loop

# Build with AI
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/build-with-ai

- **Knowledge:** an agent plugin and a skill kit that teach the DSL, the hooks
  rules, and the tools.
- **Build feedback:** `mur check` prints each diagnostic on one line with a
  fix hint.
- **Eyes on the app:** `mur devtools` and its MCP server let an agent see and
  drive the running app.
- **Docs for AI tools:** the docs site publishes `llms.txt` and a Markdown
  copy of each page.

## The tools at a glance [#the-tools-at-a-glance]

| Tool | What it gives the agent | Where to get it |
|---|---|---|
| Agent plugin | The `reactor-dev` agent and 16 skills | `plugins/reactor` in the repository, or `agentkit/plugins/reactor/` in the `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` package |
| Skill kit | `SKILL.md`, the topic files in `skills/`, and `mur` | The `reactor-skill-kit-<version>.zip` release asset |
| `mur check` | Build output with fix hints | The [mur CLI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/mur-cli) |
| Devtools MCP server | A live view of the running app, and input | The `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools` package; see [Devtools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools) |
| Docs for AI tools | `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, and a Markdown copy of each page | The docs site |

## The agent plugin [#the-agent-plugin]

The plugin is in
[`plugins/reactor`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/tree/main/plugins/reactor).
It has a manifest for GitHub Copilot CLI (`plugin.json`) and one for Claude
Code (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`). It contains:

- **The `reactor-dev` agent.** It starts every new app with
  `dotnet new reactor`, drafts the component tree, writes the files, and then
  runs `mur check`.
- **16 skills.** The agent loads `reactor-getting-started` for most tasks. It
  loads a topic skill only when the task needs it, which keeps the context
  small.

| Skill | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `reactor-getting-started` | The mental model, hooks, common factories, gotchas, and project setup. Enough for most tasks. |
| `reactor-dsl` | The full index of public signatures, `reactor.api.txt`. |
| `reactor-build-and-check` | Building with `mur check` and fixing common diagnostics. |
| `reactor-devtools` | Driving a running app with `mur devtools`. |
| `reactor-recipes` | Single-file recipes to copy and adjust. |
| `reactor-design` | Windows 11 design rules: theme tokens, typography, accessibility. |
| `reactor-async` | `UseResource`, `UseMutation`, and `UseInfiniteResource`. |
| `reactor-forms` | `UseValidationContext`, validators, `FormField`, and masked input. |
| `reactor-navigation` | `UseNavigation`, `NavigationHost`, `NavigationView`, and `TabView`. |
| `reactor-input` | Gestures, pointer events, drag and drop, and focus. |
| `reactor-commanding` | `Command`, `UseCommand`, and keyboard shortcuts. |
| `reactor-charts` | Charts and data visualization. |
| `reactor-windowing` | Top-level windows, placement, and file pickers. |
| `reactor-docking` | `DockManager` and dockable tool windows. |
| `reactor-wrapping` | Wrapping any WinUI control with `[GenerateReactorWrapper]`. |
| `reactor-advanced` | The Win2D canvases in `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Advanced`. |

Install the plugin in your agent:

**GitHub Copilot CLI**

Copilot CLI can install a plugin from a folder in a GitHub repository:

```shell
copilot plugin install microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor:plugins/reactor
```

Run `copilot plugin list` to check that it is installed. To load the plugin
from a local folder instead, start Copilot CLI with `--plugin-dir`:

```shell
copilot --plugin-dir <repo>\plugins\reactor
```

**Claude Code**

Pass the plugin folder with `--plugin-dir`. Claude Code loads it for that
session:

```shell
claude --plugin-dir <repo>\plugins\reactor
```

In a clone of the repository, `bootstrap.ps1` also places the plugin at
`~/.claude/plugins/reactor`. It uses a symbolic link when it can, so edits in
the clone show up at once. Otherwise it copies the folder. `mur upgrade`
refreshes the copy, and `mur doctor` reports whether the plugin is there. Pass
`-SkipPlugin` to `bootstrap.ps1` to skip this step.

**From the NuGet package**

You don't need a clone. The `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` package carries the plugin.
After a restore, it is in the NuGet cache:

```text
%USERPROFILE%\.nuget\packages\microsoft.ui.reactor\<version>\agentkit\plugins\reactor
```

Pass that folder to `--plugin-dir`. The plugin then matches the Reactor
version your app uses.

### Other agents [#other-agents]

The repository has no install steps for other agents. Point the agent at the
`plugins/reactor` folder, or at the single-file skill described in the next
section.

## The skill kit [#the-skill-kit]

The skill kit is for agents that can't load plugins. It contains:

- `SKILL.md`, one file with the Reactor essentials;
- `skills/`, topic files for design, async data, forms, input, and more,
  plus `reactor.api.txt`, the index of every public signature;
- `mur` builds for x64 and Arm64.

1. **Download the kit**

    Get `reactor-skill-kit-<version>.zip` from the
    [releases page](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/releases)
    and extract it.

2. **Run the install script**

    Run it from the extracted folder:

    ```powershell
    cd reactor
    .\install-skill-kit.ps1
    ```

    The script copies the kit to `~/.claude/skills/reactor` and adds the
    matching `bin\<arch>` folder to your user `PATH`. Pass `-Path <folder>` to
    install somewhere else, or `-SkipPath` to leave `PATH` alone. `mur` needs
    the .NET 10 runtime. The script warns you if it is missing.

The same files ship in the `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` package under `agentkit/`.
If `mur` is on your `PATH`, these commands print them:

```shell
mur --skill
mur --api
```

## Build feedback with mur check [#build-feedback-with-mur-check]

`mur check` runs `dotnet build` and returns the same exit code. It prints each
diagnostic on one line. For some `REACTOR_*` rules, it adds the skill to read
and a `→ try:` line with a fix to use as-is. That makes it a better build
command for an agent than raw MSBuild output.

```shell
mur check MyApp.csproj
mur check --final MyApp.csproj
```

The default mode hides low-value warnings while the agent iterates. Run
`--final` before you finish, to see every warning. See
[Analyzers](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/analyzers#mur-check) for how the hints map to the analyzer
rules, and the [mur CLI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/mur-cli#check-your-code) page for every option.

## Let the agent see the app [#let-the-agent-see-the-app]

`mur devtools` builds the app and starts it with an MCP server inside. From
another terminal, an agent can read the visual tree and hook state, take
screenshots, and click, type, and scroll:

```shell
mur devtools
mur devtools tree --view summary
mur devtools screenshot --out shot.png
mur devtools click "#save"
```

The `reactor-devtools` skill teaches these commands, so an agent with the
plugin can use them without more setup.

You can also connect an MCP client directly. `mur devtools --print-config`
prints config for Claude Code, VS Code (`.vscode/mcp.json`), and GitHub
Copilot. That config does not include the bearer token yet, so read
[Connect an MCP client](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools#connect-an-mcp-client) first. The
token-free option is the stdio transport, where the MCP client starts the app
itself with `--devtools run --mcp-transport stdio`.

This is the only MCP server in Reactor. It describes the running app, not your
source code.

## Docs for AI tools [#docs-for-ai-tools]

The [docs site](https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/) is built
with Blume, which writes these files for each docs version:

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `llms.txt` | A list of every page, with a link and a one-line summary |
| `llms-full.txt` | The full text of every page in one file |
| `<page URL>.md` | A Markdown copy of one page. Add `.md` to the page URL. |
| `skill.md` | A short skill that tells an agent to read these docs |
| `.well-known/agent-skills/index.json` | An index that points agents at that skill |

The paths are relative to the root of a docs version, for example
`https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/latest/` for the latest
release or `https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/` for the
main branch. Give an agent `llms.txt` when it should find the right page
itself. Give it one page's `.md` copy when you know which page it needs.

## Good prompts [#good-prompts]

The skills teach a set of habits. A prompt that asks for them gets better
results:

- **Start from the template.** Ask for `dotnet new reactor`. The agent skill
  warns that hand-written project files lead to invented API names.
- **Ask for `mur check` after each batch of edits,** and for every `REACTOR_*`
  warning to be fixed. Ask for `mur check --final` at the end.
- **Ask the agent to look at the app.** A screenshot and the visual tree from
  `mur devtools` show layout and contrast bugs that a build can't.
- **Name the feature.** Words like "form validation", "navigation", or
  "docking" match a topic skill, so the agent loads the right one.

**Create a Reactor app named Notes with `dotnet new reactor`. Show a list of notes and a form to add one, with validation. Run `mur check` after each batch of edits and fix every REACTOR_* warning.**

> Create a Reactor app named Notes with `dotnet new reactor`. Show a list of
> notes and a form to add one, with validation. Run `mur check` after each batch
> of edits and fix every REACTOR_* warning.

**The Save button is cut off. Start the app with `mur devtools`, take a screenshot, read the visual tree, and fix the layout.**

> The Save button is cut off. Start the app with `mur devtools`, take a
> screenshot, read the visual tree, and fix the layout.

# Devtools
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools

There are two parts. The in-app dev menu adds a
button to your window with debug overlays and your own debug commands. The MCP
server lets `mur devtools` and AI agents read the visual tree and hook state,
take screenshots, and click or type into the app.

## Launch modes [#launch-modes]

Devtools stay off until you start the app with a `--devtools` argument. With
`dotnet run`, put it after `--`:

```
dotnet run -- --devtools app
```

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| none | A normal run. `UseDevtools()` returns `false`, and the dev menu renders nothing. |
| `--devtools app` | Turns on the dev menu, the overlays, and `UseDevtools()`. No MCP server. |
| `--devtools run [Component]` | Everything in `app`, plus the MCP server and log capture. Pass a component name to open that component instead of the app's root. `--devtools` with no verb means `run`. |
| `--devtools list [file]` | Prints the names of the app's components and exits. With a file name, it also writes the list to that file. |
| `--devtools screenshot [Component] --out shot.png` | Opens one component, saves a PNG of the window, and exits. `--out` is required. |

`--preview` is an old name for `--devtools run`. It still works, but prints a
warning.

## Set up devtools [#set-up-devtools]

Devtools need two things at build time: the package and a build switch.

1. Add the package. Reference it in Debug builds only, so a Release build
   doesn't include it:

   ```xml
   <ItemGroup Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Debug'">
     <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools" Version="0.1.0-preview.18" />
   </ItemGroup>
   ```

2. Check the build switch. `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport` decides if the devtools
   code is kept in the build. In a Debug build, the `Microsoft.UI.Reactor`
   package turns it on for you. In every other configuration it is off, and
   the trimmer removes the devtools code. To set it yourself, add it to the
   project:

   ```xml
   <ItemGroup Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Debug'">
     <RuntimeHostConfigurationOption Include="Reactor.DevtoolsSupport" Value="true" Trim="true" />
   </ItemGroup>
   ```

Then start the app with a `--devtools` argument. The build gives the app the
ability to run devtools. The argument turns them on for one session.

![How devtools turn on. The build switch Reactor.DevtoolsSupport, on by default in Debug builds, and the Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools package reference are both needed. Then the launch flag decides: --devtools app gives the in-app dev menu and overlays; --devtools run also starts the MCP server on 127.0.0.1, which mur devtools and agents can attach to; no flag gives a normal run. In a Release or Native AOT build of the same project, the switch defaults to false, so the trimmer removes the devtools code.](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/devtools/opt-in.svg)

If the switch or the package is missing and you pass a `--devtools` argument,
the app does not open a window. It prints a message that shows the
`RuntimeHostConfigurationOption` line above, then exits with code 2.

If the versions of `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` and `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools`
don't match, the app prints both versions and stops. This usually means NuGet
restored an old local package. Run `mur pack-local`, delete the app's `bin`
and `obj` folders, and build again.

You can also turn the switch on or off for one build from the command line.
`-p:ReactorDiagnostics=true` turns it on, even in Release. It also turns on
[source mapping](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/source-mapping). `-p:ReactorDiagnostics=false` turns it
off, even in Debug. Don't ship a build made with `ReactorDiagnostics=true`.

## In-app dev menu [#in-app-dev-menu]

The dev menu is a small amber button with a flyout. Put it in your title bar
or toolbar with `DevtoolsMenu(...)`. When devtools are off, `DevtoolsMenu`
returns an empty element and never calls your item list.

First, declare your debug flags. `Observable<T>` is a small value cell that
components can watch. Make the flags `static readonly`, so every component
shares one instance:

```csharp
// Observable<T> is the lightweight INPC cell that backs dev-only flags.
// Declare them as static readonly so every component shares one instance.
public static class AppFlags
{
    public static readonly Observable<bool> DebugUI = new(false);
    public static readonly Observable<bool> SlowMode = new(false);
    public static readonly Observable<bool> ForceDark = new(false);
}
```

Then build the menu. Read the flags with `ctx.UseObservable(...)` in the render
body, and pass your items to `DevtoolsMenu`:

```csharp
static class DevMenu
{
    public static Element UseTitleBar(RenderContext ctx)
    {
        // Subscribe in the render body, not inside the menu builder. The builder
        // runs only when devtools are on, so a hook call in there would be a
        // conditional hook and break hook ordering.
        //
        // Named Use* because UseObservable is a hook, and REACTOR_HOOKS_005
        // only permits hook calls from Render() or a Use*-named helper.
        var debugUI = ctx.UseObservable(AppFlags.DebugUI).Value;

        return HStack(8,
            TextBlock("My App"),
            // DevtoolsMenu renders nothing unless UseDevtools() is true,
            // so the same cost model carries over.
            DevtoolsMenu(() => new MenuFlyoutItemBase[]
            {
                ToggleMenuItem("Debug UI", debugUI,
                    v => AppFlags.DebugUI.Value = v),
                MenuSeparator(),
                MenuItem("Clear cache", () => CacheService.Clear()),
                MenuItem("Slow mode off", () => AppFlags.SlowMode.Value = false),
            })
        );
    }
}

// Stand-in for whatever your app actually caches.
static class CacheService
{
    public static void Clear() { }
}
```

The item list is a function. It runs only when devtools are on, so never call
a hook inside it. A hook there would run in some renders and not in others,
which breaks the hook order. Changing a flag re-renders every component that
reads it with `UseObservable`. See [Advanced patterns](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/advanced) for more
about observables.

After your items, the menu adds two built-in items:

| Item | What it does |
|---|---|
| Highlight reconcile changes | Toggles an overlay. After each render, controls that were mounted flash red and controls that changed flash yellow, for about 600 ms. |
| Keyed-list diagnostics | Opens a dialog that lists recent duplicate or null keys in `ListView<T>`, `GridView<T>`, `LazyVStack<T>`, and `LazyHStack<T>`. The item shows the count, or "(none)". |

The highlight overlay helps you find renders you did not expect. It does not
take input, and when it is off the reconciler collects nothing. The
[Rules of Reactor](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/rules-of-reactor) page covers the most common causes of
extra renders.

### Gate your own debug UI [#gate-your-own-debug-ui]

`UseDevtools()` returns `true` only when devtools are on for this session. Use
it to show your own debug UI:

```csharp
static class DevGate
{
    // UseDevtools() is a RenderContext extension, so it is reached from a
    // function component's ctx (or any helper you hand the ctx to) — there is
    // no Component-level forwarder. It returns true only when BOTH the
    // Reactor.DevtoolsSupport build switch and `--devtools app` (or `run`) are set.
    //
    // UseDevtools() uses no hook slot, but it is still a Use* call:
    // REACTOR_HOOKS_005 only permits Use* calls from Render() or a Use*-named
    // method, so a helper called `Shell` here would warn.
    public static Element UseShell(RenderContext ctx)
    {
        var dev = ctx.UseDevtools();

        return VStack(8,
            MainContent(),
            dev ? DebugOverlay() : Empty()
        );
    }

    private static Element MainContent() => TextBlock("App content");

    // Only *constructed* when dev is true. In retail the ternary costs one
    // bool read plus one branch — no element tree, no children reconciled.
    private static Element DebugOverlay() =>
        TextBlock("debug overlay").Opacity(0.6);
}
```

The value is fixed when the app starts. `UseDevtools()` does not use a hook
slot and never causes a render. It is still named like a hook, so call it from
`Render()` or from a helper whose name starts with `Use`. Otherwise the
`REACTOR_HOOKS_005` analyzer warns. Build the debug elements inside the
`true` branch, so a normal run doesn't create them.

## MCP server [#mcp-server]

`--devtools run` starts a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)
server inside the app. The server describes the running app, not your source
code: its windows, visual tree, hook state, screenshots, and logs. It can also
click, type, and scroll through UI Automation.

The easy way to start it is `mur devtools`. Run it from the project folder:

```
mur devtools
```

`mur devtools` finds the `.csproj` in the current folder, builds the app, and
starts it with `--devtools run`. It watches the app and starts it again after
a `reload`. Options:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `[project.csproj]` | The project to run. The default is the `.csproj` in the current folder. |
| `--component <Name>` | Open this component instead of the app's root. |
| `--mcp-port <N>` | Use a fixed port. Without it, `mur devtools` picks a free port. |
| `--print-config` | Print MCP client config for Claude Code, VS Code, and GitHub Copilot. |

Then, from a second terminal, talk to the app:

```
mur devtools session list --pretty
mur devtools tree --view summary
mur devtools screenshot --out shot.png
mur devtools click "#increment"
mur devtools state
mur devtools logs --tail 50
mur devtools shutdown
```

Each command finds the running session by itself. Run `mur devtools shutdown`
when you are done. It closes the app and frees the build output, so the next
build can write to it.

### Commands [#commands]

| Group | Commands |
|---|---|
| Look | `tree`, `screenshot`, `state`, `properties`, `styles`, `ancestors`, `resources`, `components`, `windows`, `version` |
| Act | `click`, `type`, `focus`, `invoke`, `toggle`, `select`, `scroll`, `expand`, `collapse`, `wait` |
| Change | `set-property`, `set-resource`, `fire` |
| Session | `switch`, `reload`, `windows.open`, `windows.activate`, `windows.close`, `shutdown`, `session list`, `session clean` |
| Logs and raw tools | `logs`, `call <tool> --args <json>` |

Add `--pretty` to any command for indented JSON. The exit code tells you what
happened:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | Bad arguments |
| 2 | The app could not be reached |
| 3 | Another session is already running for this project |
| 4 | No session is running |
| 5 | The tool returned an error |

### Selectors [#selectors]

Commands that act on a control take a selector:

| Selector | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| Node id | `r:main/CounterDemo.SubmitButton` | The id that `tree` returns |
| Automation id | `#increment` | `.AutomationId("increment")` |
| Name | `[name='Increment']` | The UI Automation name |
| Type path | `Button`, `Button[2]`, `StackPanel > Button` | Controls by type and position |

Give important controls an `.AutomationId(...)`. It is the most stable
selector, and it also helps [UI tests](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/testing). Node ids change after
`switch` and `reload`, so get them again with `tree`.

### Connect an MCP client [#connect-an-mcp-client]

> **Caveat:** The server listens on `127.0.0.1` only. Each launch creates a random bearer
> token and writes it, with the endpoint, to a lock file under
> `%TEMP%\reactor-devtools\`. The `mur devtools` commands read that file and
> send the token for you. The config from `mur devtools --print-config` does
> not include the token yet, so a client that uses it as-is gets
> `401 Unauthorized`.

For an MCP client that starts its own servers, launch the app with
`--devtools run --mcp-transport stdio`. The server then reads requests from
stdin and writes replies to stdout, with no port and no token.

For agents, the Reactor agent plugin includes a devtools skill that teaches
these commands. See [Build with AI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/build-with-ai).

### Logs [#logs]

In `run` mode, the app keeps the latest console output, debug output, and
trace output in memory, 4 MB by default. `mur devtools logs` reads it.
Filter with `--tail <N>`, `--filter <text>`, or
`--source stdout|stderr|debug|trace`, and add `--follow` to keep reading. To
change the buffer, start the app with `--devtools-logs-capacity <MB>`, or turn
capture off with `--devtools-logs off`. Reactor's own diagnostic events are in
the same stream; see [Diagnostics](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/diagnostics).

## Release builds and Native AOT [#release-builds-and-native-aot]

A Release build has no devtools by default. The switch is off and the trimmer
removes the devtools code. If you also reference the package only in Debug, as
shown above, it isn't in the Release build at all.

You can keep devtools in a Native AOT build for testing. The sample
[`hello-world-aot-devtools-on`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/tree/main/samples/apps/hello-world-aot-devtools-on)
shows how:

- Its project file sets the switch to `true` in every configuration and
  references the devtools project.
- Its `Program.cs` calls `ReactorDevtools.EnsureRegistered()` before
  `ReactorApp.Run`. Reactor normally loads the devtools assembly by name, and
  the AOT compiler can't see that. The direct call makes the compiler keep the
  assembly.

Under Native AOT, `properties` and `set-property` can't find dependency
properties, because their metadata is trimmed. Use a JIT build to inspect
properties. [Native AOT](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/native-aot#devtools-in-aot-builds) has the full
steps.

## Tips [#tips]

- Give the controls you want to drive an `.AutomationId(...)`. Then
  `mur devtools click "#id"` keeps working when the layout changes.
- Use `mur devtools screenshot --out shot.png` to check a layout without
  looking at the screen. It works well in scripts and for agents.
- Only one session can run for each project. If `mur devtools` exits with
  code 3, run `mur devtools shutdown` first.
- Popups are not in the `tree` output. ComboBox drop-downs, flyouts, and
  context menus live outside the window's main visual tree.
- Keep the devtools package reference in a Debug-only `ItemGroup`.

# Diagnostics
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/diagnostics

It is the debug-and-measure step of the
[Developer tools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools) loop. It is not about adding new events.

Sometimes Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) catches an exception or a failed
HRESULT and keeps going instead of throwing. In the past, the framework only
wrote a `Debug.WriteLine` message in that case. You saw it in the Visual Studio
Output window during a Debug build, but it was gone in Release, which is the
build every shipped app runs.

Spec 044 changed this. Error and HRESULT diagnostics now go through the
`Microsoft-UI-Reactor` `EventSource`. These events:

- are visible in Release builds;
- are grouped by keyword, so you turn on only the groups you need;
- allocate nothing when no listener is attached.

The devtools `logs` tool can also return these framework events, next to
stdout, stderr, and debug output. An AI agent connected to the
[devtools MCP server](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools#mcp-server) gets all of them in one call.

To add or change events, read [perf-instrumentation.md](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/perf-instrumentation)
first. It covers keywords, the `IsEnabled` gate, event IDs, and the split
between EventPipe and ETW.

![Reactor diagnostics flow — a framework catch site delegates to DiagnosticLog, which emits to ReactorEventSource for the Release path and mirrors to Debug.WriteLine in Debug builds; four consumers read the event surface: env-var / dotnet-trace capture, Visual Studio Profiler, the in-process ReactorTrace.Subscribe helper, and the reactor.logs MCP tool](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/diagnostics/flow.svg)

## The rule [#the-rule]

Audience, not severity, decides the channel. `Debug.WriteLine`
exists for the contributor working on the framework itself; the
target audience is "someone reading the Output window in Visual
Studio with their checkout open". `ReactorEventSource` exists for
the app developer, the SRE, and the support engineer; the target
audience is "someone who runs the shipped binary and needs to know
why a window failed to open".

| Audience | Channel | Visible in Release? |
|---|---|---|
| Framework contributor | `Debug.WriteLine`, `Debug.Assert` | No |
| App developer / SRE | `Microsoft-UI-Reactor` `EventSource` | Yes |
| Unreachable code | `throw new UnreachableException(...)` | Yes (as a crash) |

The two channels are complementary, not redundant. A swallowed
exception in `RenderContext` emits both — the typed event for the
app developer and a richer `Debug.WriteLine` mirror (with the
exception message) for the contributor running a Debug build. The
mirror is `[Conditional("DEBUG")]` and compiles out in Release.

> **Caveat:** Exception messages are PII-shaped and never reach the ETW payload.
> `ex.Message` can carry absolute paths, environment values, partial
> form values, and the bound user data that caused the failure. The
> typed event payload carries the exception *type* only
> (`InvalidOperationException`, `COMException`); a same-UID
> `dotnet-trace` consumer sees the type and nothing else. If you need
> the message in your own logs, attach an in-process subscriber (see
> [`ReactorTrace.Subscribe`](#in-process-subscription) below) and
> forward to a sink under your own ACL.

## What's instrumented [#whats-instrumented]

The provider's events split across a small set of keywords; spec 044
adds six subsystem keywords on top of the seven the perf-instrumentation
page documents, spec 049 added a seventh (`HotReload`), and `RenderDetail`
carries the per-component render notification. Pick the bits that match what
you're triaging:

| Keyword | Bit | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `Errors` | `0x20` | Generic `SwallowedError` / `HResultFailed` / `Warning`, plus `RenderError` and `CommitError` |
| `Hosting` | `0x80` | `WindowOpened`, `WindowClosed` (root component type and HWND, for windows opened through `ReactorApp`), `WindowDpiChanged`, `BackdropMaterializationFailed` |
| `Persistence` | `0x100` | `PersistenceRead`, `PersistenceWrite`, `PersistenceRejected` |
| `Navigation` | `0x200` | `NavigationRequested`, `NavigationCompleted`, `NavigationCancelled`, cache hit/miss/evict, transitions, deep-link |
| `Intl` | `0x400` | `IntlMissingKey` |
| `Theme` | `0x800` | `ThemeApplyFailed` |
| `Shell` | `0x1000` | `JumpList*` / `ThumbnailToolbar*` / `Tray*` (planned) |
| `HotReload` | `0x2000` | Hook-state migration across edits (spec 049) |
| `RenderDetail` | `0x4000` | `ComponentRendered` — one Verbose event per component render, with the reason |

Combine bits with bitwise-or. The most common capture-everything-
unsurprising mask is `0x1FA0` (`Errors | Hosting | Persistence |
Navigation | Intl | Theme`) — drops the verbose `State` and
`EventDispatch` keywords that produce per-state-write spam. Add
`0x2000` when you are debugging why hot reload reset a component's
state, and `0x4000` (at level `5`, Verbose) when you want one
`ComponentRendered` event per component render.

`Warning` carries a framework-authored diagnostic for a recoverable
misconfiguration the framework chose to continue past — an unresolved
`.ApplyStyle()` key, a backdrop that could not materialize. Its payload is
three strings:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `category` | Subsystem label, e.g. `Theme`, `Hosting` |
| `operation` | Stable operation identifier, e.g. `ApplyStyle` |
| `message` | Framework-authored explanation, naming the offending key or property |

The message is composed by the framework from developer-authored
identifiers, never from user data (spec 044 §6.2.1).

`RenderError` names the component whose `Render()` or effects threw. A failure
outside any component — reconciling the tree into native controls, installing
it in the host, a post-render host callback — has no owning component; when it
replaces the host's content with the error screen, Reactor raises `CommitError`
(EventId 41, `Error`) instead:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `phase` | `Reconcile` (the commit phase) or `Cleanup` (retiring a replaced root) |
| `rootComponent` | The host's root component (`FuncElement` for a root render function) |
| `exceptionType` | Exception type name only; the message is never on the payload |

### Component render notifications [#component-render-notifications]

`ComponentRendered` (EventId 40, `Verbose`, keywords `Render | RenderDetail`)
fires once each time a component's `Render()` runs — on mount, on update, and
for a host's root component, including a `Render()` that threw (whether the
framework's error fallback or an `ErrorBoundary` caught it) — and never for a
component the memo gate skipped.
It is what an inspector needs to flash the regions that just re-rendered, or to
answer *why did this render?*:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `componentName` | Component type name — `Counter`, or `ItemList<Int32>` for a generic component (`FuncElement` / `MemoElement` for function and memo components); the same name `RenderError` reports |
| `componentId` | Process-unique id of the mounted instance; stable across its re-renders |
| `reason` | `mount`, `state`, `props`, `context`, `parent`, `hotReload` or `forced` |
| `elapsedMicroseconds` | Time in `Render()` (plus the synchronous effect flush for non-root components) |

`state` means an update was requested from inside the component's subtree —
its own hook, or a descendant's: Reactor re-renders every component on the path
from the root to the one whose state changed, so ancestors report `state` too.
A host's root component reports `state` for every non-forced re-render, including
the ones the host requests itself (theme, high-contrast or animation-setting
changes).
`parent` means the parent re-rendered and nothing could skip this component (a
function component, or a propless `Component` whose `ShouldUpdate()` is true). A
function component whose consumed context changed reports `context` instead.
`hotReload` covers every re-render of a hot-reload pass, whatever else changed,
including the retry after a hook-order change. A component first created during
the pass reports `mount`.

In process, `ReactorTrace.GetComponentControl(componentId)` resolves an id to the
control whose bounds are that component's, and `ReactorTrace.TryGetComponentId(control, out id)` goes the other way,
except for a host's root: its id resolves to the root content, but that control
is often also a child component's wrapper, so the reverse lookup returns the
child's id (or nothing), never the root's. Ids
are only issued while the event is enabled, so subscribe with
`ReactorTrace.Subscribe(..., EventLevel.Verbose, (EventKeywords)0x4000)` first.
The payload carries no props, state values, keys or paths.

### Inspector diagnostics on controls [#inspector-diagnostics-on-controls]

Out-of-process inspectors (WinUI DevTools, VS Live Property Explorer) read the visual tree
through XamlDiagnostics, which cannot call into managed code. That matters most for Native
AOT apps, which have no managed agent to load. Reactor therefore publishes what it knows about each control as a string attached
property, `ReactorDiagnostics.SourceProperty` (`.ReactorSource` in XamlDiagnostics):

```
v=1|at=Pages/Main.cs:36:13|owner=Counter|element=Button|key=t1|name=incrementButton
v=1|at=App.cs:46:9|owner=App|element=Component|mounts=Counter|hooks=0:count@36;1:density@37
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `at` | DSL call site `path:line[:column]`, relative to the project directory |
| `rel` | `root` = `at` is relative to the solution root; `0` = file name only (file outside both) |
| `owner` | Component whose render produced the control (`FuncElement` / `MemoElement` for function components) |
| `element` | Element kind: `Button`, `TextBlock`, `Stack`, `Component`, … |
| `mounts` | On a component's wrapper: the component it hosts |
| `root` | On a host's root content: the host's root component |
| `key` | The element's key |
| `name` | The identifier the element was assigned to (`var title = TextBlock(…)` → `title`) |
| `hooks` | On `mounts` / `root` controls: `slot:variable@line;…` (`?` once slots are not statically known) |

Values escape `%` as `%25` and `|` as `%7C`. Readers ignore fields they do not know.

**Gating.** Publishing needs both of these:

- the `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport` build switch: on by default in Debug through `$(ReactorDiagnostics)`, and `-p:ReactorDiagnostics=true` for a Release / [Native AOT](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/native-aot) build. An explicit `ReactorDiagnostics` value wins over the default and over a `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport` item the project declares itself;
- `REACTOR_DIAGNOSTICS=1` in the environment at launch. It also turns source mapping on from startup, so elements built before the first host (a page's field initializers, say) carry their call sites.

Otherwise nothing is written, and a trimmed or AOT build without the switch does not contain the publishing code at all. Like XAML's runtime source info, paths are never absolute developer paths. See the [threat model](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/security/threat-model.md) §7.7.

**Cost.** With the switch on but `REACTOR_DIAGNOSTICS` unset (the Debug default), the cost is a
cached boolean check per control: mount, re-render, memory and first frame stay within run-to-run
noise of a build without the feature. With publishing on, every realized control carries one string
value. Measured on a Native AOT app with 50,000 controls, diagnostics mode costs about 20 B of
managed memory and 0.7 KB of native memory per control, and about 3 µs per control at mount. Values
are cached per call site, so controls without a key from the same call site share one string; a
value that is unique per control (a keyed control) costs about 0.3 KB more. An in-place re-render
whose call sites and keys did not change writes nothing. Under JIT, where a managed inspector can
read call sites from the element, each stamped control also keeps its element tag (about 0.2 KB
managed and 0.8 KB native more); Native AOT skips that tag when the call site is all it would carry,
because no managed inspector can load, and `ReactorSourceMap.GetSource` reads the published value
instead. Controls whose handler tears down child slots itself (NavigationView's pane slots, item
hosts) keep it, because unmount reaches that handler through the tag.

> **NativeAOT:** the .NET NativeAOT toolchain defaults the `EventSourceSupport`
> feature switch to `false`, which compiles the whole `EventSource` surface out.
> A NativeAOT-published app therefore emits none of these events — including
> `Warning` — until it opts back in with
> `<EventSourceSupport>true</EventSourceSupport>` in its project file. The DEBUG
> `Debug.WriteLine` mirror is unaffected.

## Capturing a trace [#capturing-a-trace]

There are four routes. Pick by where the consumer lives.

### Environment variables — zero code, file output [#environment-variables-zero-code-file-output]

For a quick local capture with no app changes, the .NET runtime can
write an EventPipe `.nettrace` file driven entirely by environment
variables. This is the right tool when an issue reproduces only in a
shipped build, on a different machine, or when you want to hand the
trace off to someone else:

```
set DOTNET_EnableEventPipe=1
set DOTNET_EventPipeOutputPath=reactor.nettrace
set DOTNET_EventPipeConfig=Microsoft-UI-Reactor:0x1FA0:5
MyApp.exe
```

The third variable is `<provider>:<keywords>:<level>`. `0x1FA0` is
the everything-unsurprising mask above; level `5` is `Verbose`. Run
the app, reproduce the issue, exit cleanly (the runtime flushes the
file on shutdown). Open the resulting `.nettrace` in Visual Studio's
Performance Profiler → Events Viewer.

### `dotnet-trace` — attach to a running process [#dotnet-trace-attach-to-a-running-process]

`dotnet-trace` is the cross-platform CLI for EventPipe capture.
Useful when the app is already running and you want to scope the
window:

```
dotnet-trace collect ^
    --process-id <pid> ^
    --providers Microsoft-UI-Reactor:0x1FA0:5 ^
    --output reactor.nettrace
```

`Ctrl+C` stops the session; the `.nettrace` lands in the working
directory. Same file format as the env-var route — same Events
Viewer workflow.

### Visual Studio Performance Profiler [#visual-studio-performance-profiler]

For a GUI workflow, the Profiler's Events Viewer accepts the same
provider:keyword:level format. Diagnostics → Performance Profiler
→ Events Viewer → Settings → Custom Provider:

```
Microsoft-UI-Reactor:0x1FA0:5
```

The timeline ties each Reactor event to the CPU sample, GC, and
network views, so you can see a `NavigationCompleted` next to the
allocation spike it caused.

### In-process subscription [#in-process-subscription]

When the consumer is the app itself — a custom log sink, a devtools
overlay, an in-app diagnostics page — `ReactorTrace.Subscribe`
returns an `IDisposable` token that fires the callback for each
event matching the filter:

```csharp
public static IDisposable Subscribe(
    Action<ReactorEvent> onEvent,
    EventLevel level = EventLevel.Verbose,
    EventKeywords keywords = (EventKeywords)(-1))
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(onEvent);
    return new Subscription(onEvent, level, keywords);
}
```

Multiple concurrent subscribers are supported; each filter is
independently active until the token is disposed. The subscriber
callback runs on the emission thread (usually the UI dispatcher when
the event originates from reconcile / render), so keep the work
minimal — the framework wraps the call in `try/catch` so a buggy
sink can't propagate to `EventSource.WriteEvent`, but the dispatcher
is still blocked for the duration. Forward to a queue if your sink
does anything expensive.

`ReactorTrace.Subscribe` is **not** a file-capture API. It exists
because in-process consumers (devtools, an `ILogger` adapter, a
custom diagnostics page) need access to the same events the env-var
route writes to disk. For a `.nettrace` file, use one of the three
routes above — they cost less and emit a richer format.

## `reactor.logs source=event` — MCP integration [#reactorlogs-sourceevent-mcp-integration]

The Reactor in-process devtools (`mur devtools`) expose a `logs` MCP
tool that drains the captured `Console.Out` / `Console.Error` /
`Debug.WriteLine` ring buffer. Spec 044 extended the tool so the
buffer also captures `Microsoft-UI-Reactor` ETW events, surfaced
under a new `source=event` filter:

```jsonc
// Request
{
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "logs",
    "arguments": { "source": "event", "tail": 20, "level": "Warning" }
  }
}

// Response — each entry now carries eventName / eventId
{
  "entries": [
    {
      "seq": 142,
      "ts": "2026-05-19T17:42:11.330Z",
      "source": "event",
      "level": "Warning",
      "text": "SwallowedError category=Hosting operation=ReactorWindow.Close exceptionType=COMException",
      "eventName": "SwallowedError",
      "eventId": 16
    }
  ],
  "nextSeq": 143,
  "dropped": 0
}
```

Existing clients that don't pass `source=event` see zero behavior
change — the `stdout` / `stderr` / `debug` filters still return their
dedicated streams. The `eventName` and `eventId` fields are present
on every entry but are `null` for non-event sources, so a client
written before spec 044 ignores them safely.

HR-style payload fields render in the same `0x{X8}` shape the
pre-migration `Debug.WriteLine` sites used (`HResultFailed
category=Shell operation=JumpList.Begin hr=0x80004002`), so log
greps that matched the old shape continue to hit.

## Patterns [#patterns]

### Reading a swallow that happened in production [#reading-a-swallow-that-happened-in-production]

A customer reports a window that won't close cleanly on a specific
machine. Capture with the env-var route, filter to the `Errors`
keyword (`0x20`) at `Warning`, and open the trace in Events Viewer.
The relevant entries will look like:

```
SwallowedError  category=Hosting  operation=ReactorWindow.Close  exceptionType=COMException
HResultFailed   category=Hosting  operation=ReactorWindow.Close  hr=0x80010108
```

The operation label is stable and developer-authored — search the
Reactor source for `"ReactorWindow.Close"` and you land on the
`DiagnosticLog.SwallowedError` call site. The exception type and HR
together pin the failure class (in this case, `RPC_E_DISCONNECTED` —
the AppWindow COM proxy was torn down before the call landed) without
ever leaking the user-visible window title.

### Wiring `ReactorTrace.Subscribe` to a per-window debug overlay [#wiring-reactortracesubscribe-to-a-per-window-debug-overlay]

A devtools overlay that wants to surface "navigation event happening
now" doesn't need a file capture — just an in-process subscription:

```csharp
public sealed class NavigationOverlay : IDisposable
{
    // ReactorEventSource is internal to Reactor, so an app names the
    // keyword by its documented bit value rather than by symbol.
    private const EventKeywords NavigationKeyword = (EventKeywords)0x200;

    private readonly IDisposable _subscription;
    private readonly Queue<string> _ring = new();

    public NavigationOverlay()
    {
        _subscription = ReactorTrace.Subscribe(
            evt =>
            {
                var line = $"{evt.EventName} {string.Join(' ',
                    Enumerable.Range(0, evt.Payload.Count)
                        .Select(i => $"{evt.PayloadNames[i]}={evt.Payload[i]}"))}";
                lock (_ring)
                {
                    _ring.Enqueue(line);
                    while (_ring.Count > 50) _ring.Dequeue();
                }
            },
            level: EventLevel.Verbose,
            keywords: NavigationKeyword);
    }

    public void Dispose() => _subscription.Dispose();
}
```

`Subscribe` already applies the keyword mask, so the callback does not
re-check `evt.Keywords`.

The callback runs on the dispatcher (most navigation events
originate there) — for a UI overlay that's actually what you want.
If the overlay forwards to a background sink instead, marshal off
the dispatcher before doing the I/O.

## Common Mistakes [#common-mistakes]

### Treating `Debug.WriteLine` as a release diagnostic [#treating-debugwriteline-as-a-release-diagnostic]

```csharp
// Don't:
try { window.AppWindow.Close(); }
catch (Exception ex)
{
    Debug.WriteLine($"Close failed: {ex}");  // disappears in Release
}
```

```csharp
private void CloseNativeWindowOnce()
{
    if (_disposed || _nativeCloseRequested) return;
    _nativeCloseRequested = true;
    try { _window.Close(); }
    catch (COMException ex) when (HResults.IsTeardownReentry(ex.HResult))
    { DiagnosticLog.SwallowedError(LogCategory.Hosting, "ReactorWindow.Close", ex); }
}
```

The first form was invisible to every shipped app. The second form
emits to `Microsoft-UI-Reactor` under `Keywords.Errors` at `Warning`
in Release (zero allocation when no consumer is attached) *and*
mirrors a richer line including `ex.Message` to `Debug.WriteLine`
in Debug builds. The narrow `catch` filter is the deliberate part:
spec 044 §6.7.2 calls for `catch (COMException ex) when (ex.HResult is
HResults.X or HResults.Y)` — never a bare `catch (COMException)`,
because the bug-class HRESULTs need to keep propagating.
`HResults.IsTeardownReentry` bundles the standard four
(`RPC_E_DISCONNECTED`, `E_HANDLE`, `RPC_E_SERVERFAULT`,
`CO_E_OBJNOTCONNECTED`); name individual constants when a call site
needs a different set.

> **Caveat:** `DiagnosticLog`, `LogCategory`, `HResults`, and `ReactorEventSource`
> are **internal to the Reactor assembly** — this pattern is the
> contract for framework code, not an API your app calls. An app that
> wants the same discipline should route its own swallows through its
> own logger; what an app consumes from Reactor is the *event stream*,
> via the four capture routes above.

### Capturing without pinning the level [#capturing-without-pinning-the-level]

```
DOTNET_EventPipeConfig=Microsoft-UI-Reactor
```

Defaults to `Verbose` plus all keywords. A typical 30-second session
on a busy app writes hundreds of megabytes — and `State` keyword
events fire once per `UseState` write, so a state-heavy screen
becomes the entire trace. Pin both:

```
DOTNET_EventPipeConfig=Microsoft-UI-Reactor:0x1FA0:5
```

`0x1FA0` is `Errors | Hosting | Persistence | Navigation | Intl |
Theme` — the everything-unsurprising mask. `:5` is `Verbose`. The
trace shrinks by an order of magnitude.

### Computing the diagnostic payload outside the IsEnabled gate [#computing-the-diagnostic-payload-outside-the-isenabled-gate]

```csharp
public static void SwallowedError(LogCategory category, string? operation, Exception? ex)
{
    // Cost-of-disabled: when no consumer enables Keywords.Errors at
    // Warning the entire branch is skipped — no enum-to-string, no
    // type-name materialization, no WriteEvent dispatch.
    if (ReactorEventSource.Log.IsEnabled(EventLevel.Warning, ReactorEventSource.Keywords.Errors))
    {
        ReactorEventSource.Log.SwallowedError(
            category.ToString(),
            operation ?? string.Empty,
            ex?.GetType().Name ?? string.Empty);
    }

    DebugSwallowedError(category, operation, ex);
}
```

`DiagnosticLog.SwallowedError` does its `category.ToString()` and
`ex.GetType().Name` work *inside* the
`ReactorEventSource.Log.IsEnabled(...)` gate, not outside. The
distinction is the entire point of the "zero-allocation when no
consumer is attached" guarantee. If a future helper materializes
the payload first and gates second, the no-allocation regression
test (`DisabledKeyword_skips_ReactorEventSource_WriteEvent_payload_marshal`)
catches it. The companion `HResultFailed` event has the same shape:

```csharp
[Event(17, Level = EventLevel.Warning, Keywords = Keywords.Errors,
    Message = "HResult failed (category={category}, op={operation}, hr=0x{hr:X8})")]
public void HResultFailed(string category, string operation, int hr)
{
    if (IsEnabled(EventLevel.Warning, Keywords.Errors))
        WriteEvent(17, category ?? string.Empty, operation ?? string.Empty, hr);
}
```

### Forwarding `ex.Message` through `ReactorTrace.Subscribe` [#forwarding-exmessage-through-reactortracesubscribe]

```csharp
// Don't — capturing the exception and forwarding its message defeats the strip:
Exception? lastEx = null;
try { /* ... */ }
catch (Exception caught)
{
    lastEx = caught;
    DiagnosticLog.SwallowedError(LogCategory.Hosting, "MyOp", caught);
}

ReactorTrace.Subscribe(evt =>
{
    // BAD: re-injects PII that the ETW payload deliberately excluded.
    _logger.Warn(evt.EventName + ": " + string.Join(",", evt.Payload) + " " + lastEx?.Message);
});
```

The framework already stripped `ex.Message` from the payload —
re-adding it from a captured local is exactly the PII leak the strip
prevented. If a sink needs the message, log it inside the `catch`
block (where the exception is in scope and the sink's ACL applies),
not at the `ReactorTrace.Subscribe` boundary.

## Tips [#tips]

**`reactor.logs source=event` is the fastest read.** Inside a
devtools session, calling the MCP tool returns the last N events
instantly without spinning up a `dotnet-trace` capture. Use the
env-var route when you need to hand a file to someone else; use the
MCP tool when you're sitting in front of the running app.

**The keyword mask is the audience pre-filter.** Subscribing on
`Keywords.Errors` alone is dramatically cheaper than `(-1)` because
the framework's hot reconcile / render paths drop their `IsEnabled`
check immediately. A long-lived broad subscription raises the cost
of every hot-path call site on the framework for as long as it
lives.

**HR fields are `0x{X8}`-rendered in `reactor.logs` text.** The MCP
tool's text rendering recognizes payload field names `hr`,
`hresult`, and `hwnd` and formats them as 8-digit uppercase hex.
This matches the pre-migration `Debug.WriteLine` shape so existing
log greps keep working.
