# Hot reload and live preview
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/hot-reload

## What survives a reload [#what-survives-a-reload]

Reactor keeps each component's `RenderContext`, and the hooks stored in it,
across a reload. Hooks are matched by call order. As long as the order of hook
calls does not change, `UseState`, `UseReducer`, `UseRef`, `UseMemo`, and
`UsePersisted` keep their values.

| Edit you make | What happens to state |
|---|---|
| Change a `Render()` body; add, remove, or reorder elements | Kept. Reactor patches the existing controls. |
| Add or remove a field on a record or class stored in a hook | Kept. Reactor copies matching fields to the new shape. A removed field is dropped. A new field gets its default value. |
| Add or remove a field on a component class | Kept. .NET gives the edited class a new type. Reactor moves the subtree to it and copies the fields that still exist. |
| Rename a component class, move it to another namespace, or change its key | Reset. Reactor treats it as a different component, so it unmounts the old one and mounts the new one with fresh state. |
| Change a stored field's type, such as `int` to `Optional<int>` | That field is not copied and gets its default value. Restart if you need the old value. |
| Add, remove, or reorder hook calls | Reset for that component. Reactor runs pending cleanups and mounts the hooks again from scratch. |

A hook-order reset cannot be avoided. When the hook order changes, the old values no
longer line up with the new hooks. Reactor resets that component instead of
showing an error, so the loop keeps running.

> **Caveat:** An effect whose dependencies did not change across a reload does not run
> again. It keeps the cleanup it captured before the reload. If an effect must
> run again on every reload, give it a dependency that changes. To keep a value
> even when the hook order changes, store it with `UsePersisted` and
> `PersistedScope.Window`, or in a static `Observable<T>` field. See
> [Persistence](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/persistence).

## Run with hot reload [#run-with-hot-reload]

Start the app with `dotnet watch` from the project folder:

```
dotnet watch run
```

`dotnet watch` builds and starts the app, then watches your `.cs` files. Your
entry point does not need anything special. It is an ordinary `ReactorApp.Run`
call:

```csharp
// Program entry point — this is the entire App.cs file:
// ReactorApp.Run<DevToolingApp>("Dev Tooling Demo");
//
// Hot reload works when the app is launched under dotnet watch. Devtools
// screenshot capture is enabled by the app project's Reactor.DevtoolsSupport
// switch and activated by launching with --devtools.
```

Here is a small app to try it with:

```csharp
class DevToolingApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (count, setCount) = UseState(0);
        var (message, setMessage) = UseState("Edit this code and save!");

        return VStack(16,
            Heading("Preview Mode Demo"),
            TextBlock(message).FontSize(16),
            HStack(8,
                Button("Click me", () => setCount(count + 1)),
                TextBlock($"Clicked {count} times").SemiBold()
            ),
            TextBox(message, setMessage, placeholderText: "Type something",
                header: "Message")
                .Width(300)
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

![A running Reactor window with the heading Preview Mode Demo, a message line, a Click me button next to a click count, and a Message text box.](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/dev-tooling/preview-app.png)

Click the button a few times. Then change the default text of `message`, or
add a new element, and save. The window updates, and the click count stays.

## The edit loop [#the-edit-loop]

1. **Start the app**

    Run `dotnet watch run` in a terminal.

2. **Edit a component**

    Change it in your editor.

3. **Save the file**

    `dotnet watch` compiles the change and applies it.

4. **See the result**

    The running window shows the new UI.

You don't start a build yourself. The app keeps running, and the window stays
where you left it.

Try it with a list. Add a few items, then change the layout code and save. The
items stay, because `UseReducer` keeps its value:

```csharp
class IterationDemo : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (items, updateItems) = UseReducer(new List<string>());
        var (input, setInput) = UseState("");

        return VStack(12,
            Heading("Iteration Cycle Demo"),
            TextBlock("Add items, then edit this code and save to see hot reload."),
            HStack(8,
                TextBox(input, setInput, placeholderText: "New item",
                    header: "New item")
                    .Width(200),
                Button("Add", () =>
                {
                    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(input))
                    {
                        updateItems(list =>
                        {
                            var next = new List<string>(list) { input };
                            return next;
                        });
                        setInput("");
                    }
                })
            ),
            ForEach(items, (item, i) => TextBlock($"  - {item}").WithKey($"{i}-{item}"))
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

![A Reactor window with the heading Iteration Cycle Demo, a short instruction, and a New item text box with an Add button.](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/dev-tooling/iteration-demo.png)

For quick experiments, skip the component class and pass a function to
`ReactorApp.Run`. Hot reload works the same way:

```csharp
// Alternative: inline function component, no class needed
// ReactorApp.Run("Quick Test", ctx =>
// {
//     var (n, setN) = ctx.UseState(0);
//     return VStack(12,
//         TextBlock($"Count: {n}").FontSize(20),
//         Button("+1", () => setN(n + 1))
//     ).Padding(24);
// });
```

See [Components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components) for function components, and the
[recipes](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes) for larger examples.

## Rude edits [#rude-edits]

Some edits cannot be applied to a running process. .NET calls them rude edits.
When `dotnet watch` sees one, it asks whether to restart the app. A restart
starts a new process, so all state is lost.

To restart without the prompt, set this environment variable before you run
`dotnet watch`:

```powershell
$env:DOTNET_WATCH_RESTART_ON_RUDE_EDIT = "1"
dotnet watch run
```

The Visual Studio extension sets this variable for you.

If a reload leaves a component in a bad state after an unusual edit, stop
`dotnet watch` and start it again. That mounts every hook from scratch.

## How Reactor applies an edit [#how-reactor-applies-an-edit]

- Reactor registers a .NET `MetadataUpdateHandler`. After the runtime applies
  an edit, the handler asks the active host to render again.
- That render skips memoization, so every component runs `Render()` with the
  new code, even if its props did not change.
- If a component's hook order changed, Reactor catches the hook-order error
  for that pass. It runs the component's cleanups, drops its hook state, and
  renders it again.

Hot reload needs the JIT. In a [Native AOT](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/native-aot) build, `MetadataUpdater.IsSupported`
is `false`, so the hot reload code is never used and the trimmer removes it.
A published app has no hot reload and no cost from it.

## Live preview in your editor [#live-preview-in-your-editor]

You can also see the running app next to your code. Both editor extensions
run the app under `dotnet watch`, so hot reload works there too.

| Editor | How the preview works |
|---|---|
| Visual Studio 2026 | The real app window is embedded in a tool window. Small edits update in place. After a rude edit, the extension shows the new process in the same place, usually within about 10 seconds. |
| VS Code | A panel shows screenshots of the running app and a component picker. Click the image to bring the real window to the front. |

See [Visual Studio and VS Code extensions](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/vs-extension) to install and use
them. The `mur` CLI has no preview command.

## Tips [#tips]

- Keep `dotnet watch` running between edits. You don't need to restart it.
- Read the terminal. If an edit does not compile, `dotnet watch` prints the
  error. Fix it and save again.
- Keep components small. A small `Render()` is quick to run again and easy to
  check.
- Keep the hook order stable while you iterate. Adding a hook resets that
  component's state.
- To change a type's shape without losing data, add a new field instead of
  changing the type of an existing one.

## Next Steps [#next-steps]

- **[Developer tools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools)**: the whole inner loop
- **[Visual Studio and VS Code extensions](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/vs-extension)**: live preview in your editor
- **[Devtools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools)**: inspect and drive the running app
- **[Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks)**: the state that hot reload keeps
- **[Persistence](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/persistence)**: keep state across reloads and restarts

# mur CLI
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/mur-cli

## Install mur [#install-mur]

`mur` is not published to NuGet.org. Get it in one of two ways.

**From a release.** Download `reactor-skill-kit-<version>.zip` from the
[GitHub releases](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/releases).
It contains the agent skills and `mur` builds for x64 and Arm64. Extract it,
then run:

```powershell
cd reactor
.\install-skill-kit.ps1
```

The script copies the kit to `~/.claude/skills/reactor` and adds the
`bin\<arch>` folder to your user `PATH`. Pass `-Path <folder>` to install
somewhere else, or `-SkipPath` to leave `PATH` alone. This `mur` needs the
.NET 10 runtime. If you don't have it, install it with
`winget install Microsoft.DotNet.Runtime.10`. Open a new terminal, then check:

```powershell
mur --version
```

**From source.** In a clone of the repository, run `./bootstrap.ps1`. It packs
the CLI into `local-nupkgs/` and installs it as a .NET global tool
(`Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Cli`). Pass `-SkipMurInstall` to pack it without
installing it. The manual steps are in
[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#manual-setup).

## Create a project [#create-a-project]

For most apps, use a project template, not `mur`:

```powershell
winapp new -t reactor -n MyApp
```

[Installation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/install) covers the templates and the `dotnet new` commands.

`mur --create <Name>` is for work inside a clone of the Reactor repository. It
writes a folder with `Program.cs`, a `.csproj`, a `.sln`, and
`Assets/AppIcon.ico`. The project references `..\src\Reactor\Reactor.csproj`,
so create it in the root of the clone. The name must start with a letter or an
underscore, and can contain letters, digits, underscores, and dots.

`mur templates status` tells you if `dotnet new reactor` works on this
machine:

| Exit code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | The Reactor templates are installed. |
| 1 | `mur` could not list the `dotnet new` templates. |
| 2 | The template pack is installed, but it has no Reactor templates. |
| 3 | The template pack is not installed. Run `winapp new` once to install it. |

## Check your code [#check-your-code]

`mur check` builds the project and prints one line for each diagnostic, with a
hint on how to fix it:

```text
mur check [<path>] [options] [-- <dotnet build arguments>]
```

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `<path>` | The project, solution, or folder to build. The default is the current folder. |
| `--strict` | Rank every warning as an error, so all warnings print. It does not change the exit code. |
| `--final` | Print every diagnostic, with nothing hidden. Use it before you merge. |
| `--quiet` | Print errors only. |
| `--suggest-threshold <N>` | Change how close a name must be to get a "did you mean" suggestion. `0` turns suggestions off. |
| `--emit-threshold <N>` | Change the score a warning needs before it prints in the default mode. |
| `--disable-rule <Id>` | Turn off one hint rule. You can repeat it. |
| `--list-rules` | List the hint rules and exit. |
| `--trace <file>` | Write a trace of what `mur check` did to a file. |

Without a mode option, `mur check` prints errors and the warnings most likely
to matter, and hides info messages. It passes `--nologo`, `-v:m`, and the
platform of your machine to `dotnet build`, unless you pass your own after
`--`. The exit code is the exit code of the build. To fail on warnings in
CI, pass `-- -p:TreatWarningsAsErrors=true`.

[Analyzers](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/analyzers#mur-check) explains how `mur check` relates to the
`REACTOR_*` analyzers. The
[rule reference](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/reference/mur-check-did-you-mean.md)
lists every hint.

## Drive a running app [#drive-a-running-app]

`mur devtools` builds your app, starts it with the devtools MCP server, and
restarts it after a reload. In a second terminal, commands such as
`mur devtools tree`, `mur devtools screenshot --out shot.png`, and
`mur devtools click "#id"` act on the running app.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `mur devtools [project.csproj]` | Build and start the app with devtools. |
| `mur devtools --component <Name>` | Open one component instead of the app's root. |
| `mur devtools --mcp-port <N>` | Use a fixed port. |
| `mur devtools --print-config` | Print MCP client config for Claude Code, VS Code, and GitHub Copilot. |
| `mur devtools session list` | List the running sessions. |
| `mur devtools session clean` | Remove lock files left by sessions that are no longer running. Add `--dry-run` to only list them. |
| `mur devtools <verb> ...` | Run one devtools command against the running app. |

[Devtools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools#mcp-server) lists every verb, the selectors, and the
exit codes.

## Localize [#localize]

The `mur loc` commands work with `.resw` resource files. Run them from the
project folder.

| Command | What it does | Main options |
|---|---|---|
| `mur loc extract` | Find text in your source code that should be localized, and write it to `.resw` files. | `--source <dir>` (default `.`), `--output <dir>` (default `Strings/en-US/`), `--rewrite` to change the source to use the new keys, `--dry-run` |
| `mur loc translate` | Translate the `.resw` files with AI. | `--target <locales>` (required, for example `fr-FR,ar-SA`), `--source <dir>` (default `Strings/en-US/`), `--missing-only`, `--model <name>` |
| `mur loc validate` | Check message syntax, and check that each translation uses the same parameters as the source. | `--resources <dir>` (default `Strings/`), `--default-locale <locale>` (default `en-US`) |
| `mur loc status` | Show how much of each locale is translated. | `--resources <dir>`, `--default-locale <locale>` |
| `mur loc prune` | Find keys that the code no longer uses, and remove them. | `--source <dir>`, `--resources <dir>` (default `Strings/en-US/`), `--dry-run` to only list them |

`mur loc translate` uses the GitHub Copilot SDK, so it needs a GitHub Copilot
subscription and a signed-in `gh` CLI. The default model is `gpt-5.4-mini`.
You can also set it with the `COPILOT_MODEL` environment variable. Each
translation is marked as an AI draft that needs review. See
[Localization](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/localization) for the full workflow.

## Help for AI agents [#help-for-ai-agents]

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `mur --skill` | Print the Reactor `SKILL.md` reference. |
| `mur --api` | Print `reactor.api.txt`, a list of every public Reactor signature. |
| `mur --regen-api` | Rebuild the API index from the source. Only works in a clone of the repository. |

If you don't have `mur`, the NuGet package also contains the API index, at
`%USERPROFILE%\.nuget\packages\microsoft.ui.reactor\<version>\agentkit\reactor.api.txt`.
[Build with AI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/build-with-ai) explains how agents use these files.

## Work on Reactor itself [#work-on-reactor-itself]

These commands are for a clone of the Reactor repository. Most of them stop
with an error when you run them anywhere else.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `mur pack-local` | Pack the framework from your working tree into `<repo>/local-nupkgs/`. Options: `--version` (default `0.0.0-local`), `--configuration` (default `Debug`). |
| `mur clean-local` | Remove the local packages, their NuGet cache entries, and old local templates. |
| `mur upgrade` | After `git pull`: pack the framework again, install the template pack if it is missing, and refresh the agent plugin and the Visual Studio extension. Options: `--skip-plugin`, `--skip-vs-extension`. |
| `mur doctor` | Check the .NET SDK, `mur`, the local packages, the template pack, and the agent plugin. Add `--verbose` for more detail. |

`mur upgrade` does not update `mur` itself, because a running program can't
replace its own file. Run `./bootstrap.ps1` again for that.

The docs build is not part of `mur`. `mur docs` prints the new command and
exits. See the
[doc pipeline guide](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/contributing/doc-pipeline.md).

## Design files [#design-files]

`mur figma watch <figma-url>` checks a Figma file for changes, every 10 seconds
by default (`--interval <seconds>`). When the file changes, it prints one line
of JSON. An agent can read that line and fetch the new design. It needs a Figma
API key. `mur` reads it from the `FIGMA_API_KEY` environment variable first.
If that is not set, it looks for an MCP server entry that sets
`FIGMA_API_KEY` in `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`, and then in
`.vscode/mcp.json`.

# Visual Studio and VS Code extensions
Source: https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/vs-extension

Each one starts the app with
`dotnet watch` and devtools turned on, so edits reach the preview as described
in [Hot reload and live preview](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/hot-reload). The Visual Studio extension
embeds the real app window. The VS Code extension shows screenshots of it.

Both extensions are experimental. The Visual Studio extension is the least
stable part of Reactor. Expect install problems, races while a solution loads,
window and DPI issues, and breaking changes. Use it to try the embedded preview
and to send feedback, not as your only way to run the app.

| | Visual Studio extension | VS Code extension |
|---|---|---|
| Editor | Visual Studio 2026 (version 18.x) | VS Code 1.85 or later |
| Preview | The real app window, embedded in a tool window. Mouse, keyboard, and focus work. | Screenshots of the app in a panel. It is not interactive. |
| Get it | `Reactor.VsExtension.vsix` from GitHub Releases, or `bootstrap.ps1` | Run it from source in `src/vscode-reactor` |
| Starts the app with | `dotnet watch run --project <csproj> -- --devtools run --embed` | `dotnet watch run --project <csproj> -- --devtools run --vscode` |
| Marketplace | Not listed | Not published |

## Visual Studio extension [#visual-studio-extension]

The extension adds a **Reactor Preview** tool window. It finds the project of
the file you are editing and starts it under `dotnet watch`. Then it places the
app's window inside the tool window. You can click, type, open popups, and
inspect the accessibility tree, because it is the real WinUI window.

### Requirements [#requirements]

- Visual Studio 2026 (version 18.x): Community, Professional, or Enterprise, on
  x64 or Arm64. Visual Studio 2022 is not supported.
- The .NET 10 SDK on `PATH`.
- Visual Studio must not run as administrator. If it does, the tool window
  shows an error and does not start the app, because Windows can drop input
  between an elevated and a non-elevated process.
- The app you preview must use Windows App SDK 1.6 or later and declare
  PerMonitorV2 DPI awareness in its project file:

  ```xml
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ApplicationHighDpiMode>PerMonitorV2</ApplicationHighDpiMode>
  </PropertyGroup>
  ```

- Windows 11 23H2 or later is recommended.

### Install [#install]

Pick one of these:

**From a release**

Download `Reactor.VsExtension.vsix` from
[GitHub Releases](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/releases),
close Visual Studio, and double-click the file. It installs for your user
account. The file may be unsigned, so Visual Studio can show a warning.

**With bootstrap.ps1**

In a source checkout, `bootstrap.ps1` builds the VSIX and installs it into the
newest Visual Studio 2026 that has the **Visual Studio extension development**
workload. If no such instance exists, it skips this step. Pass
`-SkipVsExtension` to skip it on purpose. Later, `mur upgrade` refreshes the
extension; see [mur CLI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/mur-cli).

**Build it yourself**

This also needs the **Visual Studio extension development** workload:

```powershell
# Build the VSIX
pwsh -File src\vs-reactor\Build-Vsix.ps1
# The file is src\vs-reactor\Reactor.VsExtension\bin\Debug\Reactor.VsExtension.vsix

# Or build and install it in one step (close Visual Studio first)
pwsh -File src\vs-reactor\Reinstall-Vsix.ps1
```

If the restore cannot reach nuget.org, pass `-NuGetSource <url>` or
`-NuGetConfig <path>` to either script. A plain `dotnet build` of the
extension project makes a VSIX for CI checks only. It cannot be installed.

To work on the extension itself, open `src\vs-reactor` in Visual Studio, set
`Reactor.VsExtension` as the startup project, and press F5. Visual Studio starts
a separate Experimental instance (`/RootSuffix Exp`) with the extension loaded.

### Open the preview [#open-the-preview]

1. **Load the solution**

    Open a solution that contains a Reactor app, and
    wait until it has loaded.

2. **Open a component**

    Open a `.cs` file that contains a component (a class
    that derives from `Component`).

3. **Show the tool window**

    Choose **View > Other Windows > Reactor Preview**.
    The command is also on the **Tools** menu.

If the active file belongs to a loaded project, the preview starts right away.
If not, the tool window opens empty. Open a component file, then select
**Preview Active File** on the tool window's toolbar.

### Tool window [#tool-window]

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Preview Active File** | Starts the preview for the project that contains the active file. Use it to switch to another project. |
| **Stop Preview** | Stops the app. |
| **Force Reload** (toolbar), **↻** (next to the picker) | Stops the app and starts it again. Use it when a build, a hot reload, or the start-up handshake gets stuck. |
| Component picker | Lists the components of the project. By default it follows the active editor and shows the first component in that file. When you pick a component yourself, it stays selected until you pick another one. |
| **Reactor Preview** output pane | Shows the `dotnet watch` output, the port and token handshake, and errors. Check it first when something goes wrong. |

The picker only follows files in the project that is running. A file from
another project does not switch the preview. Select **Preview Active File** to
start that project instead.

### Edits and rude edits [#edits-and-rude-edits]

- Most edits, such as changes inside `Render`, apply in place through hot
  reload. The embedded window stays where it is.
- A rude edit, such as a change to a record's shape, makes `dotnet watch`
  rebuild and start the app again. The extension finds the new process and
  embeds it in the same place, usually within about 10 seconds.
- If the `dotnet watch` process exits on its own, the extension starts it again
  once. If it exits a second time, the tool window shows **Preview crashed**.

### Packaged apps [#packaged-apps]

Packaged (MSIX) projects work without changes. Apps made from the Reactor
templates already reference `Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp`, which
provides the run support the preview needs. The extension sets
`WinAppRunUseExecutionAlias=true` for the app it starts, so the app keeps its
console output and can report its port and token. A project that you converted
to MSIX by hand must add that package first. To preview the app unpackaged,
set `<WindowsPackageType>None</WindowsPackageType>`.

### Known limits [#known-limits]

- Visual Studio and the app must use the same DPI awareness. On a mismatch, the
  extension retries once in owner mode: the app window floats above Visual
  Studio instead of inside the tool window. If that fails too, the tool window
  shows an error.
- There are no settings yet. A **Tools > Options** page is planned.
- The control reference graph is not shown in Visual Studio yet. Use the
  VS Code panel or the devtools `references` tool.

For more fixes, see the
[troubleshooting section of the extension README](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/src/vs-reactor/README.md#troubleshooting).
The design is in
[spec 056](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/specs/056-visual-studio-embedded-preview.md).

## VS Code extension [#vs-code-extension]

The VS Code extension opens a **Reactor Preview** panel beside the editor. The
app runs in its own window. The panel shows screenshots of that window and
updates them while the app runs. It is not on the Visual Studio Marketplace.

### Install from source [#install-from-source]

You need Node.js with npm, and the .NET SDK on `PATH`.

1. **Open the extension folder**

    Open the `src/vscode-reactor` folder of a
    source checkout in VS Code.

2. **Install the build dependencies**

    ```powershell
    npm install
    ```

3. **Start the extension**

    Press F5 and pick **Run Extension**. VS Code
    compiles the extension and opens a second window, the Extension
    Development Host, with the extension loaded.

4. **Open your app**

    In that window, open your Reactor app folder.

### Commands [#commands]

Run these from the Command Palette:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Reactor: Preview Component** | Starts the preview for the active C# file. It finds the nearest `.csproj` above the file and runs `dotnet watch run --project <csproj> -- --devtools run --vscode`. |
| **Reactor: Connect to Preview** | Connects the panel to an app you started yourself. It asks for the `CAPTURE_PORT` and `CAPTURE_TOKEN` values that the app prints when it runs with `--devtools run --vscode`. |
| **Reactor: Stop Preview** | Stops the app and closes the panel. |
| **Reactor: Focus Preview Window** | Brings the real app window to the front. The status bar item does the same. |

### The preview panel [#the-preview-panel]

- A component picker lists the components of the project. Pick one to switch.
  The app does not restart.
- When you switch to another C# file in the same project, the preview switches
  to the first component in that file. A file from another project starts that
  project.
- **Focus Window**, or a click on the image, brings the real window to the
  front so you can interact with it.
- **References** shows the control reference graph of the current tree, with
  cycles and unresolved references.
- The status text shows **Building...** while `dotnet watch` rebuilds and
  **Live** when frames arrive.
- The **Reactor Preview** output channel shows the app's output.

If the app uses an older Reactor package without devtools, the extension
starts it again with the old `--preview --vscode` flags.

## Tips [#tips]

- Check the **Reactor Preview** output pane or channel first. It shows the
  `dotnet watch` output and the handshake.
- Restart the preview before you assume the app is broken. The extensions are
  rougher than the framework.
- For a preview with no editor, run `mur devtools` in the project folder. See
  [Devtools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools).
- Both extensions need a debug build with devtools available. See
  [Devtools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools) to set it up.
